title.vi: M01 · Vi mạch tích hợp và mạch logic: bài tập có số của Jaeger (đáp án in sẵn)
title.en: M01 · Integrated circuits and logic circuits: Jaeger numeric exercises (printed answers)

note.vi: Mỗi phần là một khung EXERCISE của Jaeger 5e kèm ANSWERS in ngay dưới. Thời gian là giả định của site (6 phút mỗi bài); mỗi bài 1 điểm. Bài có ghi “cần hình” dùng hình vẽ trong sách ở trang đã nêu.
note.en: Each part is an EXERCISE box of Jaeger 5e with its printed ANSWERS. The time limit is this site's assumption (6 minutes per exercise); 1 mark each. Parts marked “figure needed” refer to the figure in the book at the page given.

problems.text: A certain TTL gate has the following values for its logic levels: VOH = 3.6 V, VOL = 0.4 V, VI H = 2.0 V, VI L = 0.8 V. What are the noise margins for this TTL gate?

Suppose the waveforms in Fig. 6.5 are those of an ECL gate with VL = −2.6 V and VH = −0.6 V, and t1 = 100 ns, t2 = 105 ns, t3 = 150 ns, and t4 = 153 ns. What are the values of V10%, V90%, V50%, tr, and tf ?
(a) What is the power-delay product at low power for the logic gate characterized by Fig. 6.6? (b) What is the PDP at P = 3 mW? (c) At 20 mW?
(a) Calculate the power supply current I DD if the voltage at node Y is 203 mV. (b) Repeat for 132 mV. (c) Repeat for 64.4 mV.
What is the dynamic power dissipated by alternately charging and discharging a 1-pF capacitor between 2.5 V and 0 V at a frequency of 32 MHz? At 3.2 GHz?

Suppose vI = 1 V for the CMOS inverter in Fig. 7.4. (a) What is the range of values of vO for which MN is saturated and MP is in the triode region? (b) For which values are both transistors saturated? (c) For which values is MP saturated and MN in the triode region?
The (W/L) N of MN in Fig. 7.4 is 10/1. What is the value of (W/L) P required to form a symmetrical inverter?

Equate the expressions for the drain currents of MN and MP to show that vO = vI occurs for a voltage equal to VDD/2 in a symmetrical inverter. What voltage corresponds to vO = vI in an inverter with KR = 10 and VDD = 4 V? For KR = 0.1 and VDD = 4 V?
What is the value of KR for a CMOS inverter in which (W/L) P = (W/L) N? Calculate the noise margins for this value of KR with VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, and VT P = −0.6 V.
Calculate the average propagation delay of the reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 for C = 1 pF. Repeat for C = 0.2 pF.
An inverter must drive a 5-pF load capacitance with τ p = 1 ns. Scale the reference inverter to achieve this delay.
What would be the W/L ratios in Ex. 7.1 if the threshold voltages of the transistors were +0.5 V and −0.5 V?
What are the new equations [similar to Eqs. (7.16) and (7.17)] for τ PH L and τ PLH for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, and VT P = −0.6 V?
problems.answer: τ PH L = 2.4RonnC = 1.26C/Kn; τ PLH = 2.4RonpC = 1.26C/K p

problems.text: What are the new equations [similar to Eqs. (7.16) and (7.17)] for τ PH L and τ PLH for VDD = 3.3 V, VT N = 0.75 V, and VT P = −0.75 V?
problems.answer: τ PH L = 2.4RonnC = 0.94C/Kn; τ PLH = 2.4RonpC = 0.94C/K p

problems.text: (a) What is the power-delay product for the symmetrical reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 operating from VDD = 2.5 V and driving an average load capacitance of 100 fF? (b) Repeat for a 3.3-V supply. (c) Repeat for a 1.8-V supply.

title.vi: M02 · Bộ khuếch đại thuật toán (op-amp): bài tập có số của Jaeger (đáp án in sẵn)
title.en: M02 · The operational amplifier: Jaeger numeric exercises (printed answers)

note.vi: Mỗi phần là một khung EXERCISE của Jaeger 5e kèm ANSWERS in ngay dưới. Thời gian là giả định của site (6 phút mỗi bài); mỗi bài 1 điểm. Bài có ghi “cần hình” dùng hình vẽ trong sách ở trang đã nêu.
note.en: Each part is an EXERCISE box of Jaeger 5e with its printed ANSWERS. The time limit is this site's assumption (6 minutes per exercise); 1 mark each. Parts marked “figure needed” refer to the figure in the book at the page given.

problems.text: (a) What input bias point should be chosen for the amplifier in Fig. 10.13 to provide the maximum possible linear input signal magnitude? What are the maximum input and output signal amplitudes? (b) What is the voltage gain if the amplifier input is biased at VID = −1.0 V?
Write an expression for vO(t) for the amplifier in Fig. 10.13 if vID(t) = (0.25 + 0.75 sin 1000πt) V. What dc bias appears as part of the output voltage?
Suppose an amplifier is operating with vo = +10 V. What is the input voltage vid if (a) A = 100? (b) A = 10,000? (c) A = 120 dB?
Find Av, vo, ii, and io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.19 if R1 = 68 kΩ, R2 = 360 kΩ, and vi = 0.5 V.
If VI = 2 V, R1 = 4.7 kΩ, and R2 = 24 kΩ, find I I , I2, I O, and VO in Fig. 10.19. Why is the symbol VI being used instead of vi, and so on?
problems.answer: 0.426 mA, 0.426 mA, −0.426 mA, −10.2 V; the problem is stated specifically in terms of dc values.

problems.text: We wish to convert a 25-μA sinusoidal current to a voltage with an amplitude of 5 V using a transresistance amplifier. What value of R2 is required? If ii = 50 sin 2000πt μA, what is the amplifier output voltage?
What are the voltage gain Av, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.22 if R1 = 2 kΩ, R2 = 36 kΩ, and vI = −0.2 V?
What are the voltage gain in dB and the input resistance of the amplifier shown here? If vi = 0.25 V, what are the values of vo and io? vi vo io 1 kΩ 39 kΩ 100 kΩ R3 R2 R1
Design a noninverting amplifier (choose R1 and R2 from Appendix A) to have a gain of 54 dB, and the current io ≤0.1 mA when vo = 10 V.
problems.answer: Two possibilities of many: (220 Ω and 110 kΩ) or (200 Ω and 100 kΩ)

problems.text: What are the voltage gain Av, input resistance Rin, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifiers in Ex. 10.6 if R1 = 1.5 kΩ, R2 = 30 kΩ, and vi = 0.15 V?
Add a resistor to the noninverting amplifier circuit to change its input resistance to 2 kΩ.
problems.answer: Set resistor R3 = 2 kΩ in the schematic on page 548.

problems.text: What is the summing amplifier output voltage vo in Fig. 10.24 if v1 = 2 sin 1000πt V, v2 = 4 sin 2000πt V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ, and R3 = 3 kΩ? What are the input resistances presented to sources v1 and v2? What is the current supplied by the op amp output terminal?
problems.answer: (−6 sin 1000πt −6 sin 2000πt) V; 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ; (−2 sin 1000πt −2 sin 2000πt) mA

problems.text: Suppose A = 10^5, β = 1/100, and vi = 100 mV. What are A^Ideal v , T, Av, vo, and vid for the noninverting amplifier.
problems.answer: 100, 99.9, 10.0 V, 100 μV (vid is small but nonzero)

problems.text: What value of open-loop gain is guaranteed for the OP-27 op amp over the full temperature range with a load resistance of at least 2 kΩ?

A noninverting amplifier is designed with R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 39 kΩ, and an op amp with an open-loop gain of 80 dB. What are the loop gain, closed-loop gain, ideal gain and fractional gain error of the amplifier?
What value of open-loop gain is required to achieve an output resistance of 0.1 Ω in the amplifier in Ex. 11.2.

A noninverting amplifier must have a closed-loop gain of 40 dB and an output resistance of less than 0.1 Ω. The only op amp available has an output resistance of 200 Ω. What is the minimum open-loop gain of the op amp that will meet the requirements?

Suppose a noninverting amplifier has Rid = 1 MΩ, with R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 390 kΩ, and the open-loop gain is 80 dB. What is the input resistance of the overall amplifier? What are the currents I−and I1 for a dc input voltage VI = 1 V? Is I−≪I1?
Find the input resistance Rin of an inverting amplifier that has R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, Rid = 1 MΩ, and A = 100 dB. What is the deviation of Rin from its ideal value?
problems.answer: 1001 Ω; 1 Ω out of 1000 Ω or 0.1 percent

problems.text: (a) What is the actual output voltage in the circuit in Fig. 11.31(b) if Vos = 1 mV and A = 60 dB? (b) Calculate the output voltage for the circuit in Fig. 11.31(a).
Repeat the calculation in Ex. 11.10 if the noninverting amplifier gain is set to 50 and the offset voltage is 2 mV?
An inverting amplifier is designed with R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 39 kΩ. What value of resistance should be placed in series with the noninverting input terminal for bias current compensation?
problems.answer: 975 Ω. Note that 1 kΩ is the closest 5 percent resistor value.

problems.text: An integrator has R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 pF, VOS = 1.5 mV, and I B2 = 100 nA. How long will it take vO to saturate (reach VCC or VEE) after the power supplies are turned on if VCC = VEE = 15 V?
What is the maximum guaranteed value for the output current of the OP-27A operational amplifier (see MCD website for specification sheets)?

Design a noninverting amplifier to have a gain of 20 dB and to develop a peak output voltage of at least 20 V when connected to a load resistance of at least 5 kΩ. The op amp output current specification states that the output current must be less than 5 mA. Choose acceptable values of R1 and R2 from the table of 5 percent resistor values in Appendix A.
problems.answer: Some possibilities: 27 kΩ and 3 kΩ; 270 kΩ and 30 kΩ; 180 kΩ and 20 kΩ; but not 18 kΩ and 2 kΩ because of tolerances.

problems.text: The CMRR specification of 80 dB in Example 11.12 actually corresponds to −10^4 ≤ CMRR ≤+10^4. What range of output voltages may occur?
What is the voltage gain in Ex. 11.13 if the CMRR is improved to 80 dB? If the differential-mode gain were only 60 dB?
An op amp has a gain of 100 dB at dc and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is fB? Write the transfer function for the gain of the op amp.

An op amp has a dc gain of 90 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the cutoff frequency of the op amp? If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 40 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.

An op amp has a dc gain of 90 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the cutoff frequency of the op amp? If the op amp is used to build an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 50 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the inverting amplifier.

An op amp has a dc gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 10 MHz. What is the upper-cutoff frequency of the op amp itself? If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 60 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.

Suppose that an op amp has a slew rate of 0.5 V/μs. What is the largest sinusoidal signal amplitude that can be reproduced without distortion at a frequency of 20 kHz? If the amplifier must deliver a signal with a 10-V maximum amplitude, what is the full-power bandwidth corresponding to this signal?

problems.text: What are the voltage gain Av, output voltage VO, output current I O, and the current in source V2 for the amplifier in Ex. 10.7 if V1 = 3 V and V2 = 5 V?
What are the voltage gain Av, output voltage VO and output current I O for the amplifier in Fig. 10.25 if R1 = 2 kΩ, R2 = 36 kΩ, V1 = 8 V, and V2 = 8.25 V?
What is the cutoff frequency for the low-pass circuit in Ex. 10.8 if R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, and C = 200 pF?
Find the midband gain, cutoff frequency, and bandwidth of the amplifier with this transfer function: Av(s) = 250s (s + 250π)
What is the cutoff frequency for the high-pass circuit in Ex. 10.9 if R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, and C = 0.1 μF?
Find the magnitude and phase of the voltage gain in Ex. 10.10 for ω = 1 rad/s and ω = 5 rad/s.
Find the magnitude and phase of the following transfer function for ω = 0.95, 1.0, and 1.10. Av(s) = 20 s^2 + 1 s^2 + 0.1s + 1
Find the midband gain, lowerand upper-cutoff frequencies, and bandwidth of the amplifier with the following transfer function: Av(s) = − 2 × 10^7s (s + 100)(s + 50000)
Write an expression for the phase of the transfer function above. What is the phase shift for w = 0, 100, 50000, and ∞?
Design an active low-pass filter (choose the values of R1, R2, and C) with fH = 3 kHz, Rin = 10 kΩ, and Av = 26 dB.
problems.answer: Calculated values: 10 kΩ, 200 kΩ, 265 pF; Appendix A values: 10 kΩ, 200 kΩ, 270 pF

problems.text: Design an active high-pass filter (choose the values of R1, R2, and C) with fL = 5 kHz, a high frequency gain of 20 dB, and an input resistance of 18 kΩ at high frequencies.
problems.answer: Calculated values: 18 kΩ, 180 kΩ, 1770 pF; Appendix A values: 18 kΩ, 180 kΩ, 1800 pF.

problems.text: Suppose the input voltage vi(t) to an integrator is a 500-Hz square wave with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 10 V and 0 dc value. (a) What type of waveform appears at the output of the integrator? (b) Choose the values of R and C in the integrator so that the peak output voltage will be 10 V and Rin = 10 kΩ.
What is the output voltage of the circuit in Fig. 10.35 if R = 20 kΩ, C = 0.02 μF, and vi = 2.5 sin 2000πt V?

Suppose diode D1 in Fig. 12.51 has an “on-voltage” of 0.6 V, and the op amp is operating with ±10-V power supplies. What are the voltages vO and v1 for the circuit if vI = +1 V? For vI = −1 V? What is the minimum Zener breakdown voltage for the diode?

Suppose the diodes in Fig. 12.53 have “on-voltages” of 0.6 V, and the op amp is operating with ±15-V power supplies. What are the voltages vO and v1 for the circuit if R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 68 kΩ, and vI = +2 V? For vI = −2 V? Estimate the most negative input voltage for which the circuit will operate properly. What is the minimum Zener breakdown voltage specification for the diodes assuming they are both the same?
What is the dc output voltage of the ac voltmeter circuit if R1 = 3.24 kΩ, R2 = 10.2 kΩ, R3 = 20 kΩ, R4 = 20 kΩ, and VI = 2 V?
If VCC = +10 V = −VEE, R1 = 1 kΩ, and R2 = 9.1 kΩ, what are the values of the switching thresholds for the Schmitt-trigger circuit in Figs. 12.56 through 12.61 and the magnitude of the hysteresis?
What is the frequency of oscillation of the circuit in Fig. 12.62 if VCC = +5 V, −VEE = −5 V, R1 = 6.8 kΩ, R2 = 6.8 kΩ, R = 10 kΩ, and C = 0.001 μF?

For the monostable multivibrator circuit in Fig. 12.64, VCC = +5 V = VEE, R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 18 kΩ, R = 11 kΩ, and C = 0.002 μF. What is the pulse width of the one shot? What is the minimum time between trigger pulses for this circuit?

problems.text: What are the decimal values of the following 8-bit binary fractions? (a) 0.01100001 (b) 0.10001000.
A 12-bit D/A converter has VREF = 5.12 V. What is the output voltage for a binary input code of (101010101010)? What is VLSB? What is the size of the MSB?
What are the offset voltage and step size for the nonideal converter in Fig. 12.21 if the endpoints are at 0.100 and 0.800VFS?
Suppose a 1-kΩ resistor is used for the MSB in an 8-bit converter similar to that in Fig. 12.24. What are the other resistor values?
problems.answer: 2 kΩ; 4 kΩ; 8 kΩ; 16 kΩ; 32 kΩ; 64 kΩ; 128 kΩ; 500 Ω

problems.text: A high-speed microprocessor must drive a 64-bit data bus in which each line has a capacitive load C of 50 pF, and the logic swing is 2.5 V. The bus drivers must discharge the load capacitance from 2.5 V to 0 V in 0.8 ns, as depicted in Fig. P6.31. Draw the waveform for the current in the output of the bus driver as a function of time for the indicated waveform. What is the peak current in the microprocessor chip if all 64 drivers are switching simultaneously? Bus driver and switching waveform.
answer: Current of one driver iC = C·ΔV/Δt
156.2 mA (a rectangular pulse of this height lasting 800.0 ps, zero before and after)
Peak current for all 64 drivers switching together (2.5 V in 0.8 ns)
With the values drawn in the figure (3.3 V in 1 ns)
165.0 mA per driver, 10.56 A for 64 drivers
problems.how: The load capacitance is discharged by the driver along the linear fall of the figure: iC = −C·dvO/dt = C·ΔV/Δt, constant during the fall. The 64 lines add: Ipeak = 64·C·ΔV/Δt. Numerical differentiation of the ramp and integration of the current (charge C·ΔV) confirm it.
assume: The statement says a 2.5 V swing in 0.8 ns, while the waveform of Fig. P6.31 is drawn from 3.3 V with a fall time labelled 1 ns: the statement's numbers are used and the figure's numbers are also given.
problems.circuit: Fig. P6.31 (p.349): inverter-type bus driver (supplies V+ and V−) discharging the load capacitance C (50 pF) with the current iC flowing from the capacitor into the output; below, vO(t) falls linearly from the high level to 0 V in the time marked 1 ns.

1.25 A (a rectangular pulse of this height lasting 100.0 ps, zero before and after)

With a 3.3 V swing as drawn in the figure

problems.text: A particular interconnection between two logic gates in an IC chip runs one-half the distance across a 7.5-mm-wide die. The interconnection line is insulated from the substrate by silicon dioxide. If the line is 1.5 μm wide and the oxide (εox = 3.9εo and εo = 8.85 × 10^−14 F/cm) beneath the line is 1 μm thick, what is the total capacitance of this line assuming that the capacitance is three times that predicted by the parallel plate capacitance formula? Assume that the silicon beneath the oxide represents a conducting ground plane.
problems.how: C = εox·L·W/tox with L = 3.75 mm, W = 1.5 μm, tox = 1 μm, then ×3.

problems.text: Scale the sizes of the resistors and transistors in the five inverters in Fig. 6.24 to change the power dissipation level to 2 mW.
answer: 199.7 μW (IDD = 79.86 μA, checked from the resistor design and from the switching and load devices of (b))
2 mW / 200.0 μW = 10.02 ≈ 10 (the exact factor is rounded to 10 since the reference power is 0.2 mW)
problems.how: In ratioed logic the voltage levels depend only on W/L ratios, so multiplying every W/L by k multiplies every drain current and the power by k and leaves VH and VL unchanged (Sec. 6.11.3); a resistor is divided by k. The reference gates of Fig. 6.24 dissipate 0.2 mW (checked: 2.3 V/28.8 kΩ = 79.9 μA; the switching transistor 2.22/1 and the saturated-load pair of (b) carry the same current in the square-law model), so 2 mW needs k = 10.
assume: Power is taken as the static power VDD·IDD with the output low (0.2 mW) for all five reference designs; the book says only "power dissipation level".
The load sizes in parentheses are the velocity-saturation versions printed in the figure.
problems.circuit: Fig. 6.24 (p.355): five NMOS inverter designs, VDD = 2.5 V: (a) 28.8 kΩ resistor load (L/W = 2880), MS 2.22/1; (b) saturated load ML 1/1.68 (1/1.56), MS 4.71/1; (c) linear load (gate at +4 V) ML 1/5.72 (1/3.81), MS 2.22/1; (d) depletion load ML 1.81/1, MS 2.22/1; (e) pseudo-NMOS ML 1/1.11 (1/1.28), MS 2.22/1.

problems.text: (a) Scale the transistor sizes in Fig. 6.30(b) to decrease the gate power by a factor of 8. (b) Scale the transistor sizes in Fig. 6.30(b) to increase the gate power by a factor of 3.5.
problems.how: Power scaling (Sec. 6.11.3): all W/L ratios of the gate are multiplied by the same factor, which multiplies every current and the power by that factor and leaves the logic levels unchanged: factor 1/8 for (a), 3.5 for (b).
assume: Fig. 6.30(b): depletion-load NMOS gate with ML = 1.81/1, MA = MB = 4.44/1 and MC = MD = 8.88/1 (as drawn; the figure also shows the 4.44/1 equivalents of the two blocks).
W/L ratios below 1 (e.g. 0.226/1) mean a transistor longer than wide.
problems.circuit: Fig. 6.30 (p.356): NMOS gate with a depletion-mode load ML (1.81/1) from +2.5 V to the output Y and a switching network to ground: transistor A (4.44/1) in series with B (4.44/1), with C and D (8.88/1 each, in series with each other) in parallel with A.

problems.text: Calculate the values of K ^(′) n and K ′ p for NMOS and PMOS transistors with a gate oxide thickness of 10 nm and 5 nm. Assume that μn = 500 cm^2/V · s, μp = 200 cm^2/V · s, and the relative permittivity of the gate oxide is 3.9. (ε0 = 8.854 × 10^−14 F/cm).
problems.how: K′ = μ·Cox″ with Cox″ = εox/tox, εox = 3.9·8.854×10⁻¹⁴ F/cm, 1 nm = 10⁻⁷ cm.

problems.text: (a) The n-well in a CMOS process covers an area of 1 cm × 0.5 cm, and the junction saturation current density is 500 pA/cm^2. What is the total leakage current of the reverse-biased well? (b) Suppose the drain and source regions of the NMOS and PMOS transistors are 2 μm × 5 μm, and the saturation current density of the junctions is 100 pA/cm^2. If the chip has 20 million inverters, what is the total leakage current due to the reverse-biased junctions when vO = 2.5 V? Assume VDD = 2.5 V and VSS = 0 V. (c) When vO = 0 V?
answer: (b) vO = 2.5 V: one reverse-biased junction per inverter (NMOS drain)
(c) vO = 0 V: the PMOS drain is the reverse-biased junction
problems.how: I = J·A; per inverter one 2 μm × 5 μm drain junction is reverse biased; × 20 million inverters.
assume: The n-well of part (a) is counted separately; the totals with the well are shown in brackets.

problems.text: A particular interconnection between two logic gates in an IC chip runs one-half the distance across a 10-mm-wide die. If the line is 1 μm wide and the oxide (εr = 3.9, ε0 = 8.854 × 10^−14 F/cm) beneath the line is 1 μm thick, what is the total capacitance of this line, assuming that the capacitance is three times that predicted by the parallel plate capacitance formula? Assume that the silicon beneath the oxide represents a conducting ground plane.
problems.how: C = εox·L·W/tox with L = 5 mm, W = 1 μm, tox = 1 μm, then ×3.

problems.text: The CMOS inverter in Fig. P7.5 has VDD = 2.5 V and VSS = 0 V. What are the values of VH and VL for this inverter? (b) Repeat for VDD = 1.8 V. (c) Repeat for VDD = 1 V and −VSS = −1 V.
answer: VH = VDD = 2.5 V, VL = VSS = 0 V
VH = VDD = 1.8 V, VL = VSS = 0 V
VH = VDD = 1.0 V, VL = VSS = -1.0 V
problems.how: In a static CMOS inverter one transistor is always cut off in each logic state, so the output reaches the supply rails: VH = VDD and VL = VSS (−VSS = −1 V means the lower rail is at −1 V). The numerical transfer curve (full square-law model) at the two extreme inputs confirms it.
assume: W/L ratios and thresholds do not matter for the levels.
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.5 (p.404): CMOS inverter: PMOS MP (source to VDD) above NMOS MN (source to −VSS/ground), gates tied to vI, drains tied to vO.

problems.text: The CMOS inverter in Fig. P7.5 has VDD = 3.3 V, VSS = 0 V, (W/L)N = 4/1, and (W/L)P = 10/1. What are the values of VH and VL for this inverter? (b) Repeat for (W/L)N = 6/1 and (W/L)P = 15/1.
problems.how: Static CMOS inverter: VH = VDD and VL = 0 whatever the W/L ratios (one transistor is cut off in each state and the other is in the triode region with zero current); the numerical transfer curve confirms it for these sizes.
assume: The W/L ratios are given but do not change VH and VL.
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.5 (p.404): CMOS inverter: PMOS MP (source to VDD) above NMOS MN (source to −VSS/ground), gates tied to vI, drains tied to vO.

problems.text: The CMOS inverter in Fig. P7.5 has VDD = 2.5 V, VSS = 0 V, (W/L)N = 4/1, and (W/L)P = 10/1. What are the values of VH and VL for this inverter? (b) Repeat for (W/L)N = 4/1 and (W/L)P = 4/1.
problems.how: Static CMOS inverter: VH = VDD and VL = 0 whatever the W/L ratios (one transistor is cut off in each state and the other is in the triode region with zero current); the numerical transfer curve confirms it for these sizes.
assume: The W/L ratios are given but do not change VH and VL.
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.5 (p.405): CMOS inverter: PMOS MP (source to VDD) above NMOS MN (source to −VSS/ground), gates tied to vI, drains tied to vO.

problems.text: The CMOS inverter in Fig. P7.5 has VDD = 1.8 V and VSS = 0 V. If VT N = 0.45 V and VT P = −0.45 V, what are the regions of operation of the transistors for (a) VI = VL? (b) VI = VH? (c) VI = VO = 1.65 V?
answer: NMOS (vGS = 0 V, vDS = 1.8 V): cutoff; PMOS (vSG = 1.8 V, vSD = 0 V): triode
NMOS (vGS = 1.8 V, vDS = 0 V): triode; PMOS (vSG = 0 V, vSD = 1.8 V): cutoff
NMOS (vGS = 1.65 V, vDS = 1.65 V): saturation; PMOS (vSG = 0.15 V, vSD = 0.15 V): cutoff
problems.how: A transistor is cut off if vGS ≤ VT, in the triode region if vDS < vGS − VT and saturated if vDS ≥ vGS − VT (PMOS with the source-referenced magnitudes vSG, vSD, |VTP|). In the static states one transistor is off and the other is in the triode region with vDS = 0.
assume: Point (c) is just a pair of voltages (the PMOS is cut off there, so it is not a dc operating point of the circuit).
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.5 (p.405): CMOS inverter: PMOS MP (source to VDD) above NMOS MN (source to −VSS/ground), gates tied to vI, drains tied to vO.

problems.text: The CMOS inverter in Fig. P7.5 has VDD = 2.5 V and VSS = 0 V. If VT N = 0.60 V and VT P = −0.60 V, what are the regions of operation of the transistors for (a) VI = VL? (b) VI = VH? (c) VI = VO = 1.25 V?
answer: NMOS (vGS = 0 V, vDS = 2.5 V): cutoff; PMOS (vSG = 2.5 V, vSD = 0 V): triode
NMOS (vGS = 2.5 V, vDS = 0 V): triode; PMOS (vSG = 0 V, vSD = 2.5 V): cutoff
NMOS (vGS = 1.25 V, vDS = 1.25 V): saturation; PMOS (vSG = 1.25 V, vSD = 1.25 V): saturation
problems.how: A transistor is cut off if vGS ≤ VT, in the triode region if vDS < vGS − VT and saturated if vDS ≥ vGS − VT (PMOS with the source-referenced magnitudes vSG, vSD, |VTP|). In the static states one transistor is off and the other is in the triode region with vDS = 0.
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.5 (p.405): CMOS inverter: PMOS MP (source to VDD) above NMOS MN (source to −VSS/ground), gates tied to vI, drains tied to vO.

problems.text: (a) Calculate the voltage at which vO = vI for a CMOS inverter with Kn = K p. (Hint: Always remember that iDN = iDP.) Use VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.6 V, VT P = −0.6 V. (b) What is the current IDD from the power supply for vO = VI if (W/L)N = 2/1? (c) Repeat the calculation in (a) for a CMOS inverter with Kn = 2.5K p. (d) What is the current IDD from the power supply for vO = VI if (W/L)N = 2/1?
problems.how: KR = Kn/Kp; vO = vI where both devices are saturated: vI = (VDD + VTP + VTN√KR)/(1 + √KR); IDD = (Kn/2)(vI − VTN)² with Kn = K′n·2 = 200 μA/V².
assume: K′n = 100 μA/V² (Table 7.1).

problems.text: (a) Repeat Prob. 7.10 for VDD = 3.3 V, VT N = 0.75 V, and VT P = −0.75 V. (b) Repeat Prob. 7.10 for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.60 V, and VT P = −0.50 V.
answer: (a) VDD = 3.3 V, VTN = 0.75 V, VTP = −0.75 V
(b) VDD = 2.5 V, VTN = 0.60 V, VTP = −0.50 V
problems.how: Same method as Problem 7.10.
assume: K′n = 100 μA/V².

problems.text: (a) Repeat Prob. 7.10 for VDD = 1.8 V, VT N = 0.45 V and VT P = −0.45 V. (b) Repeat Prob. 7.10 for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.75 V and VT P = −0.65 V. (c) Repeat Prob. 7.10 for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.65 V and VT P = −0.75 V.
answer: (b) VDD = 2.5 V, VTN = 0.75 V, VTP = −0.65 V
(c) VDD = 2.5 V, VTN = 0.65 V, VTP = −0.75 V
problems.how: Same method as Problem 7.10.
assume: K′n = 100 μA/V².

problems.text: (a) The CMOS gate in Fig. P7.14 is called pseudo- NMOS. Find VH and VL for this gate. (b) Repeat for VDD = 2.5 V. (c) Repeat for VDD = 1.8 V.
problems.how: Pseudo-NMOS: the PMOS gate is grounded, so it is always on. vI = 0: the NMOS is off and VH = VDD. vI = VDD: the NMOS (Kn = 5·100 μA/V²) is in the triode region and the PMOS (Kp = 40 μA/V², vSG = VDD) is in saturation: ½Kp(VDD − |VTP|)² = Kn[(VDD − VTN)VL − VL²/2], so VL = (VDD − VTN) − √[(VDD − VTN)² − Kp(VDD − |VTP|)²/Kn]. A bisection on the full piecewise model gives the same value.
assume: VTN = 0.6 V and VTP = −0.6 V, K′n = 100 and K′p = 40 μA/V² (problem-set defaults).
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.14 (p.405): pseudo-NMOS gate: PMOS MP with its gate grounded (W/L = 1/1) from VDD (= 3.3 V) to the output, NMOS MN (W/L = 5/1) with the input vI from the output to ground.

problems.text: What is the switching threshold (where does vI = vO) for a minimum size inverter in which both W/L ratios are 2/1 if VDD = 2.5 V and VT N = −VT P = 0.6 V?
problems.how: W/L = 2/1 for both: Kn/Kp = K′n/K′p = 2.5, vI = (VDD + VTP + VTN√KR)/(1 + √KR).

problems.text: What is the switching threshold (where does vI = vO) for a minimum size inverter in which both W/L ratios are 2/1 if VDD = 1.8 V and VT N = −VT P = 0.45 V?
problems.how: Same method as Problem 7.15.

problems.text: What are the noise margins of a minimum size CMOS inverter in which both W/L ratios are 2/1 and VDD = 2.5 V and VT N = −VT P = 0.6 V?
problems.how: Eqs. (7.7)–(7.12) with KR = 2.5, checked against the simulated transfer curve (slope = −1 points).

problems.text: What are the noise margins for a symmetrical CMOS inverter operating with VDD = 3.3 V and VT N = −VT P = 0.75 V? (b) Repeat for a CMOS inverter having (W/L)N = (W/L)P operating with VDD = 3.3 V and VT N = −VT P = 0.75 V.
problems.how: Eq. (7.14) for KR = 1 (checked numerically); Eqs. (7.7)–(7.12) for KR = 2.5.

problems.text: The outputs of two CMOS inverters are accidentally tied together, as shown in Fig. P7.22. What is the voltage at the common output node if the NMOS and PMOS transistors have W/L ratios of 20/1 and 40/1, respectively? What is the current in the circuit?
answer: Output voltage (both outputs tied: MP1 on, MN2 on, MN1 and MP2 off)
Current from VDD through MP1 and MN2
problems.how: Left inverter input 0 V: MP1 (40/1) on, MN1 off; right inverter input 2.5 V: MN2 (20/1) on, MP2 off. The current of MP1 equals that of MN2: Kp[(VDD − |VTP|)(VDD − vO) − (VDD − vO)²/2] = Kn[(VDD − VTN)vO − vO²/2] (both in the triode region), a quadratic in vO; the bisection on the full piecewise model gives the same value, and the current follows from either transistor.
assume: K′n = 100, K′p = 40 μA/V², VTN = 0.6 V, VTP = −0.6 V; the NMOS transistors are 20/1 and the PMOS 40/1.
problems.circuit: Fig. P7.22 (p.405): the outputs of two CMOS inverters tied together: left input 0 V (MP1, MN1), right input +2.5 V (MP2, MN2), both between +2.5 V and ground; the current I flows from MP1 through MN2.

problems.text: A CMOS inverter is to be designed to drive a single TTL inverter (which will be studied in Chapter 9). When vO = VL, the CMOS inverter must sink a current of 1.5 mA and maintain VL ≤0.6 V. When vO ≥VH, the CMOS inverter must source a current of 60 μA and maintain VH ≥2.4 V. What are the minimum W/L ratios of the NMOS and PMOS transistors required to meet these specifications? Assume VDD = 5 V.
problems.how: Output low: NMOS (vGS = 5 V) in the triode region, iD = Kn[(VDD−VTN)vDS − vDS²/2] = 1.5 mA at vDS = 0.6 V. Output high: PMOS in the triode region, iD = Kp[(VDD−|VTP|)vSD − vSD²/2] = 60 μA at vSD = 2.6 V.

problems.text: (a) What are the rise time, fall time, and average propagation delay for a symmetrical CMOS inverter with (W/L)N = 2/1, (W/L)P = 5/1, VDD = 2.5 V, and C = 0.3 pF? (b) Repeat for VDD = 2.0 V. (c) Repeat for VDD = 1.8 V.
answer: τP = 1.5 ns, tf = 3.0 ns, tr = 3.0 ns
problems.how: τPHL = 2.4·Ronn·C with Ronn = 1/[Kn(VDD − VTN)], τPLH likewise with Kp(VDD + VTP); tr = 2τPLH, tf = 2τPHL, τP = average. The book gives two estimates: Eq. (7.15)/(7.18) with 1.2·Ron·C and, after the SPICE comparison of Fig. 7.15, the revised Eq. (7.23) with 2.4·Ron·C. Both are listed.
assume: VTN = −VTP = 0.6 V for all three supplies (the statement gives no other value).

problems.text: (a) Repeat problem 7.24(a) if the inverter is asymmetrical with VT N = 0.55 V and VT P = −0.65 V. What is the switching threshold vI (where does vO = vI)? (b) Repeat for VDD = 1.8 V. (c) Repeat for VDD = 3.3 V.
answer: τP = 1.503 ns, tf = 2.88 ns, tr = 3.13 ns
problems.how: As Problem 7.24(a) with VTN = 0.55 V, VTP = −0.65 V; threshold vI = (VDD + VTP + VTN√KR)/(1 + √KR), KR = Kn/Kp = 1. The book gives two estimates: Eq. (7.15)/(7.18) with 1.2·Ron·C and, after the SPICE comparison of Fig. 7.15, the revised Eq. (7.23) with 2.4·Ron·C. Both are listed.

Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: (a) Scale the reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 to achieve a 0.3 ns delay with C = 0.5 pF. (b) What is the delay of the new inverter if C = 1.5 pF?
problems.how: Performance scaling, Eq. (7.20): τP′ = [(W/L)/(W/L)′]·(C′/Cref)·τref with the reference inverter of Fig. 7.12 ((W/L)N = 2/1, (W/L)P = 5/1, τref = 3.16 ns for 1 pF). The scaled sizes were put back into the delay equation (7.15, 1.2·Ron·C with the new Kn, Kp) and reproduce the target delay. (The book's own exercise for 5 pF and 1 ns prints 31.5/1 and 78.8/1; this method gives 31.6/1 and 78.9/1: 0.3 % rounding of τref.)
assume: The revised delay estimate (Eq. 7.23, 2.4·Ron·C) would double τref but leaves the scaling rule unchanged only if the reference delay is taken from the same equation; the book's reference value 3.16 ns/pF is used.
problems.circuit: Fig. 7.12 (p.406): reference inverter: PMOS (W/L = 5/1) above NMOS (W/L = 2/1), gates tied to vI, drains to vO with the load capacitance C; VDD = 2.5 V.

problems.text: (a) Scale the reference inverter in Fig. 7.12 to achieve a 0.4 ns delay with C = 2 pF. (b) What is the delay of the new inverter if C = 3 pF?
problems.how: Performance scaling, Eq. (7.20): τP′ = [(W/L)/(W/L)′]·(C′/Cref)·τref with the reference inverter of Fig. 7.12 ((W/L)N = 2/1, (W/L)P = 5/1, τref = 3.16 ns for 1 pF). The scaled sizes were put back into the delay equation (7.15, 1.2·Ron·C with the new Kn, Kp) and reproduce the target delay. (The book's own exercise for 5 pF and 1 ns prints 31.5/1 and 78.8/1; this method gives 31.6/1 and 78.9/1: 0.3 % rounding of τref.)
assume: The revised delay estimate (Eq. 7.23, 2.4·Ron·C) would double τref but leaves the scaling rule unchanged only if the reference delay is taken from the same equation; the book's reference value 3.16 ns/pF is used.
problems.circuit: Fig. 7.12 (p.406): reference inverter: PMOS (W/L = 5/1) above NMOS (W/L = 2/1), gates tied to vI, drains to vO with the load capacitance C; VDD = 2.5 V.

problems.text: (a) Calculate the sensitivity Kn = (Kn/τp) (dτp/dKn) of the propagation delay τp in Eq. (7.18) to changes in Kn. If the IC processing causes Kn to be 25 percent below its nominal value, what will be the percentage change in τp? (b) Calculate the sensitivity S VT N = (VT N/τp)(dτp/dVT N) of the propagation delay τp in Eq. (7.18) to changes in VT N. If the IC processing causes VT N to change from a nominal value of 0.75 V to 0.85 V, what will be the percentage change in τp?
answer: τp increases by 33.33 % exactly (25.0 % by the linearised sensitivity)
problems.how: τp ∝ 1/[Kn(VDD − VTN)] from Eq. (7.18); the sensitivity of a power law is its exponent.
assume: VDD = 2.5 V in part (b) (not given in the statement).

problems.text: Resize the transistors in Fig. 7.20 based upon the 1-V saturation velocity case in Table 7.3 to achieve the same propagation delay as the non velocity saturated case.
problems.how: Table 7.3 (symmetrical inverter of Fig. 7.12 with C = 0.2 pF) gives τP = 0.71 ns without velocity saturation and 0.89 ns with VSAT = 1 V, so every W/L must be multiplied by 0.89/0.71 to recover the same delay (and by a further factor for a shorter delay): τP is inversely proportional to W/L at fixed load (Eq. 7.20). Anchor: the book's exercise for the inverter gives 2.51/1 and 6.27/1, reproduced by 2·1.2535 and 5·1.2535.
assume: The same factor is applied to every transistor of the circuit (the relative sizes that equalise the on-resistances are kept).
Fig. 7.20 contains the reference inverter (b) and the two-input NOR gate (c); both are resized.
problems.circuit: Fig. 7.20 (p.407): reference inverter (PMOS 5/1, NMOS 2/1) and the two-input NOR gate (series PMOS 10/1, parallel NMOS 2/1), VDD = 2.5 V.

Anchor: the book's exercise for the inverter gives 2.51/1 and 6.27/1, reproduced by 2·1.2535 and 5·1.2535.

problems.text: A high-performance CMOS microprocessor design requires 500 million logic gates and will be placed in a package that can dissipate 100 W. (a) What is the average power that can be dissipated by each logic gate on the chip? (b) If a supply voltage of 1.8 V is used, what is the average current that must be supplied to the chip?
problems.how: P/N and I = P/VDD.

problems.text: A certain packaged IC chip can dissipate 5 W. Suppose we have a CMOS IC design that must fit on one chip and requires 10 million logic gates. What is the average power that can be dissipated by each logic gate on the chip? If the average gate must switch at 100 MHz, what is the maximum capacitive load on a gate for VDD = 3.3 V, 2.5 V and 1.8 V.
problems.how: P = 5 W/10⁷ gates; Eq. (7.24) P = C·VDD²·f solved for C at f = 100 MHz.

problems.text: (a) The n-well in a CMOS process covers an area of 5 mm × 10 mm, and the saturation current density of thejunctionis400pA/cm^2.Whatisthetotalleakage current of the reverse-biased well? (b) Suppose the drain and source regions of the NMOS and PMOS transistors are each 0.5 μm × 1.25 μm in size, and the saturation current density of the junction is 150 pA/cm^2. If the chip has 200 million inverters, what is the total leakage current when vO = 2.5 V? Assume VDD = 2.5 V. (b) Repeat for vO = 0 V.
answer: (b) vO = 2.5 V: reverse-biased NMOS drain junctions
(c) vO = 0 V: reverse-biased PMOS drain junctions
problems.how: I = J·A; the well is 0.5 cm × 1 cm; each drain is 0.5 μm × 1.25 μm = 6.25×10⁻⁹ cm²; × 200 million inverters.
assume: The well leakage of part (a) is not added to (b) and (c).

problems.text: A high-speed CMOS microprocessor has a 64-bit address bus and performs a memory access every 2 ns. Assume that all address bits change during every memory access and that each bus line represents a load of 25 pF. (a) How much power is being dissipated by the circuits that are driving these signals if the power supply is 2.5 V? (b) Repeat for 3.3 V.
problems.how: P = N·C·VDD²·f with f the full switching cycle rate: each line changes at every 2 ns access, so a charge-discharge cycle lasts 4 ns (f = 250 MHz).
assume: If f were taken as the access rate 500 MHz the powers double.

problems.text: An NMOS transistor is to be used as a power switch to disable one core of a multicore processor chip that operates from a 2.5 V power supply. When the core is enabled, its current is 4 A. What is the W/L ratio of the NMOS transistor if the voltage drop across the transistor must be less than 100 mV? If L = 1 μm, estimate the area of the transistor.
problems.how: Deep triode: R = 1/[Kn(VGS − VTN)] with VGS = 2.5 V.
assume: VTN = 0.6 V and K′n = 100 μA/V² (not given in the statement).

problems.text: CMOS with a PDP of 50 fJ is to be used in a chip design that requires 100 million gates. The chip will be placed in a package that can safely dissipate 40 W. What is the minimum logic gate delay that can be used in the design if all the gates operate at the same speed and 20 percent of the gates are switching at any given time?
problems.how: Each switching gate dissipates PDP/τ; 0.2 × 10⁸ gates × PDP/τ ≤ 40 W.

problems.text: (a) CMOS inverter has (W/L)N = 15/1, (W/L)P = 15/1,and VDD = 3.3V.Whatisthepeak current in the logic gate and at what input voltage does it occur? (b) Repeat for VDD = 2.5 V.
answer: peak IDD = 496.5 μA at vI = 1.414 V
peak IDD = 190.3 μA at vI = 1.104 V
problems.how: Both devices saturated at vI = switching threshold: IDD,max = (Kn/2)(vI − VTN)², Kn = 15·K′n.
assume: VTN = −VTP = 0.6 V, K′n = 100, K′p = 40 μA/V².

problems.text: (a) Repeat Prob. 7.57(a) for VDD = 1.8 V. (b) Repeat for VDD = 2.5 V, VT N = 0.55 V, and VT P = −0.65 V.
answer: peak IDD = 40.53 μA at vI = 0.8325 V
(b) VDD = 2.5 V, VTN = 0.55 V, VTP = −0.65 V
peak IDD = 190.3 μA at vI = 1.054 V
problems.how: As Problem 7.57.
assume: Part (a) keeps VT = ±0.6 V (not restated).

problems.text: (a) CMOS inverter has (W/L)N = 2/1, (W/L)P = 5/1, and VDD = 3.3 V. Assume VT N = −VT P = 0.8 V. What is the peak current in the logic gate and at what input voltage does it occur? (b) Repeat for VDD = 2.0 V with VT N = −VT P = 0.5 V.
answer: peak IDD = 72.25 μA at vI = 1.65 V
peak IDD = 25.0 μA at vI = 1.0 V
problems.how: Symmetrical inverter: Kn = Kp = 200 μA/V², vI = VDD/2.

problems.text: (a) Repeat Prob. 7.59(a) for VDD = 2.0 V, VT N = 0.45 V, and VT P −0.55 V. (b) Repeat Prob. 7.59(a) for VDD = 2.0 V, VT N = 0.55 V, and VT P = −0.45 V.
answer: peak IDD = 25.0 μA at vI = 0.95 V

problems.text: What is the power-delay product for the inverter in Prob. 7.24? How much power does the inverter dissipate if it is switching at a frequency of 100 MHz?
answer: Check with PDP = Pav·τP using τP of Problem 7.24(a)
problems.how: Eq. (7.28) is the lower bound of the PDP; the last line is the same quantity from Pav·τP (about 5 % lower because Eq. 7.28 assumes the 80 % transition-time rule).

problems.text: The values of IE E and RC in Fig. 9.6 are changed to 5 mA and 200 Ω, respectively. What are the new values of VH, VL, VREF, and ∆V ?
problems.how: Eqs. (9.12)–(9.18): the follower outputs are one VBE below the collector levels. With Q1 off the collector is at 0 V (minus R1·IEE if the common resistor R1 is present), with the current switched in it is IEE·RC lower: VH = −R1·IEE − VBE, VL = VH − IEE·RC, VREF = (VH + VL)/2. Check by KCL with βF = 40 (base currents of the followers included): ΔV = 0.9756 V and VH = -0.7005 V, i.e. the neglected iB·RC terms are below 6 %.
assume: The follower resistors R = 42 kΩ are unchanged (follower current ≈ 0.1 mA).

(IEE changed to 5 mA and RC to 200 Ω).

(IEE = 1 mA, RC = 600 Ω, follower currents I3 = I4 = 0.3 mA).

answer: VOH = -0.85 V, VOL = -1.45 V, VREF = -1.15 V (ΔV = 0.6 V unchanged)
VOH = -0.95 V, VOL = -1.55 V, VREF = -1.25 V (ΔV = 0.6 V unchanged)
Follower resistors for the same 0.1 mA currents (VEE = −5.2 V)
R ≈ (VOH + 5.2 V)/0.1 mA: 43.5 kΩ (a) and 42.5 kΩ (b) instead of 42 kΩ (optional)

(b) If IE E = 0.3 mA, R1 = 3.33 kΩ, RC = 2 kΩ, and VREF = −2 V, what are the values of VH, VL, and the logic swing ∆V ? (c) Are the input and output levels of this gate compatible with each other?
answer: VH = −IEE·R1 − VBE = -1.699 V, VL = -2.299 V, ΔV = IEE·RC = 0.6 V
(c) input levels expected with VREF = −2 V
VREF ± ΔV/2 = -1.7 V and -2.3 V; output levels -1.699 V and -2.299 V: compatible: the outputs equal the input levels
problems.how: With R1 in the common collector path the collector levels are −IEE·R1 (current switched away) and −IEE·R1 − IEE·RC; the emitter followers subtract VBE = 0.7 V. The logic levels sit symmetrically about VREF = −2 V only if VREF = (VH + VL)/2 = −2.0 V, which holds here. KCL check with βF = 40 agrees within 6 %.
assume: Part (a) is a drawing (emitter followers on both outputs, as in Fig. 9.6) and is not reproduced.
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.4 (p.506): current switch: Q1 (input vI) and Q2 (base at VREF) with RC in each collector, a common resistor R1 from ground to the two collector resistors, tail current source IEE to −VEE; emitter followers (as in Fig. 9.6) are added to the two outputs.

problems.text: Emitter followers are added to the outputs of the circuit in Fig. P9.4 in the same manner as in Fig. 9.6. (a) Draw the new circuit. (b) What are the values of RC, VH, VL, and VREF if IE E = 1.5 mA, R1 = 800 Ω, and ∆V = 0.4 V?
problems.how: ΔV = IEE·RC gives RC; VH = −IEE·R1 − VBE; VL = VH − ΔV; VREF = (VH + VL)/2. KCL check with βF = 40 agrees within 6 %.
assume: Part (a) is a drawing and is not reproduced.
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.4 (p.506): current switch: Q1 (input vI) and Q2 (base at VREF) with RC in each collector, a common resistor R1 from ground to the two collector resistors, tail current source IEE to −VEE; emitter followers (as in Fig. 9.6) are added to the two outputs.

problems.text: What is the minimum logic swing ∆V required for an ECL gate to have a noise margin of 0.1 V at room temperature?
problems.how: Solve NM = ΔV/2 − VT[1 + ln(ΔV/VT − 1)] = 0.1 V numerically (the NM grows with ΔV).
assume: Room temperature: VT = 25 mV (the value the book uses in Section 9.3).

problems.text: Suppose that an ECL gate is to be designed to operateoverthe−55^(°)Cto+75^(°)Ctemperaturerangeand must maintain a minimum noise margin of 0.1 V over that full range. What is the value of the logic swing of this ECL gate at room temperature?
answer: -55 °C: VT = 18.8 mV, ΔV needed for NM = 0.1 V
27 °C: VT = 25.86 mV, ΔV needed for NM = 0.1 V
75 °C: VT = 30.0 mV, ΔV needed for NM = 0.1 V
ΔV ≥ 0.4128 V (set by the hottest case, +75 °C)
problems.how: NM falls as VT = kT/q rises, so the +75 °C end of the range sets ΔV; the same ΔV then gives NM > 0.1 V at lower temperatures.
assume: ΔV = IEE·RC is taken as temperature independent.

problems.text: Suppose the output in Fig. P9.81 is accidentally shorted to ground. (a) Calculate the emitter current in the circuit if RS = 0 and βF = 100. (b) Repeat for RS = 130 Ω.
answer: IB = (VCC − VBE − VD1)/RC = 2.25 mA, IE = (βF + 1)·IB = 227.2 mA
βF·IB = 225.0 mA would need 29.2 V across RS, so Q4 saturates (VCE = 0.15 V): IC = (VCC − VD1 − VCEsat)/RS = 31.92 mA, IE = IC + IB = 34.17 mA (saturated)
problems.how: With the output shorted to ground the base current is set by RC alone: IB = (5 − 0.7 − 0.7)/1.6 kΩ. Without RS the transistor is forward active: IE = (βF + 1)IB. With RS = 130 Ω the collector current cannot exceed (VCC − VD − VCEsat)/RS, so the transistor saturates and the emitter current is limited to that value plus IB. KVL around the collector branch checks that VC stays above VD1 + VCEsat.
assume: VBE = VD1 = 0.7 V, VCEsat = 0.15 V (Table 9.3); the output short circuit holds vO = 0 V.
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.81 (p.511): TTL totem-pole output stage: VCC = +5 V; RC = 1.6 kΩ to the base of Q4 and RS = 130 Ω to its collector; emitter of Q4 through diode D1 to the output vO, which sinks the load current iL (here shorted to ground).

problems.text: Prior to the availability of Schottky diodes, the Baker clamp circuit in Fig. P9.99 was used to prevent saturation. What is the collector-emitter voltage of the transistor in this circuit assuming that iB > iC/βF? What are iD1, iD2, and iC if iBB = 250μA,iCC = 1mA,βF = 20,andβR = 2?
answer: vCE = vBE + vD2 − vD1 = vBE ≈ 0.7 V: the base-collector junction stays at about 0 V, so the transistor is not saturated
problems.how: Baker clamp: D2 feeds the base, D1 returns the excess base drive to the collector. KCL at the base node: iBB = iD1 + iD2; at the collector node: iC = iCC + iD1; the transistor stays at the edge of the forward-active region, iB = iD2 = iC/βF. Solving gives iD1 = (iBB − iCC/βF)/(1 + 1/βF). The loop vCE = vBE + vD2 − vD1 gives 0.7 V for identical diodes.
assume: Ideal identical diodes and forward-active operation (βR = 2 is not needed).
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.99 (p.513): Baker clamp: current source iBB into the node joined to the base through diode D2 and to the collector through diode D1; current source iCC into the collector; emitter grounded.

problems.text: What is the logic function of the gate in Fig. P9.102. Find VH, VL, and VREF for the circuit, assuming VE E = −3 V, RC = 3.3 kΩ, and RE = 2.4 kΩ. Assume VBE = 0.7 and VD = 0.4 V for the Schottky diode. –VEE
answer: Y = A + B + C (OR): Y is the collector of QR, which is off (Y = 0 V) when any input transistor is on
0 V (QR off, no current in RC)
-0.8 V: the Schottky diode clamps the collector of QR at VREF − VD (without the clamp RC would drop 2.61 V)
problems.how: The three input transistors and QR share the emitter resistor RE; with all inputs low QR conducts and the collector level would be −IE·RC (IE = (VREF − VBE + VEE)/RE), far below VREF, so the Schottky diode clamps it at VREF − VD. With VREF centred between the levels, VREF = VL/2 and VL = VREF − VD give VREF = −VD = −0.4 V and VL = −0.8 V; then IE = 0.79 mA, so the clamp is indeed active.
assume: VREF is taken centred between VH and VL as in Eq. (9.18a) (the statement does not say how VREF is chosen).
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.102 (p.513): ECL OR gate: input transistors A, B, C (collectors to ground) and the reference transistor QR (Schottky-clamped, base at VREF, collector Y through RC to ground) with emitters tied to RE and −VEE.

problems.text: Estimate iB and iC of the Schottky transistor in Fig. P9.103 if the external collector terminal is open. Assume the forward voltage of the Schottky diode is 0.45 V.
answer: VCE = VBE − VSchottky = 0.25 V > VCEsat = 0.15 V: forward active
problems.how: With the external collector open the whole collector current is supplied through the Schottky diode from the base node, so the current from the resistor splits as iin = iB + iC = (βF + 1)iB with βF = 40 (Table 9.3) and iin = (5 − 0.7)/4 kΩ.
assume: βF = 40 and VBE = 0.7 V (Table 9.3) are used; the Schottky forward voltage is 0.45 V as given.
problems.circuit: Fig. P9.103 (p.513): Schottky-clamped transistor Q1: the base is fed from +5 V through 4 kΩ, the emitter is grounded and the external collector terminal is open (i = 0).

problems.text: The power dissipation of a particular IC chip is 50 W, and the chip will contain 50 million logic gates. The gates must have an average propagation delay of 1 ns. (a) What is the power-delay product of the logic family? (b) What is the lowest PDP that can be plotted on the graph in Fig. 9.51?
answer: (b) lowest PDP on the graph (lower left corner: 0.1 mW × 0.1 ns)
the required PDP is below the lowest value that can be plotted (ratio 0.1)
problems.how: PDP = (chip power/number of gates) × delay; the corner of the graph of Fig. 9.51 (0.1 mW, 0.1 ns) gives the smallest plottable PDP, 10 fJ (axes read from the vector drawing).
assume: The graph limits (0.1 mW … 100 mW, 0.1 ns … 100 ns) are read from the axis labels of Fig. 9.51.
problems.circuit: Fig. 9.51 (p.513): power-delay graph: propagation delay 0.1–100 ns against power dissipation 0.1–100 mW (log axes) with lines of constant PDP (50 pJ, 1 pJ, 100 fJ) and points for the logic families (74LS: 2 mW, 10 ns; ECL 100K: about 40 mW, 0.7 ns); the gate on the left is the Schottky TTL gate.

problems.text: The power dissipation of a particular IC chip is limited to 100 W, and the chip will contain 250 million logic gates. The gates must have an average propagation delay of 0.25 ns. (a) What is the powerdelay product of the logic family? (b) What is the lowest PDP that can be plotted on the graph in Fig. 9.51?
answer: (b) lowest PDP on the graph (lower left corner: 0.1 mW × 0.1 ns)
the required PDP is below the lowest value that can be plotted (ratio 0.01)
problems.how: PDP = (chip power/number of gates) × delay; the corner of the graph of Fig. 9.51 (0.1 mW, 0.1 ns) gives the smallest plottable PDP, 10 fJ (axes read from the vector drawing).
assume: The graph limits (0.1 mW … 100 mW, 0.1 ns … 100 ns) are read from the axis labels of Fig. 9.51.
problems.circuit: Fig. 9.51 (p.514): power-delay graph: propagation delay 0.1–100 ns against power dissipation 0.1–100 mW (log axes) with lines of constant PDP (50 pJ, 1 pJ, 100 fJ) and points for the logic families (74LS: 2 mW, 10 ns; ECL 100K: about 40 mW, 0.7 ns); the gate on the left is the Schottky TTL gate.

problems.text: A low-power ECL gate has a 0.5-pJ PDP. (a) What will be the gate delay for a gate operating at a power level of 0.3 mW? (b) What power is required for the gate to achieve a delay of 1 ns?
problems.how: PDP = P·τ (Eq. 9.x, definition of the power-delay product).

problems.text: The 74LS gate in Fig. 9.51 is redesigned to operate at a power of 5 mW. (a) What is the gate delay of the new design? Assume a constant power-delay product. (b) What power is required to achieve a delay of 0.3 ns?
answer: PDP of the 74LS gate read from Fig. 9.51
problems.how: Constant power-delay product: τ = PDP/P. The 74LS point of Fig. 9.51 was read from the vector drawing (log interpolation between the axis labels: 1.99 mW, 10.0 ns).
assume: Reading of the graph: about 2 mW and 10 ns for 74LS (±3 %).
problems.circuit: Fig. 9.51 (p.514): power-delay graph: propagation delay 0.1–100 ns against power dissipation 0.1–100 mW (log axes) with lines of constant PDP (50 pJ, 1 pJ, 100 fJ) and points for the logic families (74LS: 2 mW, 10 ns; ECL 100K: about 40 mW, 0.7 ns); the gate on the left is the Schottky TTL gate.

problems.text: The ECL-100K gate in Fig. 9.51 is redesigned to operate at a power of 10 mW. (a) What is the gate delay of the new design? Assume a constant powerdelay product. (b) What power is required to achieve a delay of 0.2 ns?
answer: PDP of the ECL 100K gate read from Fig. 9.51
problems.how: Constant power-delay product: τ = PDP/P. The ECL 100K point of Fig. 9.51 was read from the vector drawing (39.6 mW, 0.70 ns).
assume: Reading of the graph: about 40 mW and 0.7 ns for ECL 100K (±3 %).
problems.circuit: Fig. 9.51 (p.514): power-delay graph: propagation delay 0.1–100 ns against power dissipation 0.1–100 mW (log axes) with lines of constant PDP (50 pJ, 1 pJ, 100 fJ) and points for the logic families (74LS: 2 mW, 10 ns; ECL 100K: about 40 mW, 0.7 ns); the gate on the left is the Schottky TTL gate.

problems.text: CML with a PDP of 25 fJ is to be used in a chip design that requires 50,000 gates. The chip will be placed in a package that can safely dissipate 20 W. What is the minimum logic gate delay that can be used in the design if all the gates operate at the same speed?
problems.how: All gates dissipate the same power: P = 20 W/50,000, τ = PDP/P.

title.vi: M02 · Bộ khuếch đại thuật toán (op-amp): problem Jaeger không có đáp án in (site tự giải và kiểm) · phần 1/4
title.en: M02 · The operational amplifier: Jaeger problems without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site) · part 1 of 4

note.vi: Sách không in đáp án các problem này. Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. Bài có hình trong sách thì hình được cắt từ PDF và đặt dưới đề, kèm mô tả mạch bằng lời. Thời gian là giả định (8 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: The circuit inside the box in Fig. P10.27 contains only resistors and diodes. The terminal VO is connected to some point in the circuit inside the box. (a) Is the largest possible value of VO most nearly 0 V, −9 V, +6 V, or +15 V? Why? (b) Is the smallest possible value of VO most nearly 0 V, −9 V, +6 V, or +15 V? Why?
problems.how: A network of resistors and diodes contains no source: every node voltage is a weighted average of the voltages of the nodes it is connected to (a diode can only lower it), so no node can lie above the highest supply (+15 V) or below the lowest (−9 V). VO can come close to +15 V (tied to that terminal through a small resistance and a conducting diode) and to −9 V, but not to +6 V or 0 V as extremes: those are intermediate values.
assume: Random resistor–diode networks fed from +15 V, −9 V and 0 V were solved (300 networks, ideal 0.6 V diodes): all node voltages stayed between -9.00 V and 15.00 V, inside the limits.
The “most nearly” answers are the limits; the exact extremes also lose a diode drop.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.27 (p.578): a box containing only resistors and diodes with the terminals +15 V, −9 V, ground and the output vO.

problems.text: (a) The input voltage applied to the amplifier in Fig. P10.28 is vI = VB + VM sin 1000t. What is the voltage gain of the amplifier for small values of VM if VB = 0.6 V? What is the maximum value of VM that can be used and still have an undistorted sinusoidal signal at vO? (b) Write expressions for vI(t) and νO(t).
answer: 0.1 V (the segment is straight between vI = 0.5 V and 0.7 V)
vO(t) = 8 − 40·VM sin 1000t V (for VM = 0.1 V: 8 − 4 sin 1000t V)
problems.how: The amplifier is linear only where the transfer curve is straight: around vI = 0.6 V the curve falls from (0.5 V, 12 V) to (0.7 V, 4 V), a slope of −40; the bias point is vO = 8 V, so vO = 8 − 40(vI − 0.6).
assume: The vertices (0.3, 14), (0.5, 12), (0.7, 4), (0.9, 2) were read from the figure.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.28 (p.579): transfer characteristic vO (0 to 14 V) versus vI (0 to 1.2 V) of an amplifier: 14 V up to 0.3 V, then a straight fall through (0.5 V, 12 V) and (0.7 V, 4 V) to 2 V at 0.9 V, then flat.

problems.text: The input signal to an audio amplifier is described by vI = (0.5 + 0.25 sin 1200πt) V, and the output is described by vO = (2 + 4 sin 1200πt + 0.8 sin 2400πt + 0.4 sin 3600πt) V. What is the voltage gain of the amplifier? What order harmonics are present in the signal? What is the total harmonic distortion in the output signal?
answer: 2nd (1200 Hz) and 3rd (1800 Hz) harmonics; fundamental 600 Hz
problems.how: Gain = amplitude of the 600 Hz output component / input amplitude (the dc terms are not part of the gain). THD checked with an FFT of the waveform.

problems.text: The input signal to an audio amplifier is a 1-kHz sine wave with an amplitude of 4 mV, and the output is described by vO = (5 sin 2000πt + 0.5 sin 6000πt +0.20 sin 10,000πt) V. What is the voltage gain of the amplifier? What order harmonics are present in the signal? What is the total harmonic distortion in the output signal?
answer: 3rd (3 kHz) and 5th (5 kHz); only odd harmonics
problems.how: Gain = 5 V/4 mV at 1 kHz; THD = √(0.5² + 0.2²)/5 checked with an FFT.

problems.text: Suppose the VTC for an amplifier is described by vO = 10 tanh (2vI) volts. (a) Plot the VTC. (b) Calculate the distortion based upon the first three frequency components in the output if vI = 0.75 sin 2000πt volts. 10.7 The Differential Amplifier Model
answer: Distortion from the first three components
12.09 % (the VTC is odd, so the 2nd harmonic is zero)
problems.how: Fourier components of 10·tanh(1.5·sin ωt) found with an FFT and by direct integration; THD = √(V2² + V3²)/V1. The plot of part (a) is not reproduced.

problems.text: A differential amplifier connected in the circuit in Fig. P10.38 has the parameters listed below with RI = 5 kΩ and RL = 600 Ω. (a) Find the overall voltage gain Av, current gain Ai, and power gain AP for the amplifier, and express the results in dB. (b) What is the amplitude VI of the sinusoidal input signal needed to develop a 20-V peak-to-peak signal at vo? vid Rid
answer: (b) amplitude of vi for 20 V p-p at vo
problems.how: Voltage divider RI–Rid at the input, the gain A = 60 dB = 1000, and the divider Ro–RL at the output: Av = [Rid/(Rid + RI)]·A·[RL/(RL + Ro)]; ii = vi/(RI + Rid), io = vo/RL; AP = Po/Pi = Av·Ai.
assume: AP is taken as Av·Ai (source voltage and source current), the textbook definition of power gain from vi and ii.
RI = 5 kΩ and RL = 600 Ω are given in the statement; Rid = 1 MΩ, Ro = 25 Ω and A = 60 dB are the parameters listed under it.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.38 (p.579): an amplifier model: signal source vi in series with RI drives the amplifier input resistance Rid (voltage vid across it); the output is a dependent source A·vid in series with Ro driving the load RL (Rid = 1 MΩ, Ro = 25 Ω, A = 60 dB; RI = 5 kΩ, RL = 600 Ω).

problems.text: Suppose that the amplifier in Fig. P10.38 has been designed to match the source and load resistances in Prob. 10.38 with the parameters below. (a) What is the amplitude of the input signal vi needed to develop a 15-V peak-to-peak signal at vo? (b) How much power is dissipated in the amplifier when 0.5 W is delivered to the load resistor?
answer: (a) amplitude of vi for 15 V p-p at vo
(b) io, vo for 0.5 W in RL
(b) power dissipated in the amplifier model
in Ro: 0.8333 W; in Rid: 427.0 μW; total ≈ 0.8338 W (the dependent source delivers 1.333 W)
problems.how: Av = [Rid/(Rid + RI)]·A·[RL/(RL + Ro)] with RI = 5 kΩ, RL = 600 Ω (Problem 10.38); for 0.5 W in RL the load current is √(PL/RL) and the amplifier dissipates io²·Ro in its output resistance plus vid²/Rid in its input resistance.
assume: The statement says the amplifier is “designed to match” the source and load of Problem 10.38, but its listed Ro = 1 kΩ is not 600 Ω: the load RL = 600 Ω is kept.
Powers are for sinusoidal peak amplitudes: the 0.5 W is taken as the power in RL with io, vo as the rms-equivalent quantities (the ratios do not change).
“Power dissipated in the amplifier” is read as the loss in the model resistances Ro and Rid; the dependent source supplies it.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.38 (p.580): an amplifier model: signal source vi in series with RI drives the amplifier input resistance Rid (voltage vid across it); the output is a dependent source A·vid in series with Ro driving the load RL (Rid = 5 kΩ, Ro = 1 kΩ, A = 30 dB).

problems.text: An amplifier has a sinusoidal output signal and is delivering 100 W to a 50-Ω load resistor. What output resistance is required if the amplifier is to dissipate no more than 2 W in its own output resistance?
problems.how: The same current flows in RL and Rout: P ∝ R, so Rout/RL ≤ 2 W/100 W.

problems.text: The input to an amplifier comes from a transducer that can be represented by a 1-mV voltage source in series with a 50-kΩ resistor. What input resistance is required of the amplifier for vid ≥0.99 mV?
problems.how: vid = 1 mV·Rin/(Rin + 50 kΩ) ≥ 0.99 mV.

problems.text: Suppose a differential amplifier has A = 120 dB, and it is operating in a circuit with an open-circuit output voltage vo = 15 V. What is the input voltage vid? How large must the voltage gain be for vid ≤1 μV? What is the input current i+ if Rid = 1 MΩ?
problems.how: vid = vo/A; A = 120 dB = 10⁶.

problems.text: An almost ideal op amp has an open-circuit output voltage vo = 10 V and a gain A = 106 dB. What is the input voltage vid? How large must the voltage gain be to make vid ≤1 μV?
problems.how: vid = vo/A with A = 10^(106/20).

problems.text: What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance of the amplifier in Fig. P10.44 if R1 = 12 kΩ and R2 = 120 kΩ? (b) Repeat for R1 = 160 kΩ and R2 = 330 kΩ? (c) Repeat for R1 = 4.3 kΩ and R2 = 270 kΩ?
answer: Av = -10.0 (20.0 dB), Rin = 12.0 kΩ, Rout = 0 (ideal op amp)
Av = -2.062 (6.288 dB), Rin = 160.0 kΩ, Rout = 0 (ideal op amp)
Av = -62.79 (35.96 dB), Rin = 4.3 kΩ, Rout = 0 (ideal op amp)
problems.how: Figure P10.44 is the inverting amplifier: Av = −R2/R1, Rin = R1, Rout = 0 for the ideal op amp.
assume: Figure P10.44 read from the book page: inverting amplifier.

problems.text: (a) What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance of the amplifier in Fig. P10.44 if R1 = 4.7 kΩ and R2 = 220 kΩ? Express the voltage gain in dB. (b) Repeat for R1 = 47 kΩ and R2 = 2.2 MΩ.
answer: Av = -46.81 (33.41 dB), Rin = 4.7 kΩ, Rout = 0 (ideal op amp)
Av = -46.81 (33.41 dB), Rin = 47.0 kΩ, Rout = 0 (ideal op amp)
problems.how: As Problem 10.44: both circuits have the same gain, 10× different input resistance.
assume: Figure P10.44 read from the book page: inverting amplifier.

problems.text: Write an expression for the output voltage vo(t) of the circuit in Fig. P10.44 if R1 = 750 Ω, R2 = 9.1 kΩ, and vi(t) = (0.05 sin 4638t) V. Write an expression for the current ii(t).
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier: v− = 0, so ii = vi/R1 and vo = −R2·ii.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.44 (p.580): inverting amplifier: vI (source with the resistor R1) → R1 → the − input, feedback resistor R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded; the currents iI and io are marked.

problems.text: R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 220 kΩ in the amplifier circuit in Fig. P10.44. (a) What is the output voltage if vi = 0? (b) What is the output voltage if a dc signal VI = 0.22 V is applied to the circuit? (c) What is the output voltage if an ac signal vI = 0.15 sin 2500 πt V is applied to the circuit? (d) What is the output voltage if the input signal is vI = 0.22 −0.15 sin 2500 πt V? (e) What is the input current iI for parts (b), (c), and (d). (f) What is the op amp output current iO for the input signals in parts (b), (c), and (d)? (g) What is the voltage at the inverting input of the op amp for the input signal in part (d)?
answer: (f) op-amp output current iO = vO/R2 (into R2)
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier with gain −R2/R1 = −10: vO = −10·vI, iI = vI/R1, iO = vO/R2 (the only load of the output is R2), v− = v+ = 0.
assume: No power-supply limits are given, so no clipping is applied.
iO is the current leaving the op-amp output towards R2 (arrow direction of the figure); iO = iI by KCL at the summing node.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.44 (p.580): inverting amplifier: vI (source with the resistor R1) → R1 → the − input, feedback resistor R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded; the currents iI and io are marked.

problems.text: The amplifier in Fig. P10.44 has R1 = 7.5 kΩ, R2 = 150 kΩ and operates from ±12-V power supplies. (a) If vI = −0.2 + Vi sin 2000πt volts, write an expression for the output voltage. (b) What is the maximum value of Vi for an undistorted output? (c) Repeat if vI = 0.6+Vi sin 2000πt volts.
answer: vO = −12 − 20·Vi sin 2000πt V: the dc output is already at the −12 V limit, so any Vi > 0 clips the negative peaks: largest undistorted Vi = 0
problems.how: Gain −R2/R1 = −20; the output may swing only between the supplies (±12 V).
assume: The output is assumed to reach the supply voltages exactly.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.44 (p.580): inverting amplifier: vI (source with the resistor R1) → R1 → the − input, feedback resistor R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded; the currents iI and io are marked.

problems.text: The amplifier in Fig. P10.44 has R1 = 8.2 kΩ, R2 = 160 kΩ and operates from ±12-V power supplies. (a) What is the voltage gain Av = vo/vi of the circuit? (b) Suppose input source vi is not ideal but actually has a 1.5 kΩ source resistance. What is the voltage gain Av = vo/vi?
answer: (b) with a 1.5 kΩ source resistance in series with the source
problems.how: The source resistance adds to R1 because the − input is a virtual ground: the input resistance of the stage is R1, so Av = −R2/(R1 + Rs).
assume: Av = vo/vi with vi the open-circuit source voltage.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.44 (p.581): inverting amplifier: vI (source with the resistor R1) → R1 → the − input, feedback resistor R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded; the currents iI and io are marked.

problems.text: The amplifier in Fig. P10.44 has R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ and operates from ±10-V power supplies. (a) If vI = 0.5+Vi sin 5000πt volts, write an expression for the output voltage. (b) What is the maximum value of Vi for an undistorted output? (c) Repeat if vI = −0.25 + Vi sin 2000πt volts.

problems.text: (a) The amplifier in Prob. 10.45(a) utilizes resistors with 5 percent tolerances. What are the nominal and worst-case values of the voltage gain and input resistance? (b) Repeat for Prob. 10.44(b). (c) Repeat for Prob. 10.44(c).
answer: nominal |Av| = 46.81 (33.41 dB); worst case 42.35 to 51.74 (32.54 to 34.28 dB); Rin nominal 4.7 kΩ, worst case 4.465 kΩ to 4.935 kΩ
nominal |Av| = 2.062 (6.288 dB); worst case 1.866 to 2.28 (5.419 to 7.157 dB); Rin nominal 160.0 kΩ, worst case 152.0 kΩ to 168.0 kΩ
nominal |Av| = 62.79 (35.96 dB); worst case 56.81 to 69.4 (35.09 to 36.83 dB); Rin nominal 4.3 kΩ, worst case 4.085 kΩ to 4.515 kΩ
problems.how: |Av| = R2/R1: the largest gain has R2 +5 % and R1 −5 %, the smallest the reverse; Rin = R1 ± 5 %.
assume: Same circuit as Problem 10.44 (Figure P10.44).

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier with an input resistance of 15 kΩ and a gain of 28 dB. Choose values from the 1-percent resistor table in Appendix A.
problems.how: |Av| = R2/R1 with Rin = R1; R2 taken from the nearest value of the E96 table.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier with an input resistance of 2 kΩ and a gain of 40 dB. Choose values from the 1-percent resistor table in Appendix A.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier with an input resistance of 100 kΩ and a gain of 13 dB. Choose values from the 1-percent resistor table in Appendix A.

problems.text: The current generated by some transducer falls in the range of ±2.5 μA, and its source resistance is 100 kΩ. A transresistance amplifier is needed to convert the current to a voltage between ±5 V. What value of R is required?
problems.how: Transresistance amplifier (virtual ground): vO = −iS·R, so R = 5 V/2.5 μA; the 100 kΩ source resistance does not matter.

problems.text: What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance of the amplifier in Fig. P10.60 if R1 = 8.2 kΩ and R2 = 750 kΩ? Express the voltage gain in dB.
problems.how: Ideal noninverting amplifier (Jaeger Eq. 10.53 and the examples of §10.9).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.60 (p.581): noninverting amplifier: vi drives the + input, R2 from the output to the − input and R1 from the − input to ground; the input current ii and the output current io are marked.

problems.text: Write an expression for the output voltage vo(t) of the circuit in Fig. P10.60 if R1 = 910 Ω, R2 = 8.2 kΩ, and vi(t) = (0.04 sin 9125t) V.
problems.how: Ideal noninverting amplifier.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.60 (p.581): noninverting amplifier: vi drives the + input, R2 from the output to the − input and R1 from the − input to ground; the input current ii and the output current io are marked.

problems.text: What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance of the amplifier in Fig. P10.60 if R1 = 30 kΩ and R2 = 120 kΩ? (b) Repeat for R1 = 18 kΩ and R2 = 300 kΩ. (c) Repeat for R1 = 3.3 kΩ and R2 = 390 kΩ.
problems.how: Av = 1 + R2/R1, infinite input resistance and zero output resistance for the ideal op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.60 (p.581): noninverting amplifier: vi drives the + input, R2 from the output to the − input and R1 from the − input to ground; the input current ii and the output current io are marked.

problems.text: R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 360 kΩ in the amplifier circuit in Fig. P10.60. (a) What is the output voltage if vI = 0? (b) What is the output voltage if a dc signal VI = 0.33 V is applied to the circuit? (c) What is the output voltage if an ac signal vi = 0.18 sin 3250 πt V is applied to the circuit? (d) What is the output voltage if the input signal is vI = 0.33 −0.18 sin 3250πt V? (e) Write an expression for the input currentiI for parts (b), (c), and (d). (f) Write an expression for the op amp output current iO for the input signals in parts (b), (c) and (d). (g) What is the voltage at the inverting input of the op amp for the input signal in part (d)?
answer: 0 for all three (ideal op amp, infinite input resistance)
(f) op-amp output current iO = vO/(R1 + R2)
problems.how: Ideal noninverting amplifier: vO = (1 + R2/R1)·vI = 17.36·vI; the only load of the output is R2 + R1 to ground.
assume: No supply limits are given, so no clipping is applied.

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier with a gain of 23 dB. Choose values from the 1 percent resistor table in Appendix A, and use values that are no smaller than 2 kΩ.
problems.how: Av = 1 + R2/R1; R2 from the E96 table.
assume: R1 = 10 kΩ chosen; other pairs also work.

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier with an input resistance of 100 kΩ and a gain of 6 dB. Choose values from the 1-percent resistor table in Appendix A, and use values that are no smaller than 2 kΩ.
answer: R3 = 100 kΩ from the + input to ground
problems.how: The ideal noninverting amplifier has infinite input resistance, so the 100 kΩ is set by a resistor R3 to ground at the input; Av = 1 + R2/R1.
assume: R1 = 10 kΩ chosen.

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier with a gain of 46 dB. Choose values from the 1-percent resistor table in Appendix A, and use values that are no smaller than 1 kΩ.
problems.how: Av = 1 + R2/R1; R2 from the E96 table.

problems.text: Write an expression for the output voltage vo(t) of the circuit in Fig. P10.69 if R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ, R3 = 47 kΩ, v2(t) = (0.01 sin 3770t) V, and v1(t) = (0.04 sin 10000t)V.Writeanexpressionfor the voltage appearing at the summing junction (v−).
problems.how: Ideal summing amplifier: v− = 0, the currents v1/R1 and v2/R2 add and flow through R3.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.69 (p.582): inverting summing amplifier: v1 through R1 and v2 through R2 to the − input v−, R3 from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: The summing amplifier can be used as a digitally controlled volume control using the circuit in Fig. P10.70. The individual bits of the 4-bit binary input word (b1b2b3b4) are used to control the position of the switches with the resistor connected to 0 V if bi = 0 and connected to the input signal vI if bi = 1. (a) What is the output voltage vO with the data input 0110 if vI = 2 sin 4000πt V? (b) Suppose the input changes to 1011. What will be the new output voltage? (c) Make a table giving the output voltages for all 16 possible input combinations.
answer: (c) all 16 codes: vO amplitude (V) = −(n/16)·2 V, n = 8b1 + 4b2 + 2b3 + b4
problems.how: Each switch connects its resistor to vI (bi = 1) or to 0 V (bi = 0); the summing amplifier with feedback resistor R gives vO = −(b1·R/2R + b2·R/4R + b3·R/8R + b4·R/16R)·vI = −(n/16)·vI.
assume: b1 is the bit of the 2R resistor (the most significant) and b4 the bit of the 16R resistor, as drawn.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.70 (p.582): summing amplifier with feedback resistor R and four input resistors 2R, 4R, 8R, 16R, each switched by a bit b1…b4 either to 0 V (bi = 0) or to the input vI (bi = 1).

problems.text: (a) What is the gain of the circuit in Fig. P10.72 if Av = vo/(v1 −v2) and R = 10 kΩ? (b) What is the input resistance presented to v2? (c) What is the input resistance at terminal v1? (d) What is the output voltage if v1 = 3 V and v2 = 1.5 cos 8300πt V? (e) What is the output voltage if v1 = [3 − 1.5 cos 8300πt] V and v2 = 1.5 sin 8300πt V?
answer: R = 10.0 kΩ (for v2 = 0; in general i1 depends on v2 also)
problems.how: Difference amplifier with R1 = R3 = R and R2 = R4 = 10R: vO = −(R2/R1)(v1 − v2) = −10(v1 − v2) (Jaeger Eq. 10.64); Rin2 = R + 10R and Rin1 = R for v2 = 0.
assume: Av is defined as vo/(v1 − v2), so it is negative for this connection (v1 on the inverting side).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback from the output to the − input; v2 through R to the + input with 10R from the + input to ground.

problems.text: (a) What are the voltages at all the nodes in the difference amplifier in Fig. P10.72 if V2 = 3.2 V, V1 = 3.1 V, and R = 100 kΩ? (b) What is amplifier output current IO? (c) What are the currents entering the circuit from v1 and v2?
answer: (b) output current IO (into the 10R feedback resistor, leaving the output)
(c) currents entering from v1 and v2
problems.how: Ideal op amp: v+ = v2·10R/(11R) = v−; vO = −10(V1 − V2); currents from Ohm's law.
assume: IO is the current delivered by the op-amp output through the feedback resistor (no other load).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier with R = 100 kΩ: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback, v2 through R to the + input with 10R to ground.

problems.text: Find vO, i1 and i2 for the difference amplifier in Fig. P10.72 if v2 = 2 sin 1000πt V, v1 = (2 sin 1000πt + 2 sin 2000πt) V, and R = 15 kΩ.
answer: vO = −20 sin 2000πt V (the common-mode term 2 sin 1000πt cancels)
problems.how: Ideal difference amplifier with R = 15 kΩ and 10R: v1 − v2 = 2 sin 2000πt, so vO = −10(v1 − v2); v+ = v− = (10/11)v2 gives the input currents.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier with R = 15 kΩ: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback, v2 through R to the + input with 10R to ground; i1 and i2 are the currents drawn from the sources.

problems.text: Calculate the worst-case output voltage for the circuit in Fig. P11.63 if VOS = 2 mV, IB1 = 100 nA, and IB2 = 95 nA. What is the ideal output voltage? What is the total error in this circuit? Is there a better choice for the value of R1? If so, what is the value?
answer: |VO| = 37.0 mV (VOS = ±2 mV, IB1 = 100 nA at the + input, IB2 = 95 nA at the − input); the two polarities give -37.0 mV and 7.0 mV
R1 = R2·R3/(R2 + R3) = 90.91 kΩ makes the dc drops of the two bias currents cancel; the worst-case error then is only the offset-voltage term and the offset current: 27.0 mV (instead of 37.0 mV)
problems.how: With no input, VO = (1 + R2/R3)(VOS − IB1·R1) + R2·IB2 (superposition of offset voltage and bias currents; Jaeger Eq. 11.101); choosing R1 = R2‖R3 cancels the bias-current drops except for the offset current.
assume: IB1 enters the + input and IB2 the − input; the worst-case polarity of VOS is the one that adds to the bias-current term.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.63 (p.677): noninverting-type amplifier with no signal: R1 = 100 kΩ from the + input to ground, R3 = 100 kΩ from the − input to ground, feedback resistor R2 = 1 MΩ from the output to the − input.
