problems.text: The amplifier in Fig. P11.67 is to be designed to have a gain of 46 dB. What values of R1 and R2 should be used in order to meet the gain specification and minimize the effects of bias current errors?
answer: bias-current compensation: R1‖R2 = 10 kΩ (the resistance seen by the + input)
nearest standard values R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 2.0 MΩ
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier gain 1 + R2/R1; the input-bias currents cause equal dc drops (and cancel) when the resistance at the − input, R1‖R2, equals the resistance 10 kΩ at the + input.
assume: Both conditions determine R1 and R2 exactly; standard values give 46.06 dB.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.67 (p.677): noninverting amplifier: the source vi in series with a 10 kΩ resistor drives the + input; R2 from the output to the − input and R1 from the − input to ground.

problems.text: The op amp in the circuit of Fig. P11.68 has an open-loop gain of 10,000, an offset voltage of 1 mV, and an input-bias current of 100 nA. (a) What is the output voltage for an ideal op amp? (b) What is the actual output voltage for the worst-case polarity of offset voltage? (c) What is the percentage error in the output voltage compared to the ideal output voltage? 0.005 V 100 k Ω
answer: (b) actual output voltage for the worst-case polarity of VOS (also with the finite gain A = 10,000 and IB = 100 nA)
-0.36349 V (the other polarity gives -0.54563 V; finite gain alone: -0.45536 V)
(c) percentage error compared with the ideal output
problems.how: Superposition: the signal gain (1 + R2/R1) with the finite-gain correction 1/(1 + 1/T), plus the offset term (1 + R2/R1)·VOS and the bias-current term (IB·(R2 − (1 + R2/R1)·Rs)).
assume: The 0.005 V source is drawn with its − terminal at the 1 kΩ resistor (+ at ground), so vi = −5 mV at the + input; the error percentages are the same for +5 mV.
The input-bias currents of both inputs are taken equal (100 nA) as no offset current is given.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.68 (p.677): noninverting amplifier: a 0.005 V source (− terminal towards the amplifier) in series with 1 kΩ drives the + input; 100 kΩ from the output to the − input and 1.1 kΩ from the − input to ground.

problems.text: The output-voltage range of the op amp in Fig. P11.69 is equal to the power supply voltages. What are the values of VO and V−for the amplifier if the dc input VI is (a) −1 V and (b) +2 V?
answer: VO = -10.0 V, V− = 0.4615 V (the ideal -13.6 V is beyond the supply: the output saturates at -10.0 V and V− = (VI·R2 + VO·R1)/(R1 + R2))
problems.how: Inverting amplifier with gain −R2/R1 = −6.8 and ±10 V supplies: if the ideal output is inside the supplies V− = 0; otherwise the output is clamped at the supply and V− follows from the divider of VI and VO (the op amp is no longer in feedback).
assume: The output saturates at exactly the supply voltage.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.69 (p.678): inverting amplifier: VI through 1 kΩ to the − input (V−), 6.8 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded; supplies +10 V and −10 V.

problems.text: The 6.8-kΩ resistor in Fig. P11.69 is replaced by a 10-kΩ resistor. What are the values of Vo and V−if the dc input VI is (a) 0.5 V and (b) 1.2 V?
answer: VO = -10.0 V, V− = 0.1818 V (ideal -12.0 V: saturated at -10.0 V)
problems.how: As Problem 11.69 with the feedback resistor 10 kΩ: gain −10.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.69 (p.678): inverting amplifier: VI through 1 kΩ to the − input, the feedback resistor (10 kΩ here instead of 6.8 kΩ) from the output to the − input, + input grounded; supplies ±10 V.

problems.text: What are the voltages VO and VI D in the op amp circuit in Fig. P11.73 for dc input voltages of (a) VI = 300 mV and (b) VI = 600 mV if the output-voltage range of the op amp is limited to the power supply voltages.
answer: VO = 12.0 V, VID = VI − V− = 12.0 pV
VO = 15.0 V, VID = VI − V− = 225.0 mV
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier of gain 1 + 39 = 40 with ±15 V supplies: for VI = 0.3 V the output is 12 V and VID ≈ 0; for 0.6 V the ideal 24 V is beyond +15 V, the op amp saturates and VID = VI − VO·R1/(R1 + R2) ≠ 0.
assume: The output saturates at exactly the supply voltage; VID is the voltage between the inputs (V+ = VI).
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.73 (p.678): noninverting amplifier: VI on the + input, 39 kΩ from the output to the − input and 1 kΩ from the − input to ground; supplies +15 V and −15 V.

problems.text: Repeat Prob. 11.73 if the 1-kΩ resistor in Fig. P11.73 is replaced by a 910-Ω resistor.
answer: VO = 13.16 V, VID = VI − V− = 13.16 pV
VO = 15.0 V, VID = VI − V− = 258.0 mV
problems.how: As Problem 11.73 with the 1 kΩ resistor replaced by 910 Ω: gain 1 + 39/0.91 = 43.86.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.73 (p.678): noninverting amplifier: VI on the + input, 39 kΩ from the output to the − input and 910 Ω (instead of 1 kΩ) from the − input to ground; supplies ±15 V.

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier with Av = 46 dB that can deliver a ±10-V signal to a 10-kΩ load resistor. Your op amp can supply only 1.5 mA of output current. Use standard resistor 5 percent values in your design. What is the gain of your design?
answer: R1 = 110 Ω, R2 = 22 kΩ → gain 201.0 (46.06 dB); output current at ±10 V = 1.452 mA ≤ 1.5 mA
problems.how: The op amp must supply the load current plus the current in R1 + R2: 10 V/10 kΩ + 10 V/(R1 + R2) ≤ 1.5 mA.
assume: R1 = 100 Ω would need R1 + R2 ≈ 19.95 kΩ, just under the limit, so 110 Ω is used.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier with Av = 43 dB that can deliver ±15 V to a 5-kΩ load resistor. Your op amp can supply only 4 mA of output current. Use standard resistor 5 percent values in your design. What is the gain of your design?
answer: R1 = 110 Ω, R2 = 16 kΩ → gain -145.5 (43.25 dB); output current = 3.938 mA ≤ 4 mA
problems.how: Inverting: the feedback current is vo/R2 (virtual ground): 15/5k + 15/R2 ≤ 4 mA → R2 ≥ 15 kΩ; R1 ≈ R2/141.
assume: 110 Ω and 16 kΩ are 5 % values; the ideal ratio 141 would be 15 kΩ/106 Ω.

problems.text: What is the minimum value of R in the circuit in Fig. P11.78 if the maximum op amp output current is 5 mA and the current gain of the transistor is βF ≥60?
answer: 10 V (the op amp makes the emitter follow its + input)
maximum emitter current for IB ≤ 5 mA
problems.how: The op amp forces the emitter (the − input) to 10 V, so IE = 10 V/R; the op amp supplies only the base current IB = IE/(βF + 1) ≤ 5 mA, i.e. IE ≤ 61 × 5 mA.
assume: VBE is inside the loop and does not matter; βF = 60 is the minimum value.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.78 (p.678): an op amp whose + input is at +10 V and whose output drives the base of an npn transistor with collector at +25 V; the emitter is fed back to the − input and goes through R to ground.

problems.text: (a) Design a single-stage inverting amplifier with a gain of 46 dB using an operational amplifier. The input resistance should be as low as possible while achieving the op amp output drive capability mentioned here. The amplifier must be able to produce the signal vo = (10 sin 1000t) V at its output when an external load resistance RL ≥5 kΩ is connected to the output of the amplifier. You have an operational amplifier available whose output is guaranteed to deliver ±10 V into a 4-kΩ load resistance. Otherwise, the amplifier is ideal. (b) If the amplifier input signal is vi = V sin 1000t, what is the largest acceptable value for the input signal amplitude V ? (c) What is the input resistance of your amplifier?
answer: (a) R2 (the feedback current must fit in the remaining 0.5 mA)
problems.how: Output guaranteed ±10 V into 4 kΩ → 2.5 mA; the 5 kΩ load takes 2 mA, so 10 V/R2 ≤ 0.5 mA → R2 ≥ 20 kΩ; Rin = R1 = R2/|Av|.

problems.text: The resistors the difference amplifier Fig. P11.80 are slightly mismatched due to their tolerances. (a) What are the differential-mode and common-mode input voltages if v1 = 3 V and v2 = 3 V? (b) What is the output voltage? (c) What would be the output voltage if the resistor pairs were matched? (d) What is the CMRR?
answer: vid = v1 − v2 = 0 V; vic = (v1 + v2)/2 = 3 V
vo = 107.1 mV (= Acm·3 V with Acm = 0.035711)
problems.how: vo = Ad·vid + Acm·vic with Acm = [R4/(R3 + R4)](1 + R2/R1) − R2/R1 (R1 = 10.1 k, R2 = 99 k, R3 = 9.9 k, R4 = 101 k) and Ad from the exact nodal solution; a matched amplifier would have Acm = 0.
assume: The op amp is ideal; the mismatch alone produces the common-mode gain.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.80 (p.679): difference amplifier with slightly mismatched resistors: v1 through 10.1 kΩ to the − input and 99 kΩ feedback; v2 through 9.9 kΩ to the + input and 101 kΩ from the + input to ground; ideal op amp.

problems.text: The resistors the difference amplifier Fig. P11.80 are slightly mismatched due to their tolerances. (a) What is the amplifier output voltage if v1 = 3.90 V and v2 = 4.10 V? (b) What would be the output voltage if the resistor pairs were matched? (c) What is the error in amplifying (v1 −v2)?
problems.how: Exact nodal solution of the mismatched difference amplifier for v1 = 3.90 V and v2 = 4.10 V; the matched amplifier gives −10(v1 − v2) = 2 V.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.80 (p.679): difference amplifier with slightly mismatched resistors: v1 through 10.1 kΩ to the − input and 99 kΩ feedback; v2 through 9.9 kΩ to the + input and 101 kΩ from the + input to ground; ideal op amp.

problems.text: The op amp in the amplifier circuit in Fig. P11.80 is ideal and v1 = (10 sin 120πt + 0.25 sin 5000πt) V v2 = (10 sin 120πt −0.25 sin 5000πt) V (a) What are the differential-mode and commonmode input voltages to this amplifier? (b) What are the differential-mode and common-mode gains of this amplifier? (c) What is the common-mode rejection ratio of this amplifier? (d) Find vo.
answer: vid = v1 − v2 = 0.5 sin 5000πt V; vic = (v1 + v2)/2 = 10 sin 120πt V
vo = Ad·vid + Acm·vic = -4.91 sin 5000πt + 0.3571 sin 120πt V
problems.how: Superposition of the differential part (gain Ad) and the common-mode part (gain Acm), both from the exact nodal solution of the mismatched resistors of Fig. P11.80 (ideal op amp).
assume: The signs follow the connection of Fig. P11.80 (Ad ≈ −10).
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.80 (p.679): difference amplifier with slightly mismatched resistors: v1 through 10.1 kΩ to the − input and 99 kΩ feedback; v2 through 9.9 kΩ to the + input and 101 kΩ from the + input to ground; ideal op amp.

problems.text: The multimeter in Fig. P11.83 has a common-mode rejection specification of 86 dB. What possible range of voltages can be indicated by the meter?
answer: error of the reading, VCM/CMRR (CMRR = 86 dB = 19,953)
problems.how: A meter with finite CMRR indicates vd ± vcm/CMRR: the 5 V common-mode level produces an error of about 0.25 mV on the 10 mV reading (2.5 %).
assume: The sign of the error is unknown, so the reading can be anywhere in ± the error.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.83 (p.679): an analog dc multimeter: its + terminal is connected to the top of a 0.01 V source in series with a 5 V source, and its − terminal to the node between the two sources (so the meter should read 0.01 V with a 5 V common-mode level).

problems.text: (a) We would like to measure the voltage (V = V1 −V2) appearing across the 20-kΩ resistor in Fig. P11.84 with a voltmeter. What is the value of V ? What is the common-mode voltage associated with V (VC M = (V1 + V2)/2)? What CMRR is required of the voltmeter if we are to measure V with an error of less than 0.01 percent? (b) Repeat if the 10-kΩ resistor is changed to 100 Ω.
problems.how: Series divider: I = 15 V/(15 k + Rm + 15 k); the meter measures V = V1 − V2 = Rm·I with the common-mode level VCM = (V1 + V2)/2; an error below 0.01 % of V needs CMRR > VCM/(10⁻⁴·V).
assume: The statement says “the 20-kΩ resistor” but the figure and part (b) show a 10 kΩ resistor between V1 and V2: the figure value is used.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.84 (p.679): a 15 V source in series with 15 kΩ, then 10 kΩ, then 15 kΩ back to the source (ground at the bottom); V1 is the node between the first 15 kΩ and the 10 kΩ, V2 the node between the 10 kΩ and the last 15 kΩ; the voltmeter reads V = V1 − V2 across the 10 kΩ.

problems.text: The common-mode rejection ratio of the difference amplifier in Fig. P11.85 is most often limited by the mismatch in the resistor pairs and not by the CMRR of the amplifier itself. Suppose that the nominal value of R is 10 kΩ and its tolerance is 0.025 percent. What is the worst-case value of the CMRR in dB?
problems.how: Difference amplifier: vo = −(R2/R1)v1 + (R4/(R3 + R4))(1 + R2/R1)v2, so Adm = ½[(R4/(R3 + R4))(1 + R2/R1) + R2/R1] and Acm = (R4/(R3 + R4))(1 + R2/R1) − R2/R1. With all four resistors R(1 ± 0.025 %) the worst CMRR = |Adm/Acm| occurs at a corner of the tolerance box (16 corners checked, 3000 random sets are never worse); the closed forms were checked against the exact nodal solution.
assume: Only the resistor mismatch is considered (the op amp is ideal); the result is the CMRR of the amplifier, not of the op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.85 (p.679): difference amplifier with four equal resistors R: v1 through R to the − input, R from the output to the − input; v2 through R to the + input, R from the + input to ground.

problems.text: (a) A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 2 MHz. What is the open-loop bandwidth of the op amp? (b) A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a bandwidth of 20 Hz. What is the unity-gain frequency of the op amp? (c) A single-pole op amp has unity-gain-bandwidth product of 30 MHz and a bandwidth of 200 Hz. What is the open-loop gain of the op amp?
problems.how: fT = A0·BW (gain-bandwidth product); 100 dB = 10⁵.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 92 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 1 MHz. What is the open-loop bandwidth of the op amp? (a) The op amp is used in a noninverting amplifier designed to have an ideal gain of 32 dB. What is the bandwidth of the noninverting amplifier? (b) Repeat for an inverting amplifier with and ideal gain of 32 dB.
problems.how: Single-pole op amp: closed-loop BW = fT·β with β = 1/Av (noninverting) or 1/(1 + |Av|) (inverting).

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the open-loop bandwidth of the op amp? (a) The op amp is used in a voltage follower. What is the amplifier’s bandwidth? (b) Repeat for a unity-gain inverting amplifier.
problems.how: β = 1 for the follower, β = 1/2 for the unity-gain inverter.

problems.text: Repeat problem 11.89 if fT = 10 MHz.
problems.how: As Problem 11.89 with fT = 10 MHz.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 94 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 4 MHz. A noninverting amplifier is needed with bandwidth of at least 20 kHz. (a) What is the maximum closed loop-gain that a noninverting amplifier can have and still meet the frequency response specification? (b) What is the maximum closed loop-gain that an inverting amplifier can have and still meet the frequency response specification?
problems.how: BW = fT/Av (noninverting), fT/(1 + |Av|) (inverting) ≥ 20 kHz with fT = 4 MHz. The open-loop gain (94 dB) only fixes the open-loop bandwidth, 80 Hz.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 86 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz. What is the open-loop bandwidth of the op amp? (a) The op amp is used in a noninverting amplifier with a gain of 3. What is the amplifier’s bandwidth? (b) Repeat for an inverting amplifier with a gain of 3. Using Feedback to Control Frequency Response
problems.how: BW = fT/Av and fT/(1 + |Av|).

problems.text: The voltage gain of an amplifier is described by (a) What are the mid-band gain and upperand lower-cutoff frequencies of this amplifier? (b) If this amplifier is used in a feedback amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 100, what are the upperand lower-cutoff frequencies of the closed-loop amplifier? (c) Repeat for a closed-loop gain of 40.
answer: T0 = Aβ = 100.0; closed-loop mid-band gain 99.01; fL = 9.901 Hz (≈ fL/(1 + T0) = 9.901 Hz), fH = 101.0 MHz (≈ fH(1 + T0) = 101.0 MHz)
T0 = Aβ = 250.0; closed-loop mid-band gain 39.84; fL = 3.984 Hz (≈ fL/(1 + T0) = 3.984 Hz), fH = 251.0 MHz (≈ fH(1 + T0) = 251.0 MHz)
problems.how: A(s) = 2π×10¹⁰ s/[(s + 2000π)(s + 2π×10⁶)]: band-pass with mid-band gain 10⁴. Feedback with β = 1/Acl multiplies the upper cutoff by (1 + Aβ) and divides the lower cutoff by it; exact −3 dB points were found numerically from Acl = A/(1 + βA) and agree within 2 %.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 86 dB, a unity-gain frequency of 5 MHz, and an output resistance of 250 Ω. The op amp is used in an inverting amplifier with an ideal gain of 20. (a) Find an expression for the output impedance of the amplifier. (b) Sketch a Bode plot for the output impedance as a function of frequency.
answer: zero at 250.6 Hz, pole at 238.3 kHz
flat at 262.8 mΩ up to 250.6 Hz, rises 20 dB/decade (inductive) to Ro = 250 Ω at 238.3 kHz, then flat
problems.how: Zout = Ro/(1 + T(s)) with T(s) = A(s)β, A(s) = A0/(1 + s/ωH), β = R1/(R1 + R2) = 1/21 for the inverting gain 20, ωH = ωT/A0.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 86 dB, a unity-gain frequency of 2.5 MHz, and an input resistance of 100 kΩ. The op amp is used in a noninverting amplifier with an ideal gain of 20. (a) Find an expression for the input impedance of the amplifier. (b) Sketch a Bode plot for the input impedance as a function of frequency.
answer: Rid(1 + T0 + s/ωH)/(1 + s/ωH) with Rid = 100 kΩ, T0 = 997.6, ωH = 787.3 rad/s (125.3 Hz)
pole at 125.3 Hz, zero at 125.1 kHz
flat at 99.86 MΩ up to 125.3 Hz, falls 20 dB/decade (capacitive) to Rid = 100 kΩ at 125.1 kHz, then flat
problems.how: Zin = Rid(1 + T(s)), T(s) = A(s)β with β = 1/20 for the noninverting gain 20, ωH = ωT/A0.

problems.text: A single-pole op amp has an open-loop gain of 97 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 2 MHz. Find an expression for the transfer function of the lowpass filter in Fig. 10.32 if R1 = 5.1 kΩ, R2 = 51 kΩ, and C = 1600 pF. Make a Bode plot comparing the ideal and the actual transfer functions.
answer: Ao = 70795.0 (97 dB), fT = 2.0 MHz, pole fb = fT/Ao = 28.25 Hz

The Bode plot itself is not drawn here: the poles, zeros and gains above define it.
assume: The "Bode plot" part of the statement is not reproduced; the transfer function and its poles/zeros are given instead.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.32 (p.681): inverting low-pass filter: input resistor R1 to the − input, R2 in parallel with C in the feedback path, + input grounded.

problems.text: The summing amplifier can be used as a digitally controlled volume control using the circuit in Fig. P10.70. The individual bits of the 4-bit binary input word (b1b2b3b4) are used to control the position of the switches with the resistor connected to 0 V if bi = 0 and connected to the input signal vI if bi = 1. (a) What is the output voltage vO with the data input 0110 if vI = 2 sin 4000πt V? (b) Suppose the input changes to 1011. What will be the new output voltage? (c) Make a table giving the output voltages for all 16 possible input combinations.
answer: (c) all 16 codes: vO amplitude (V) = −(n/16)·2 V, n = 8b1 + 4b2 + 2b3 + b4
problems.how: Each switch connects its resistor to vI (bi = 1) or to 0 V (bi = 0); the summing amplifier with feedback resistor R gives vO = −(b1·R/2R + b2·R/4R + b3·R/8R + b4·R/16R)·vI = −(n/16)·vI.
assume: b1 is the bit of the 2R resistor (the most significant) and b4 the bit of the 16R resistor, as drawn.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.70 (p.582): summing amplifier with feedback resistor R and four input resistors 2R, 4R, 8R, 16R, each switched by a bit b1…b4 either to 0 V (bi = 0) or to the input vI (bi = 1).

problems.text: (a) What is the gain of the circuit in Fig. P10.72 if Av = vo/(v1 −v2) and R = 10 kΩ? (b) What is the input resistance presented to v2? (c) What is the input resistance at terminal v1? (d) What is the output voltage if v1 = 3 V and v2 = 1.5 cos 8300πt V? (e) What is the output voltage if v1 = [3 − 1.5 cos 8300πt] V and v2 = 1.5 sin 8300πt V?
answer: R = 10.0 kΩ (for v2 = 0; in general i1 depends on v2 also)
problems.how: Difference amplifier with R1 = R3 = R and R2 = R4 = 10R: vO = −(R2/R1)(v1 − v2) = −10(v1 − v2) (Jaeger Eq. 10.64); Rin2 = R + 10R and Rin1 = R for v2 = 0.
assume: Av is defined as vo/(v1 − v2), so it is negative for this connection (v1 on the inverting side).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback from the output to the − input; v2 through R to the + input with 10R from the + input to ground.

problems.text: (a) What are the voltages at all the nodes in the difference amplifier in Fig. P10.72 if V2 = 3.2 V, V1 = 3.1 V, and R = 100 kΩ? (b) What is amplifier output current IO? (c) What are the currents entering the circuit from v1 and v2?
answer: (b) output current IO (into the 10R feedback resistor, leaving the output)
(c) currents entering from v1 and v2
problems.how: Ideal op amp: v+ = v2·10R/(11R) = v−; vO = −10(V1 − V2); currents from Ohm's law.
assume: IO is the current delivered by the op-amp output through the feedback resistor (no other load).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier with R = 100 kΩ: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback, v2 through R to the + input with 10R to ground.

problems.text: Find vO, i1 and i2 for the difference amplifier in Fig. P10.72 if v2 = 2 sin 1000πt V, v1 = (2 sin 1000πt + 2 sin 2000πt) V, and R = 15 kΩ.
answer: vO = −20 sin 2000πt V (the common-mode term 2 sin 1000πt cancels)
problems.how: Ideal difference amplifier with R = 15 kΩ and 10R: v1 − v2 = 2 sin 2000πt, so vO = −10(v1 − v2); v+ = v− = (10/11)v2 gives the input currents.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.72 (p.583): difference amplifier with R = 15 kΩ: v1 through R to the − input and 10R feedback, v2 through R to the + input with 10R to ground; i1 and i2 are the currents drawn from the sources.

problems.text: Find the poles and zeros of the following transfer functions: (a) Ai(s) (s^2 + 51s + 50)(s^2 + 13,000s + 3 × 10^7) = − 10^5(s^2 + 51s + 50) s^5 + 1000s^4 + 50,000s^3 + 20,000s^2 + 13,000s + 3 × 10^7
problems.how: (a): s² + 51s + 50 = (s + 1)(s + 50) and s² + 13000s + 3×10⁷ = (s + 3000)(s + 10000); (b): numerator (s + 1)(s + 50), denominator roots found numerically (rebuilt to check).
assume: Part (b): Av(s) = −10⁵(s² + 51s + 50)/(s⁵ + 10³s⁴ + 5×10⁴s³ + 2×10⁴s² + 1.3×10⁴s + 3×10⁷), as printed; its denominator has a complex pair in the right half-plane (unstable), which is what the printed coefficients give.

answer: 10.0 Hz, 10000.0 Hz (poles at 10 Hz and 10 kHz)
problems.how: Midband: s ≫ 20π, s ≪ 2π×10⁴: Av = 2π×10⁷/(2π×10⁴) = 10³. The −3 dB frequencies are found by a numerical sweep and agree with the pole frequencies.

problems.text: What are Amid in dB, fH, fL, and the BW in Hz for the amplifier described by What type of amplifier is this?
problems.how: Av(0) = 2π×10⁶/200π = 10⁴; single pole at 200π rad/s = 100 Hz.

problems.text: What are Amid in dB, fH, fL, and the BW in Hz for the amplifier described by
problems.how: For s ≫ 200π the gain is 10⁴; zero at the origin and pole at 200π rad/s = 100 Hz (Eq. 10.78).

problems.text: What are Amid in dB, fH, fL, the BW in Hz, and the Q for the amplifier described by
problems.how: ω0 = √10¹⁴ = 10⁷ rad/s, ω0/Q = 10⁵ rad/s so Q = 100; at ω0 |Av| = 5×10⁶/10⁵ = 50. Cutoffs by a numerical sweep; fL·fH = f0².

problems.text: What are Amid in dB, fH, fL, and the BW in Hz for the amplifier described by
answer: fL, fH (−3 dB edges of the notch)
problems.how: Numerator zeros on the jω axis at ω = 10⁶ rad/s (gain 0); far from it Av → −20. Edges found numerically; BW = ω0/(2πQ) = 1.59 kHz.

problems.text: What are Amid in dB, fH, fL, and the BW in Hz for the amplifier described by (s + 20π)(s + 50π)(s + 2π × 10^5)(s + 2π × 10^6) What type of amplifier is this?
answer: 10 Hz, 25 Hz, 100 kHz, 1 MHz; double zero at 0
problems.how: Between 25 Hz and 100 kHz: Av ≈ 4π²×10¹⁴/(4π²×10¹¹) = 10³. The two low poles are close, so the exact lower −3 dB point (numerical) lies a little above 25 Hz.

problems.text: (a) Write an expression for the transfer function of a low-pass voltage amplifier with a gain of 26 dB and fH = 5 MHz. (b) Repeat if the amplifier exhibits a phase shift of 180^(°) at f = 0.
problems.how: Single-pole low-pass amplifier, Eq. (10.66).

problems.text: (a) Write an expression for the transfer function of a voltage amplifier with a gain of 40 dB, fL = 400 Hz, and fH = 100 kHz. (b) Repeat if the amplifier exhibits a phase shift of 180^(°) at f = 0.
answer: the same with a minus sign in front
problems.how: Band-pass amplifier = high-pass × low-pass; midband gain A0 requires ωH ≫ ωL.

problems.text: The input to an low-pass amplifier with a gain of 10 dB is vS = 1 sin(1000πt) + 0.333 sin(3000πt) (a) If the phase shift of the amplifier at 500 Hz is 10^(°), what must be the phase shift at the other two frequencies if the shape of the output waveform is to be the same as that of the input waveform? Write an expression for the output signal. (b) Use the computer to check your answer by plotting the input and output waveforms.
answer: linear in frequency: 10° at 500 Hz, 30° at 1500 Hz, 50° at 2500 Hz (each frequency delayed by the same time 55.6 μs)
problems.how: No waveform distortion needs equal gain and a time delay td constant: phase = −ω·td. At 500 Hz 10° = 360°·500·td gives td = 55.6 μs.
assume: The phase shifts are taken as lags (delays).

problems.text: Find the midband gain in dB and the upper cutoff frequency for the low-pass filter in Ex. 10.8 if R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, and C = 0.01 μF.
Find the midband gain in dB and the upper cutoff frequency for the low-pass filter in Ex. 10.8 if R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 1.5 kΩ, and C = 0.02 μF.
problems.how: Same formulas as Problem 10.95.

problems.text: (a) Design a low-pass filter using the circuit in Ex. 10.8 to provide a loss of no more than 0.5 dB at low frequencies and a cutoff frequency of 20 kHz if R1 = 620 Ω. (b) Pick standard values from the tables in Appendix A.
answer: (a) C for fH = 20 kHz (R2 = that minimum)
R1 = 620 Ω, R2 = 11 kΩ → loss 0.4763 dB, C = 13.56 nF → 13 nF gives fH = 20.86 kHz
problems.how: Loss at low frequency = −20·log₁₀[R2/(R1+R2)] ≤ 0.5 dB gives R2 ≥ 16.9·R1; then C = 1/[2π(R1‖R2)fH].
assume: Standard values from the 5 % series (620 Ω and 11 kΩ).

problems.text: (a) What are the low-frequency voltage gain (in dB) and cutoff frequency fH for the amplifier in Fig. 10.32 if R1 = 2 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, and C = 0.001 μF? (b) Repeat for R1 = 3.3 kΩ, R2 = 56 kΩ, and C = 100 pF?
problems.how: Low-pass inverting amplifier (Jaeger Fig. 10.32): Av(s) = −(R2/R1)/(1 + sR2C), so the low-frequency gain is −R2/R1 and the −3 dB frequency fH = 1/(2πR2C).
assume: The gain in dB is 20 log|Av|; the minus sign (inversion) is shown separately.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.32 (p.585): low-pass amplifier: vi through R1 to the − input; the feedback is R2 in parallel with C from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Design a low-pass amplifier (i.e., choose R1, R2, and C) to have a low-frequency input resistance of 10 kΩ, a midband gain of 20 dB, and a bandwidth of 20 kHz. (b) Choose element values from the tables in Appendix A.
problems.how: Active low-pass amplifier (inverting, C across R2): Av = −(R2/R1)/(1 + sR2C); Rin = R1, |Av| = 10, fH = 1/(2πR2C).
assume: Circuit: inverting amplifier with C in parallel with R2 (Section 10.10.2/10.10.5).

problems.text: Find the midband gain in dB and the upper cutoff frequency for the high-pass filter in Ex. 10.9 if R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 82 kΩ, and C = 0.01 μF.
answer: Cutoff frequency (the high-pass has a LOWER cutoff fL; fH is infinite)
problems.how: Ex. 10.9: Av = [R2/(R1+R2)]·s/(s + ωL), ωL = 1/[(R1 + R2)C]. (The statement says "upper" but only the lower cutoff exists.)

problems.text: Find the midband gain in dB and the upper cutoff frequency for the high-pass filter in Ex. 10.9 if R1 = 8.2 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ, and C = 0.02 μF.
problems.how: Same formulas as Problem 10.101.

problems.text: (a) Design a high-pass filter using the circuit in Ex. 10.9 to provide a loss of no more than 0.5 dB at high frequencies and a cutoff frequency of 20 kHz if R1 = 390 Ω. (b) Pick standard values from the tables in Appendix A.
answer: (a) R2 for loss ≤ 0.5 dB at high frequency
problems.how: Loss = −20·log₁₀[R2/(R1+R2)] ≤ 0.5 dB gives R2 ≥ 16.9·R1; C = 1/[2π(R1 + R2)fL].
assume: Standard values from the 5 % series.

problems.text: What are the high-frequency voltage gain (in dB) and cutoff frequency fL for the amplifier in Fig. 10.33 if R1 = 4.2 kΩ, R2 = 20 kΩ, and C = 560 pF? (b) Repeat for R1 = 2.7 kΩ, R2 = 56 kΩ, and C = 0.002 μF.
problems.how: High-pass inverting amplifier (Jaeger Fig. 10.33): Av(s) = −(R2/R1)·sR1C/(1 + sR1C): the high-frequency gain is −R2/R1 and the −3 dB frequency fL = 1/(2πR1C).
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.33 (p.585): high-pass amplifier: vi through C in series with R1 to the − input; feedback resistor R2 from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Design a high-pass filter (choose R1, R2, and C) to have a high frequency input resistance of 20 kΩ, a gain of 20 dB, and a lower cutoff frequency of 1 kHz. (b) Choose element values from the tables in Appendix A.
problems.how: Active high-pass amplifier (inverting, C in series with R1): Rin(high f) = R1, |Av| = R2/R1 = 10, fL = 1/(2πR1C) (same form as Example 10.10).

problems.text: The input voltage to the integrator circuit in Fig. 10.34 is given by vi = 0.1 sin 2000πt V. What is the output voltage if R = 12 kΩ, C = 0.005 μF, and vo(0) = 0?
problems.how: Ideal integrator (Jaeger Fig. 10.34): vo(t) = vo(0) − (1/RC)∫ vi dτ; with vi = 0.1 sin ωt, ω = 2000π, vo = (0.1/(RCω))(cos ωt − 1).
assume: The dc offset −0.265 V comes from vo(0) = 0: the output starts at 0 V and swings below it.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.34 (p.585): integrator: vi through R to the − input and the capacitor C from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: The input voltage to the integrator circuit in Fig. 10.34 is a rectangular pulse with an amplitude of 5 V and a width 1 ms. Draw the waveform at the output of the integrator if the pulse starts at t = 0, R = 10 kΩ, and C = 0.1 μF. Assume vo = 0 for t ≤0. (b) Repeat for vo(0) = −2.5 V.
answer: for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 ms: vo(t) = −5 V × (t/1 ms) (a ramp falling 5000.0 V/s = 5 V/ms to -5.0 V at t = 1 ms); for t > 1 ms the input is 0, so vo stays at -5.0 V
the same ramp starting from −2.5 V: vo(t) = −2.5 − 5·(t/1 ms) V down to -7.5 V at t = 1 ms, then constant at -7.5 V
problems.how: RC = 10 kΩ × 0.1 μF = 1 ms, so a 5 V pulse makes the output fall 5 V per millisecond (vo = vo(0) − (1/RC)∫vi dt); after the pulse the input is 0 and the capacitor holds its charge.
assume: The op amp is ideal with no supply limit.
The waveform asked for is described by its segments and levels.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.34 (p.585): integrator: vi through R to the − input and the capacitor C from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: What is the output voltage of the differentiator circuit in Fig. 10.33 if vi(t) = 3 cos 3000πt V with C = 0.02 μF and R = 120 kΩ?
problems.how: Ideal differentiator (Jaeger Fig. 10.33/10.35): vo = −RC·dvi/dt; for vi = 3 cos ωt, vo = 3ωRC sin ωt.
assume: The result (67.9 V amplitude) shows that the ideal differentiator would need far larger supplies than a real op amp has: the high-pass of the practical circuit limits it.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.33 (p.585): differentiator: vi through C to the − input, feedback resistor R from the output to the − input; + input grounded (R and C are the values of the statement).

problems.text: (a) What is the output current IO in the circuit of Fig. P10.114 if −VE E = −10 V and R = 20 Ω? Assume that the MOSFET is saturated. (b) What is the minimum voltage VDD needed to saturate the MOSFET if VT N = 2.5 V and Kn = 0.25 A/V^2. (c) What must be the power dissipation ratings of resistor R and the FET.
answer: (a) output current IO = VEE/R (the source node is held at 0 V)
VGS = VTN + √(2·ID/Kn) = 4.5 V; saturation needs VDS ≥ VGS − VTN = 2.0 V, so VDD(min) = 2.0 V (source at 0 V)
resistor: IO²R = 5.0 W; FET at VDD(min): ID·VDS = 1.0 W (it grows as 0.5 A × VDD for a higher supply)
problems.how: The op amp (+ input grounded) forces the MOSFET source node to 0 V (virtual ground), so IO = ID = VEE/R, independent of the transistor; with ID = (Kn/2)(VGS − VTN)² the gate voltage follows.
assume: The drain is assumed connected directly to VDD; Kn follows ID = (Kn/2)(VGS − VTN)² (Jaeger).
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.114 (p.586): an op amp with + input grounded and its output driving the gate of an NMOS transistor whose drain goes to VDD and whose source is fed back to the − input and connected through R to −VEE; the output current IO is the drain current.

problems.text: (a) What is the output current IO in the circuit in Fig. P10.115 if −VE E = −15 V and R = 15 Ω? Assume that the BJT is in the forward-active region and βF = 30. (b) What is the voltage at the output of the operational amplifier if the saturation current IS of the BJT is 10^−13 A? (c) What is the minimum voltage VCC needed for forwardactive region operation of the bipolar transistor? (d) Find the power dissipation rating of the resistor R. How much power is dissipated in the transistor if VCC = 15 V?
answer: (b) op-amp output voltage = VBE (emitter at 0 V)
(c) minimum VCC for the forward-active region
VCB ≥ 0: VC ≥ VB = 0.748 V, so VCC(min) ≈ 0.748 V
resistor: IE²R = 15.0 W; transistor at VCC = 15 V: IC·VCE + IB·VBE = 14.54 W
problems.how: The op amp holds the emitter at 0 V, so IE = VEE/R = 1 A and IC = βF/(βF + 1)·IE; the base is VBE above the emitter.
assume: VT = 25 mV and the collector is tied directly to VCC; VCE = VCC because the emitter is at 0 V.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.115 (p.586): an op amp with + input grounded and its output driving the base of an npn transistor whose collector goes to VCC and whose emitter is fed back to the − input and connected through R to −VEE; the output current IO is the collector current.

problems.text: The low-pass filter in Fig. P10.117 has R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 330 kΩ, and C = 100 pF. If the tolerances of the resistors are ±10 percent and that of the capacitor is +20 percent/−50 percent, what are the nominal and worst-case values of the lowfrequency gain and cutoff frequency?
problems.how: Gain −R2/R1 and fH = 1/(2πR2C); the extremes occur at the corners of the tolerance box: gain largest for R2 high and R1 low, fH largest for R2 and C both low (R2·C smallest).
assume: All 8 tolerance corners were evaluated: the extremes above are the largest and smallest values.
problems.circuit: Fig. P10.117 (p.586): low-pass amplifier: vi through R1 to the − input; the feedback is R2 in parallel with C from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: Design a Schmitt trigger to have its switching thresholds centered at 1 V with a hysteresis of ±0.05 V, using the circuit topology in Fig. P12.111.
answer: Design equations (output 0 V / 5 V; node on the + input)
VL = 5·RB‖RF/(RA + RB‖RF) with output low, VH = VL + 5/(RF·G) with G = 1/RA + 1/RB + 1/RF
Choice RA = 10 kΩ (as in the figure)
upper 1.05 V, lower 0.95 V: centre 1.0 V, hysteresis ±0.05 V
problems.how: Fig. P12.111 topology: the + input is the node of RA (to the 5-V supply), RB (to ground) and RF (to the comparator output, 0 V or 5 V), the input signal is applied to the − input. With the output high the node voltage is VH, with the output low VL; centre 1 V and hysteresis ±0.05 V need VL = 0.95 V and VH = 1.05 V, which give RF = 9.5·RA and RB = RA/4.158.
assume: Only two conditions (centre, hysteresis) for three resistors: RA = 10 kΩ is chosen as in Fig. P12.111; the others follow (the nearest standard values should be chosen in practice).
The comparator output swings 0 V to 5 V (supply pins +5 V and ground in the figure).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.111 (p.769): Schmitt trigger: comparator (supply 5 V and ground); + input node with 10 kΩ to a 5-V source, 15 kΩ to ground and 100 kΩ to the output; the signal vS on the − input.

problems.text: (a) Design an astable multivibrator to oscillate at a frequency of 1 kHz. Use the circuit in Fig. 12.60 with symmetric supplies of ±5 V. Assume that the total current from the op amp output must never exceed 1 mA. (b) If the resistors have ±5 percent tolerances and the capacitors have ±10 percent tolerances, what are the worst-case values of oscillation frequency? (c) If the power supplies are actually +4.75 and −5.25 V, what is the oscillation frequency for the nominal resistor and capacitor design values?
answer: (a) peak output current (when the output switches)
(c) supplies +4.75 V and −5.25 V, nominal components
T1 = RC ln[(1 + βVEE/VCC)/(1 − β)], T2 = RC ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − β)]: f = 999.0 Hz
problems.how: Astable multivibrator (Eqs. 12.91, 12.94, 12.95): T = T1 + T2 with T1 = RC·ln[(1 + βVEE/VCC)/(1 − β)], T2 = RC·ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − β)]; symmetric supplies: T = 2RC·ln[(1 + β)/(1 − β)]. The current limit is met at the switching instant, when the capacitor is at −βVEE. Worst case = extreme over the 16 corners of the tolerance box (confirmed by 2000 random sets); exact event-driven numerical simulation of the capacitor reproduces the period of the design and of case (c).
assume: The statement leaves free β, R and C: β = 0.5 with R1 = R2 = 12 kΩ and R = 15 kΩ is chosen (any other choice meeting the 1 mA limit works; only the product RC·ln[(1+β)/(1−β)] matters for the frequency).
"Worst-case" means the minimum and maximum frequency over the tolerance extremes of R1, R2, R (±5 %) and C (±10 %).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.60 (p.769): astable multivibrator: comparator (op amp) with positive-feedback divider R2 (from the output) and R1 (to ground) on the + input, and R from the output to the − input with C from the − input to ground; supplies VCC and −VEE.

problems.text: Two diodes are added the circuit Fig. P12.116 to convert it to a monostable multivibrator similar to the circuit in Fig. 12.62, and the power supplies are changed to ±7.5 V. What are the pulse width and recovery time of the monostable circuit?
answer: Pulse width T = RC·ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]
Recovery time Tr = RC·ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − VD/VEE)]
problems.how: Monostable multivibrator (Eqs. 12.100 and 12.101): the capacitor starts at −VD (clamped by D2), charges toward VCC until it reaches βVCC (pulse width T) and then discharges from βVCC toward −VEE until D2 clamps it at −VD again (recovery time Tr). Numerical event simulation of the two exponentials gives the same times. Anchor: the book's exercise (Fig. 12.64: VCC = VEE = 5 V, R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 18 kΩ, R = 11 kΩ, C = 2 nF) gives 20.4 μs and 33.4 μs between triggers, which the formulas reproduce with VD = 0.7 V.
assume: The diode on-voltage is not given: VD = 0.7 V is used (it reproduces the book's exercise 20.4 μs / 33.4 μs).
R1 = 15 kΩ (to ground) and R2 = 27 kΩ (feedback) read from Fig. P12.116, with R = 51 kΩ and C = 0.033 μF; the supplies are ±7.5 V.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.116 (p.769): astable-multivibrator comparator (op amp with the output-switching symbol): + input with 15 kΩ to ground and 27 kΩ from the output; 51 kΩ from the output to the − input with 0.033 μF from the − input to ground; supply +12 V (changed to ±7.5 V in this problem) and two diodes added as in Fig. 12.62.

problems.text: Design a monostable multivibrator to have a pulse width of 20 μs and a recovery time of 5 μs. Use the circuit in Fig. 12.62 with ±5 V supplies.
answer: RC from T = RC·ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]
T = 20.0 μs, Tr = 5.0 μs; stability condition βVEE = 4.79 V > VD
problems.how: Two equations (Eqs. 12.100, 12.101) fix β and RC: the ratio T/Tr = ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)] / ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − VD/VEE)] = 4 gives β by root finding, then RC = T/ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]. R, C and R1 are then free choices.
assume: VD = 0.7 V is used (it reproduces the book's exercise 20.4 μs / 33.4 μs).
The requirement T/Tr = 4 forces β close to 1 (about 0.95): R2 must be only about 5 % of R1, so the design is sensitive to resistor tolerance; C = 100 pF and R1 = 19 kΩ are example choices.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.62 (p.769): monostable multivibrator: comparator with divider R2 (from the output) and R1 (to ground) on the + input, R from the output to the − input with C from the − input to ground; trigger diode D1 and clamp diode D2 on the − input.

title.en: M04 · Amplifier stage coupling and positive/negative feedback: Jaeger problems without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site) · part 1 of 3

note.vi: Sách không in đáp án các problem này. Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. Bài có hình trong sách thì hình được cắt từ PDF và đặt dưới đề, kèm mô tả mạch bằng lời. Thời gian là giả định (8 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: The classic feedback amplifier in Fig. 11.1 has β = 0.125. What are the loop gain T , ideal closedloop gain A^Ideal , actual closed-loop gain Av, and the fractional gain error FGE if (a) A = ∞? (b) A = 84 dB? (c) A = 20?
answer: T = inf; Aideal = 1/β = 8.0; Av = A/(1 + Aβ) = 8.0; FGE = (Av − Aideal)/Aideal = 0 %
T = 1981.1; Aideal = 1/β = 8.0; Av = A/(1 + Aβ) = 7.996; FGE = (Av − Aideal)/Aideal = -0.05045 %
T = 2.5; Aideal = 1/β = 8.0; Av = A/(1 + Aβ) = 5.7143; FGE = (Av − Aideal)/Aideal = -28.57 %
problems.how: Feedback amplifier equations (Jaeger Eq. 11.4): T = Aβ, Av = A/(1 + Aβ) = Aideal/(1 + 1/T) with Aideal = 1/β = 8; FGE = (Av − Aideal)/Aideal = −1/(1 + T).
assume: A in dB is converted with A = 10^(dB/20).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.1 (p.673): classic feedback amplifier: a summing block (vd = vi − vf) feeds the amplifier A, whose output vo drives the load and the feedback network β that returns vf = β·vo.

problems.text: A amplifier’s closed-loop voltage gain Av is described by Eq. (11.4). What is the minimum value of loop gain T required if the gain error is to be less than 0.2 percent for an ideal gain of 50 dB?
problems.how: FGE = 1/(1 + T) < 0.2 % → T > 499. The ideal gain (50 dB) does not matter for the fractional error.

problems.text: (a) Calculate the sensitivity of the closed-loop gain Av with respect to changes in open-loop gain A, S ^Av A , using Eq. (11.4) and the definition of sensitivity given below: (b) Use this formula to estimate the percentage change in closed-loop gain if the open-loop gain A changes by 10 percent for an amplifier with A = 100 dB and β = 0.01.
answer: (b) estimated change of Av for a 10 % change of A

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is built with R1 = 12 kΩ and R2 = 150 kΩ using an op amp with an openloop gain of 86 dB. What are the closed-loop gain, the gain error, and the fractional gain error for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if R1 is changed to 1.2 kΩ.
answer: Ideal Av = 13.5, T = Aβ = 1478.0, actual Av = 13.49
Ideal Av = 126.0, T = Aβ = 158.4, actual Av = 125.2
problems.how: Eqs. (11.4)–(11.6) with β = R1/(R1 + R2); checked with an exact nodal solution of the circuit.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is built with R2 = 47 kΩ and R1 = 6.2 kΩ using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 94 dB. What are the closed-loop gain, the gain error, and the fractional gain error for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if the open-loop gain is changed to 100 dB.
answer: Ideal Av = 8.581, T = Aβ = 5841.0, actual Av = 8.579
Ideal Av = 8.581, T = Aβ = 11650.0, actual Av = 8.58
problems.how: As Problem 11.5.

problems.text: The feedback amplifier in Fig. P11.8(a) has R1 = 1kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, RI = 0, and RL = 10 kΩ. (a) What is β? (b) If A = 92 dB, what are the loop gain T and the closed loop gain Av? (c) What are the values of GE and FGE?
answer: (b) loop gain T = Aβ and closed-loop gain Av = A/(1 + T)
(c) gain error GE = Av − Aideal, FGE = GE/Aideal
problems.how: Noninverting (series-shunt) amplifier: β = R1/(R1 + R2); T = Aβ; Av = A/(1 + Aβ).
assume: The statement gives only the open-loop gain A = 92 dB (no Rid or Ro), so the op amp is taken as having infinite input resistance and zero output resistance; then RI = 0 and RL do not change Av.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.8 (p.673): part (a): noninverting voltage amplifier: vI (with source resistance RI) drives the + input; R2 from the output to the − input and R1 from the − input to ground; load RL (four feedback amplifiers (a) to (d) are drawn).

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is built with R1 = 11 kΩ and R2 = 220 kΩ using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 86 dB. What are the closed-loop gain, the gain error, and fractional gain error for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if R1 is changed to 1.1 kΩ.
answer: Ideal Av = -20.0, T = Aβ = 950.1, actual Av = -19.98
Ideal Av = -200.0, T = Aβ = 99.27, actual Av = -198.0

problems.text: The inverting amplifier in Fig. 11.3 is implemented with an op amp with finite gain A = 80 dB. If R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 100 kΩ, what are β, T , and Av?
problems.how: Inverting amplifier with finite gain (Jaeger Eq. 11.14): β = R1/(R1 + R2), Av = −(R2/R1)/(1 + 1/T).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.3 (p.673): inverting amplifier with a finite-gain op amp A: vi through R1 to the − input (voltage vid across the inputs), R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is built with R2 = 56 kΩ and R1 = 5.6 kΩ using an op amp with an openloop gain of 94 dB. What are the closed-loop gain, the gain error, and fractional gain error for this (d) For each amplifier A: Ao = 5000, Rid = 25 kΩ, Ro = 1 kΩ. amplifier? (b) Repeat if the open-loop gain is changed to 100 dB.
answer: Ideal Av = -10.0, T = Aβ = 4556.0, actual Av = -9.998
Ideal Av = -10.0, T = Aβ = 9091.0, actual Av = -9.999
problems.how: As Problem 11.9.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is being designed to have a closed-loop gain of 36 dB. What op-amp gain is required to have the gain error less than 0.15 percent?
An inverting amplifier is being built with a closedloop gain of 46 dB. What op amp gain is required to have the gain error below 0.1 percent?
Calculate the currents i1, i2, and i−for the amplifier in Fig. 11.6 if vx = 0.1 V, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 47 kΩ, Rid = 1 MΩ, and A = 10^5. What is i+?
answer: 47.98 pA (the same current flows out of the + input side through Rid: i+ = −i−... the input current of the + terminal equals i−)
problems.how: Solve the loop: vo = A·vid, v1 = vo·R1/(R1 + R2), vid = vx − v1; then the currents from Ohm's law. The exact nodal solution of the circuit gives the same values.
assume: i+ is the current entering the + input, equal in magnitude to i− because the current flows through Rid from the + to the − terminal; the result is tiny (nanoamps).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.6 (p.674): noninverting amplifier with a finite-gain op amp (input resistance Rid between the inputs, gain A·vid): vx drives the + input; R2 from the output to the − input (current i2) and R1 from the − input to ground (current i1); i− and i+ are the input currents.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is built with R2 = 75 kΩ and R1 = 5.6 kΩ using an op amp with an openloop gain of 100 dB, an input resistance of 500 kΩ, and an output resistance of 300 Ω. What are the closed-loop gain, input resistance, and output resistance for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if the open-loop gain is changed to 94 dB.
answer: Av = 14.39, Rin = 3.474 GΩ, Rout = 43.17 mΩ (T = 6948.0); exact circuit: Av = 14.39, Rin = 3.462 GΩ, Rout = 43.62 mΩ
Av = 14.39, Rin = 1.742 GΩ, Rout = 86.13 mΩ (T = 3482.0); exact circuit: Av = 14.39, Rin = 1.735 GΩ, Rout = 87.03 mΩ
problems.how: Av = A/(1+T), Rin = Rid(1+T), Rout = Ro/(1+T)‖(R1+R2); checked with an exact nodal analysis.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is built with R1 = 15 kΩ and R2 = 150 kΩ using an op amp with an openloop gain of 86 dB, an input resistance of 200 kΩ, and an output resistance of 200 Ω. What are the closed-loop gain, input resistance, and output resistance for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if R1 is changed to 1.2 kΩ.
answer: Av = 10.99, Rin = 363.0 MΩ, Rout = 110.2 mΩ (T = 1814.0); exact circuit: Av = 10.99, Rin = 362.5 MΩ, Rout = 117.7 mΩ
Av = 125.2, Rin = 31.87 MΩ, Rout = 1.255 Ω (T = 158.4); exact circuit: Av = 125.2, Rin = 31.83 MΩ, Rout = 1.262 Ω
problems.how: As Problem 11.17.

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is built with R2 = 47 kΩ and R1 = 4.7 kΩ using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 94 dB, an input resistance of 500 kΩ, and an output resistance of 200 Ω. What are the closedloop gain, input resistance, and output resistance for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if the open-loop gain is changed to 100 dB.
answer: Av = -9.998, Rin = 4.701 kΩ, Rout = 43.89 mΩ (T = 4556.0); exact circuit: Av = -9.998, Rin = 4.701 kΩ, Rout = 44.26 mΩ
Av = -9.999, Rin = 4.7 kΩ, Rout = 22.0 mΩ (T = 9091.0); exact circuit: Av = -9.999, Rin = 4.7 kΩ, Rout = 22.19 mΩ
problems.how: Av = −(R2/R1)T/(1+T), Rin = R1 + Rid‖[R2/(1+A)] (11.37), Rout = Ro/(1+T)‖(R1+R2); checked with an exact nodal analysis.

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is built with R2 = 47 kΩ and R1 = 2.4 kΩ using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 100 dB, an input resistance of 300 kΩ, and an output resistance of 200 Ω. What are the closedloop gain, input resistance, and output resistance for this amplifier? (b) Repeat if the open-loop gain is changed to 94 dB.
answer: Av = -19.58, Rin = 2.4 kΩ, Rout = 41.16 mΩ (T = 4858.0); exact circuit: Av = -19.58, Rin = 2.4 kΩ, Rout = 41.47 mΩ
Av = -19.58, Rin = 2.401 kΩ, Rout = 82.1 mΩ (T = 2435.0); exact circuit: Av = -19.58, Rin = 2.401 kΩ, Rout = 82.73 mΩ
problems.how: As Problem 11.19.

problems.text: An op amp has Rid = 500 kΩ, Ro = 35 Ω, and A = 5×10^4. You must decide if a single-stage amplifier can be built that meets all of the specifications below. (a) Which configuration (inverting or noninverting) must be used and why? (b) Assume that the gain specification must be met and show which of the other specifications can or cannot be met. |Av| = 200 Rin ≥2 × 10^8 Ω Rout ≤0.2 Ω
answer: noninverting: only series feedback at the input can raise Rin far above the resistors (an inverting stage has Rin ≈ R1 and is limited by R1)

problems.text: An op amp has Rid = 1 MΩ, Ro = 100 Ω, and A = 1 × 10^4. Can a single-stage amplifier be built with this op amp that meets all of the following specifications? Show which specifications can be met and which cannot. |Av| = 200 Rin ≥10^8 Ω Rout ≤0.2 Ω
answer: a single stage cannot meet Rin and Rout; only the gain can
problems.how: Noninverting stage with β = 1/200 (the best choice for Rin).

problems.text: The overall amplifier circuit in Fig. P11.23 is a twoterminal network. R1 = 6.8 kΩ and R2 = 120 kΩ. What is its Th´evenin equivalent circuit if the operational amplifier has A = 7 × 10^4, Rid = 1 MΩ, and Ro = 250 Ω? What is its Norton equivalent?
answer: Thévenin voltage (open circuit) per volt of vs
In = Vth/Rth = -263.29·vs (current source) in parallel with 0.06701 Ω
problems.how: Inverting amplifier with finite A, Rid and Ro: open-circuit voltage gain ≈ −(R2/R1)·T/(1 + T) and output resistance Rth = Ro/(1 + Aβ) with β = R1/(R1 + R2) (Jaeger §11.4); the Norton current is Vth/Rth.
assume: The two-terminal network is taken between the op-amp output and ground, with vs inside the box as drawn (is = vs/R1 is the source current).
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.23 (p.675): inverting amplifier in a box (a two-terminal network): source vs with current is through R1 to the − input, R2 from the output to the − input, + input grounded; the terminals of the network are the op-amp output and ground.

problems.text: An inverting amplifier is to be designed to have a closed-loop gain of 60 dB. The only op amp that is available has an open-loop gain of 106 dB. What is the tolerance of the feedback resistors if the total gain error must be ≤1 percent? Assume that the resistors all have the same tolerances.
answer: Gain error from the finite open-loop gain alone
problems.how: Worst case: R2 low and R1 high; total gain error = 1 − (Av,actual/Av,ideal) ≤ 1 %, solved numerically with Eq. (11.17). A 0.1 % resistor is therefore adequate.

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is to be designed to have a closed-loop gain of 54 dB. The only op amp that is available has an open-loop gain of 40,000. What must be the tolerance of the feedback resistors if the total gain error must be ≤2 percent? Assume that the resistors all have the same tolerances. 11.3–11.4 Feedback Amplifier Characterization
answer: Gain error from the finite open-loop gain alone
problems.how: As Problem 11.25 with Av = A/(1 + Aβ), β = R1/(R1+R2); total error ≤ 2 %.

problems.text: An amplifier has an open-loop voltage gain of 100 dB, Rid = 40 kΩ, and Ro = 1000 Ω. The amplifier is used in a feedback configuration with a resistive feedback network. (a) What is the largest value of input resistance that can be achieved in the feedback amplifier? (b) What is the smallest value of input resistance that can be achieved? (c) What is the largest value of output resistance that can be achieved? (d) What is the smallest value of output resistance that can be achieved?
problems.how: Series feedback multiplies a port resistance by (1 + Aβ), shunt feedback divides it by (1 + Aβ); a resistive network cannot give β > 1, so the extremes use β = 1 and Aβ = A = 10⁵.
assume: β ≤ 1 for a passive resistive feedback network.

problems.text: An amplifier has an open-loop voltage gain of 90 dB, Rid = 50 kΩ, and Ro = 5000 Ω. The amplifier is used in a feedback configuration with a resistive feedback network. (a) What is the largest current gain that can be achieved with this feedback amplifier? (b) What is the largest transconductance that can be achieved with this feedback amplifier? 11.5 Voltage Amplifiers—Series-Shunt Feedback
problems.how: Negative feedback can only lower a gain below its open-loop value: for the current amplifier the open-loop (short-circuit) gain is A·Rid/Ro, for the transconductance amplifier A/Ro.

problems.text: (a) Find the closed-loop gain for the circuit in Fig. P11.8(a) if RL = 5.6 kΩ, R1 = 4.3 kΩ, R2 = 39 kΩ, and RI = 1 kΩ.
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier: Av = 1 + R2/R1; RI and RL do not matter for an ideal op amp.
assume: The statement gives no op-amp parameters (A, Rid, Ro), so the op amp is taken as ideal: with a finite A the gain would be slightly lower.
problems.circuit: Fig. P11.8 (p.675): part (a): noninverting voltage amplifier with source resistance RI, feedback divider R2 (output to − input) and R1 (− input to ground), load RL.

problems.text: The integrator in Fig. 10.34 is implemented with an op amp with finite gain A = 86 dB. If R = 24 kΩ and C = 0.01 μF, what are T (s) and Av(s)?
problems.how: Integrator with a finite-gain op amp: the feedback is through C, so β(s) = sRC/(1 + sRC), T(s) = Aβ(s) and Av(s) = Aideal(s)/(1 + 1/T(s)) with Aideal(s) = −1/(sRC) (Jaeger §11.4); algebra gives Av(s) = −A/(1 + sRC(1 + A)).
assume: The op-amp gain is taken as the constant A = 86 dB = 19,953 (no frequency dependence), as stated.
Checked against the exact frequency response of the circuit at four frequencies.

problems.text: The differentiator in Fig. 10.35 is implemented with anopampwithfinitegain A = 80dB.If R = 20kΩ and C = 0.01 μF, what are T (s) and Av(s)?
problems.how: Differentiator with a finite-gain op amp: β(s) = R_in... the feedback attenuation is β(s) = (1/sC)/(1/sC + R)... = 1/(1 + sRC) with the ideal Aideal(s) = −sRC; then Av(s) = Aideal/(1 + 1/T) = −sRC·A/(1 + A + sRC).
assume: The op-amp gain is the constant A = 80 dB = 10,000, as stated.
Checked against the exact frequency response of the circuit at four frequencies.

problems.text: The VTC for an amplifier can be expressed as vo = 15 tanh (1000 vi) V. (a) Use MAT- LAB to find the total harmonic distortion for (a) vi = 0.001 sin 2000πt V. (b) Repeat for vi = 0.002 sin 2000πt V.
problems.how: Fourier series of 15·tanh(1000·vi) found by numerical integration (odd symmetry: only odd harmonics) and checked with an FFT; THD = √(ΣVn²)/V1 up to the 39th harmonic.
assume: The statement asks for MATLAB; the same numbers are computed here with NumPy.

problems.text: An amplifier is formed by cascading the two operational amplifier stages shown in Fig. P12.2. What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance for this amplifier (a) if the op amps are ideal? (b) If the op amps have an open-loop gain of 10^5, an input resistance of 500 kΩ, and an output resistance of 200 Ω? (c) Draw the new circuit and repeat (a) and (b) if the two amplifier stages are interchanged.
answer: inverting 10.0 kΩ / 47.0 kΩ → inverting 24.0 kΩ / 360.0 kΩ
(c, stages interchanged) (b) Av (A = 1.000e+5, Rid = 500.0 kΩ, Ro = 200.0 Ω)
problems.how: Ideal op amps: Av = product of the stage gains, Rin = Rin of the first stage, Rout = 0 (Eq. 12.2). Finite op amps: Table 11.3 / Eq. (12.1): stage gain A/(1 + Aβ) (noninverting) or −(R2/R1)·T/(1 + T) (inverting) with T = Aβ, β = R1/(R1 + R2); Rin = Rid(1 + Aβ) or R1 + Rid‖R2/(1 + A); Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ); stages combined with the loading divider Rin2/(Rout1 + Rin2); the overall Rin is that of the first stage and the overall Rout that of the last. All numbers were also obtained from an exact nodal solution of the complete circuit; the book formulas agree within 8.6e-4 % in the gain and within 4.5 % in Rout (they neglect the loading of Rid on the feedback divider).
assume: Rin and Rout of the cascade are those of the first and last amplifier (ideal source, no load), as stated in Sec. 12.1.1.

note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. problems.text: What are the gain and bandwidth of the individual stages in the amplifier in Fig. P12.2 if the op amps have an Ao = 86 dB and fT = 3 MHz? problems.how: Each closed-loop stage has Av(0) = Av,ideal·T/(1 + T) with T = Ao·β, β = R1/(R1 + R2), and bandwidth f_B = β·fT (Table 11.3); the cascade is Av(s) = ΠAv_k(s) (Eq. 12.3) and its −3 dB frequency solves Eq. (12.6). Check: the full circuit with single-pole op amps (A(s) = Ao/(1 + s/ωb), ωb = 2π·fT/Ao) solved exactly at s = jω by nodal analysis gives the same −3 dB frequency within 2 % (exact: 169.2 kHz; 214.6 kHz; 242.2 kHz).
assume: Ao in dB is converted with A = 10^(dB/20); Rid = ∞ and Ro = 0 (the statement gives no other op-amp parameters).

problems.how: Each closed-loop stage has Av(0) = Av,ideal·T/(1 + T) with T = Ao·β, β = R1/(R1 + R2), and bandwidth f_B = β·fT (Table 11.3); the cascade is Av(s) = ΠAv_k(s) (Eq. 12.3) and its −3 dB frequency solves Eq. (12.6). Check: the full circuit with single-pole op amps (A(s) = Ao/(1 + s/ωb), ωb = 2π·fT/Ao) solved exactly at s = jω by nodal analysis gives the same −3 dB frequency within 2 % (exact: 77.79 kHz).
