problems.text: The op amps in Fig. P12.23 are described by Ao = 86 dB, Rid = 250 kΩ, RO = 200 Ω, and fT = 4 MHz, and the power supplies are ±15 V. (a) What are the voltage gain, input resistance, output resistance, and bandwidth of the overall amplifier? (b) Assume the offset voltage of each op amp is equivalent to +10 mV at the positive input of the op amp. If the input voltage vI = 0 V, what are the voltages (three significant digits) at each of the 10 nodes in the amplifier circuit?
answer: 35.9 kHz (exact circuit with single-pole op amps: 35.61 kHz)
(b) the 10 nodes for vI = 0 (offset +10 mV at each + input, ±15 V supplies)

vI = 0 V; v−A = 10.0 mV; vOA = 49.2 mV; v−B = 10.2 mV; vOB = -4.27 V; v−C = -3.09 V; vO = -14.9 V; V+ = 15.0 V; V− = −15.0 V; ground = 0 V. The output of the third op amp would be -21.0 V without the supply limit, so op amp C saturates at -14.9 V
problems.how: Table 11.3 / Eq. (12.1): stage gain A/(1 + Aβ) (noninverting) or −(R2/R1)·T/(1 + T) (inverting) with T = Aβ, β = R1/(R1 + R2); Rin = Rid(1 + Aβ) or R1 + Rid‖R2/(1 + A); Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ); stages combined with the loading divider Rin2/(Rout1 + Rin2); the overall Rin is that of the first stage and the overall Rout that of the last. Bandwidth: Each closed-loop stage has Av(0) = Av,ideal·T/(1 + T) with T = Ao·β, β = R1/(R1 + R2), and bandwidth f_B = β·fT (Table 11.3); the cascade is Av(s) = Π… Offsets: each op amp is replaced by an ideal-gain amplifier whose + input sits 10 mV above the external + node; when an output would pass ±15 V the amplifier is replaced by a fixed source at the rail (its feedback loop is open, Example 12.1(c)).
assume: The ten nodes are the seven circuit nodes (vI, three − inputs, three outputs) plus V+, V− and ground, as listed in Example 12.1.
Offsets of +10 mV at the + input of every op amp, output saturation exactly at ±15 V; three significant digits are shown.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.23 (p.761): three stages in cascade: a noninverting amplifier (divider 47 kΩ / 12 kΩ), an inverting amplifier (2 kΩ in, 220 kΩ feedback) and a noninverting amplifier (47 kΩ / 12 kΩ); each op amp is drawn with its supply pins (+, −); vI drives the + input of the first stage, vO is the output of the third.

problems.text: What are the nominal, minimum, and maximum values of the voltage gain, input resistance, output resistance, and bandwidth of the overall amplifier in Prob. 12.23 if the resistors all have 10 percent tolerances?
problems.how: The quantities of Prob. 12.23 (Ao = 86 dB, Rid = 250 kΩ, Ro = 200 Ω, fT = 4 MHz) are evaluated at all 2⁶ corners of the ±10 % tolerance box of the six resistors (each quantity is monotone in every resistor, so the extremes are at corners); 400 random points inside the box are checked to lie within [min, max].
assume: "Min" and "max" refer to the magnitude of the gain; the sign is the same for all corners.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.23 (p.761): three stages in cascade: a noninverting amplifier (divider 47 kΩ / 12 kΩ), an inverting amplifier (2 kΩ in, 220 kΩ feedback) and a noninverting amplifier (47 kΩ / 12 kΩ); each op amp is drawn with its supply pins (+, −); vI drives the + input of the first stage, vO is the output of the third.

problems.text: A cascade amplifier is to be designed to meet these specifications: Av = 5000 Rin ≥10 MΩ Rout ≤0.1 Ω How many amplifier stages will be required if the stages must use an op amp below? Because of bandwidth requirements, assume that no individual stage can have a gain greater than 50.
problems.how: Total gain is the product of the stage gains: 50ⁿ ≥ 5000 gives n ≥ 2.2 → 3 stages. The Rin and Rout requirements need the op-amp table that the statement refers to (not reproduced in the text).
assume: Only the gain constraint is evaluated here.

problems.text: What is the voltage gain of the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. 12.4 if R1 = 1.5 kΩ, R2 = 75 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ, and R4 = 10 kΩ. What is the output voltage if v1 = (2 + 0.1 sin 2000πt) V and v2 = 2.1 V?
answer: vo = 5.1 V -5.1·sin(2000πt) V, i.e. vo = 5.1 − 5.1·sin(2000πt) V (between 0 and 10.2 V)
problems.how: Instrumentation amplifier (Eq. 12.10 and the formula printed beside Fig. 12.4): vo = −(R4/R3)(1 + R2/R1)(v1 − v2) with v1 − v2 = (2 + 0.1 sin 2000πt) − 2.1 = −0.1 + 0.1 sin 2000πt. Checked with an exact nodal solution of the three-op-amp circuit (the middle resistor is 2R1).
assume: Ideal op amps and no supply limits (none are given); the output swing 0 … 10.2 V therefore is not clipped.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.4 (p.762): instrumentation amplifier: v1 and v2 drive the + inputs of op amps ① and ②; resistors R2, 2R1, R2 in series between their outputs (the − inputs are at the nodes v1 and v2 of the 2R1 resistor); op amp ③ with R3, R4 forms the difference amplifier.

problems.text: What is the voltage gain of the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. 12.4 if R1 = 15 kΩ, R2 = 75 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ, and R4 = 20 kΩ. What is the output voltage if v1 = (4 −0.2 sin 4000πt) V and v2 = 3.5 V?
answer: vo = -6.0 V + 2.4·sin(4000πt) V (dc -6.0 V, amplitude 2.4 V)
assume: Ideal op amps and no supply limits (none are given).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.4 (p.762): instrumentation amplifier of Fig. 12.4 (op amps ① and ② with R2, 2R1, R2; difference amplifier ③ with R3, R4).

problems.text: What are the actual values of the two input resistances Rin1 and Rin2 and the output resistance Rout of the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. 12.4 if it is constructed using operational amplifiers with A = 8 × 10^4, Rid = 1 MΩ, Ric = 800 MΩ, and Ro = 100 Ω? Assume R1 = 2 kΩ, R2 = 42 kΩ, and R3 = R4 = 10 kΩ.
problems.how: Exact nodal solution of the instrumentation amplifier with each op amp modelled by A, Rid between the inputs, 2Ric from each input to ground (Fig. 11.44) and Ro. Book estimate: op amp ① or ② is a noninverting amplifier with β = 2R1/(2R1 + R2) = 0.08696, so the source sees 2Ric (the resistor at its own + input) in parallel with Rid(1 + Aβ): Rin = 1.3 GΩ (the 2Ric at the − input is fed from the op-amp output, not from the source). the simplified entry of Table 11.3, Ric ‖ Rid(1 + Aβ), would give 717.0 MΩ; the exact nodal values are given. The output resistance is that of op amp ③, Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ3) = 2.5 mΩ with β3 = R3/(R3 + R4) = 0.5.
assume: Rin1 is measured with v2 grounded and Rin2 with v1 grounded.

The common-mode input resistance is modelled as in Fig. 11.44 (a resistor 2Ric from each op-amp input to ground); with the simplified Table 11.3 formula Ric ‖ Rid(1 + Aβ) the input resistances would be about 0.55 times smaller (ambiguity logged).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.4 (p.762): instrumentation amplifier of Fig. 12.4 (op amps ① and ② with R2, 2R1, R2 between their outputs; difference amplifier ③ with R3, R4).

problems.text: In the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. P12.38, va = 5.02 V and vb = 4.98 V. Find the values of node voltages v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6, vo, and currents i1, i2, and i3. What are the values of the commonmode gain, differential-mode gain, and CMRR of the amplifier? The op amps are ideal.
answer: Adm = vo/vid = -50.0501 (33.99 dB), vid = va − vb
problems.how: Ideal op amps: v2 = va, v3 = vb, so the current through 4.9k + 200 Ω + 4.9k is (va − vb)/200 and v1 = va + 24.5(va − vb), v4 = vb − 24.5(va − vb); then the difference amplifier gives v6 = v4·9.99/20, v5 = v6 and vo = v5(1 + 10.01/9.99) − (10.01/9.99)v1. Adm and Acm come from vo = Adm·vid + Acm·vic (vid = va − vb, vic = (va + vb)/2); the same values follow from the exact nodal solution of the circuit.
assume: Current directions follow the arrows of the figure (from the node into the op-amp output); the common-mode gain arises only from the 0.2 % mismatch of the 9.99 k / 10.01 k resistors.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.38 (p.762): instrumentation amplifier with ideal op amps: va on the + input of the upper op amp (output v1; 4.9 kΩ from v1 to its − input v2), vb on the + input of the lower op amp (output v4; 4.9 kΩ from v4 to its − input v3); 200 Ω between v2 and v3; difference amplifier: 9.99 kΩ from v1 to v5 (− input) with 10.01 kΩ feedback v5→vo, 10.01 kΩ (R3) from v4 to v6 (+ input) with 9.99 kΩ from v6 to ground; i1, i2, i3 are drawn flowing from the nodes v1, v4, vo into the op-amp outputs.

problems.text: Find the values of v1, v2, v3, v4, v5, v6, vo, i1, i2, and i3 in the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. P12.38 if va = 3 V and vb = 3 V.
problems.how: Purely common-mode input (va = vb = 3 V): no current in the 4.9k–200 Ω–4.9k chain, v1 = v2 = v3 = v4 = 3 V; the difference amplifier gives v6 = v5 = 3·0.4995 = 1.4985 V and vo = v5(1 + 10.01/9.99) − (10.01/9.99)·3 = −6.006 mV. Exact nodal solution agrees.
assume: Current directions follow the arrows of Fig. P12.38.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.38 (p.762): instrumentation amplifier with ideal op amps: va on the + input of the upper op amp (output v1; 4.9 kΩ from v1 to its − input v2), vb on the + input of the lower op amp (output v4; 4.9 kΩ from v4 to its − input v3); 200 Ω between v2 and v3; difference amplifier: 9.99 kΩ from v1 to v5 (− input) with 10.01 kΩ feedback v5→vo, 10.01 kΩ (R3) from v4 to v6 (+ input) with 9.99 kΩ from v6 to ground; i1, i2, i3 are drawn flowing from the nodes v1, v4, vo into the op-amp outputs.

title.vi: M05 · Mạch op-amp chuyên dụng và chuyển đổi A/D–D/A: problem Jaeger không có đáp án in (site tự giải và kiểm)
title.en: M05 · Special-purpose op-amp circuits and A/D–D/A conversion: Jaeger problems without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site)

note.vi: Sách không in đáp án các problem này. Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. Bài có hình trong sách thì hình được cắt từ PDF và đặt dưới đề, kèm mô tả mạch bằng lời. Thời gian là giả định (8 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: (a) What is the output voltage for the 4-bit DAC in Fig. P12.67, as shown with input data of 0110 if VREF = 2.56 V? (b) Suppose the input data changes to 1001. What will be the new output voltage? (c) Make a table giving the output voltages for all 16 possible input data combinations.
answer: (c) table of all 16 codes (vO = −VREF·N/16, LSB = VREF/16 = 0.16 V)
problems.how: The op amp with R in feedback sums the currents of the legs: vO = −R·Σ b_k·VREF/R_k = −VREF(b1/2 + b2/4 + b3/8 + b4/16) (Eq. 12.52 gives the magnitude). Exact nodal solution of the circuit for all 16 codes gives the same values.
assume: The circuit as drawn inverts, so vO is negative; Eq. (12.52) in the book quotes the same value without the minus sign.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.67 (p.764): weighted-resistor DAC: switches b1…b4 (b1 = MSB) connect resistors 2R, 4R, 8R, 16R either to ground (0) or to VREF (1); the summing node is the − input of an op amp with feedback resistor R, + input grounded; the switch settings drawn are b1 b2 b3 b4 = 0 1 1 0.

problems.text: The op amp in Fig. P12.67 has an offset voltage of +5 mV and the feedback resistor has a value of 1.05R instead of R. What are the offset and gain errors of this DAC?
answer: Gain error (deviation of the slope from the ideal converter)
+5.0 % (slope 1.05 times the ideal); at full scale (code 1111): 0.12 V more negative = 0.75 LSB
problems.how: With feedback resistor Rf = 1.05R the transfer function is vO = −1.05·VREF·N/16 + Vos·(1 + Rf/Rp): the offset voltage is amplified by the noise gain of the summing amplifier (all legs are low-impedance to ground or VREF, so the noise gain does not depend on the code) and adds to every output; the slope is 5 % high. Exact nodal solution for all 16 codes confirms both.
assume: VREF = 2.56 V from Prob. 12.67 is used (it affects only the values in LSB, not the % gain error or the offset in mV).
Offset error = output for the all-zero code, gain error = relative deviation of the slope (Sec. 12.5.2).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.67 (p.764): weighted-resistor DAC: switches b1…b4 (b1 = MSB) connect resistors 2R, 4R, 8R, 16R either to ground (0) or to VREF (1); the summing node is the − input of an op amp with feedback resistor R, + input grounded; the switch settings drawn are b1 b2 b3 b4 = 0 1 1 0.

problems.text: Fill in the missing entries for step size, differential linearity error, and integral linearity error for the DAC in the accompanying table. DIFFERENTIAL DAC LINEARITY INTEGRAL BINARY OUTPUT STEP SIZE ERROR LINEARITY INPUT VOLTAGES (LSB) (LSB) ERROR 000 0.0000 0.00 001 0.1000 010 0.3000 011 0.3500 100 0.4750 101 0.6300 110 0.7250 111 0.8750 0.00
answer: step 0.8 LSB, DNL -0.2 LSB, INL -0.2 LSB
step 1.6 LSB, DNL 0.6 LSB, INL 0.4 LSB
step 0.4 LSB, DNL -0.6 LSB, INL -0.2 LSB
step 1.0 LSB, DNL 0 LSB, INL -0.2 LSB
step 1.24 LSB, DNL 0.24 LSB, INL 0.04 LSB
step 0.76 LSB, DNL -0.24 LSB, INL -0.2 LSB
step 1.2 LSB, DNL 0.2 LSB, INL 0 LSB
problems.how: Step size = ΔVout/LSB, differential error = step − 1 LSB, integral error = actual output − ideal line through the end points, in LSB; the sum of the differential errors reproduces the integral error.

problems.text: Use Th´evenin equivalent circuits for the R-2R ladder network in Fig. P12.70 to find the output voltage for the four input combinations 0001, 0010, 0100, and 1000 if VREF = 2.50 V.
problems.how: Successive Thévenin equivalents from the left: the termination 2R in parallel with a 2R leg is R, which in series with R gives 2R again, so at every node the part of the ladder to the left looks like 2R; a switched leg therefore delivers VREF/2 to the next node and each step toward the LSB halves the contribution. For the MSB leg next to the op amp, i = VREF/(2R) and vO = −R·i = −VREF/2; the others are VREF/4, VREF/8 and VREF/16. The nodal solution of the whole ladder agrees.
assume: The word is written b4 b3 b2 b1 as in the figure, so "0001" switches b1 (the leg next to the op amp, the MSB of the converter, weight 1/2) — the four combinations give the four binary weights.
The circuit as drawn inverts, so the outputs are negative (the magnitudes are VREF/2 … VREF/16).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.70 (p.764): R-2R ladder DAC: a 2R termination to ground at the left, then three series resistors R; four legs of 2R (b4 at the left end … b1 next to the op amp) switched between ground (0) and VREF (1); the right end of the ladder is the − input (virtual ground) of an op amp with feedback R; drawn switches: b4 b3 b2 b1 = 0 1 1 0.

problems.text: A 3-bit weighted-resistor DAC similar to Fig. P12.67 is made using standard 5 percent resistors with R = 1.2 kΩ, 2R = 2.4 kΩ, 4R = 4.8 kΩ, and 8R = 9.1 kΩ. (a) Tabulate the nominal output values of this converter in a manner similar to Table 12.8. What are the values of differential linearity and integral linearity errors for the nominal resistor values? (b) What are the worst-case values of linearity error that can occur with the 5 percent resistors? (Note: this converter has a gain error. You must recalculate the “ideal” step size. It is not 0.1250 V.)
answer: (a) nominal outputs and errors (ideal step = (u(111) − u(000))/7 = 0.12598 VREF)
(a) largest errors for the nominal resistors
differential linearity error up to 0.408 LSB, integral linearity error up to 0.204 LSB
problems.how: vO/VREF = −Σ b_k R/R_k: nominal weights 0.5, 0.25 and 1.2/9.1 = 0.1319 (instead of 0.125). The gain is not the ideal one, so the ideal step is recomputed from the end points, (u111 − u000)/7 (as in Table 12.7 and Prob. 12.69); DNL = step/LSB − 1 and INL = running sum of the DNL. Worst case: the largest errors over the 16 corners of the ±5 % tolerance box of the four resistors; 20 000 random resistor sets inside the box never exceed them.
assume: The 8R resistor is 9.1 kΩ (a standard value), not 9.6 kΩ, so even the nominal converter has linearity errors.
The worst case is found at the corners of the tolerance box (checked with random sets); sign convention: the circuit inverts, the table lists the magnitudes.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.67 (p.765): weighted-resistor DAC as in Fig. P12.67 with three bits: resistors 2R = 2.4 kΩ (b1), 4R = 4.8 kΩ (b2), 8R = 9.1 kΩ (b3) and feedback R = 1.2 kΩ.

problems.text: Tabulate the output voltages for the eight binary input words for the 3-bit DAC in Fig. P12.76, and find the differential and integral linearity errors if VREF = 5.00 V, RREF = 250 Ω, and R = 1.2188 kΩ.
problems.how: With RREF the reference node moves with the data: v_ref = VREF/(1 + RREF·G) where G is the total conductance of the legs connected to it, and |vO| = R·G·v_ref. R = 1.2188 kΩ makes the full-scale code 111 equal to 7/8·VREF (zero gain error), so the ideal LSB is VREF/8; the data-dependent drop across RREF (superposition error) is what produces the linearity errors. Exact nodal solution of the circuit for all 8 codes agrees with the closed form.
assume: The circuit inverts; magnitudes are listed. The ideal step is taken from the end points; with R = 1.2188 kΩ this equals VREF/8 (verified).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.76 (p.765): weighted-resistor DAC with three bits: resistors 2 kΩ (b1), 4 kΩ (b2), 8 kΩ (b3) from the − input of the op amp (feedback R, + input grounded) to switches connected to ground (0) or to VREF through the series resistor RREF (1).

problems.text: Suppose each switch in the DAC in Fig. P12.76 has an on-resistance of 200 Ω. (a) What value of R is required for zero gain error? (b) Find the differential and integral linearity errors if VREF = 5.00 V, RREF = 0 Ω. (c) Repeat for RREF = 250 Ω.
answer: (a) R for zero gain error (code 111 → 7/8 VREF) with Ron = 200 Ω and RREF = 0
R = 0.875/Σ[1/(Rk + Ron)] = 1.0742 kΩ (Σ = 0.81459 mS); with RREF = 250 Ω the same condition gives 1.2929 kΩ
largest DNL 0.188 LSB, largest INL 0.094 LSB (step sizes in LSB: 1.048, 0.9981, 1.048, 0.8121, 1.048, 0.9981, 1.048)
(c) RREF = 250 Ω, same R as in (a)

largest DNL 0.224 LSB, largest INL 0.417 LSB (end-point LSB 0.51925 V; steps in LSB: 1.224, 1.1, 1.092, 0.8052, 0.99, 0.895, 0.8933); gain error: full scale 3.6348 V instead of 4.375 V = -16.9 % (not zero any more); with R re-trimmed to 1.2929 kΩ the gain error vanishes and the linearity errors stay the same (0.224 and 0.417 LSB) because they are measured against the end-point step
problems.how: Each leg is Rk + Ron (Ron = 200 Ω of its switch). |vO| = R·G·VREF/(1 + RREF·G) with G = Σ b_k/(Rk + Ron). The on-resistance is not binary-weighted, so the effective weights 1/(2.2k), 1/(4.2k), 1/(8.2k) are not in the ratio 4:2:1 and the converter is nonlinear. Zero gain error means |vO(111)| = 7/8·VREF. Errors are measured against the end-point step. Exact nodal solution of the circuit agrees with the closed form.
assume: Part (a) is solved with RREF = 0 (the statement does not say; the RREF = 250 Ω value is also given).
In (c) the resistor R is kept from (a); the end-point LSB is recomputed because a gain error now exists (the re-trimmed case is also shown).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.76 (p.765): weighted-resistor DAC with three bits: resistors 2 kΩ (b1), 4 kΩ (b2), 8 kΩ (b3) from the − input of the op amp (feedback R, + input grounded) to switches connected to ground (0) or to VREF through the series resistor RREF (1).

problems.text: Suppose a 10-bit DAC is built using the inherently monotonic circuit technique in Fig. 12.25. (a) If the resistor material has a sheet resistance of 50 Ω/square, and R = 500 Ω, estimate the number of squares that will be required for the resistor string. (b) If the minimum width of a resistor is 2.5 μm, what is the required length of the resistor string? Convert this length to inches.
answer: Number of resistors (Fig. 12.25 technique, 2ⁿ equal resistors)
(b) length of the string for W = 2.5 μm
problems.how: The resistor string of Fig. 12.25 has 2ⁿ equal resistors (1024 for 10 bits, the exercise in Sec. 12.5.3). A resistor of R ohms in a film of sheet resistance Rs has R/Rs squares; its length is squares × width.
assume: One square is taken as one width of length (all resistors have the minimum width, same material).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.25 (p.765): inherently monotonic DAC: a long string of equal resistors between VREF and ground, a switch tree that connects one tap to a voltage-follower op amp, decoded from the binary input (a 3-bit version has 8 resistors).

problems.text: A 14-bit ADC with VFS = 5.12 V has an output code of 10101110110010. What is the possible range of input voltages?
answer: 3.495 V ≤ vX ≤ 3.496 V (N·LSB ± ½ LSB, N·LSB = 3.496 V)
problems.how: Eq. (12.53) and Fig. 12.28: the quantization error of an ideal ADC is at most ½ LSB.
assume: Range taken as (N ± ½)·LSB as in Fig. 12.28.

problems.text: A 20-bit ADC has VFS = 2 V. (a) What is the value of the LSB? (b) What is the ADC output code for an input voltage of 1.630500 V? (c) What is the ADC output code for an input voltage of 0.997030 V?
problems.how: Code = nearest integer to vX/LSB (quantization error ≤ ½ LSB).

problems.text: A 12-bit counting converter with VFS = 5 V and fc = 1 MHz has an input voltage VX = 3.760 V. (a) What is the output code? What is the conversion time TT for this value of VX if fc = 1 MHz? (b) Repeat for VX = 4.333 V.
problems.how: The counter runs until the DAC output reaches vX: N clock periods, with N = vX/VFS·2¹² truncated (the DAC output must not exceed vX).
assume: Code obtained by truncation (counting converter stops when the DAC output first exceeds vX).

problems.text: (a) A 12-bit successive approximation ADC with VFS = 3.3 V is designed using the circuit in Fig. 12.33. What is the maximum permissible offset voltage of the comparator if this offset error is to be less than 0.1 LSB? (b) Repeat for a 20-bit ADC.
answer: LSB = VFS/2ⁿ = 805.66 μV; offset < 0.1 LSB = 80.57 μV
LSB = VFS/2ⁿ = 3.1471 μV; offset < 0.1 LSB = 314.7 nV
problems.how: The comparator offset VOS shifts every transition of the successive-approximation converter by VOS, so it is an error of VOS/LSB least-significant bits: require VOS < 0.1·VFS/2ⁿ.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.33 (p.766): successive-approximation ADC: a comparator compares the input vX with the output of a DAC driven by the successive-approximation register (SAR) and the clock; the comparator decides each bit.

problems.text: ing converter. (a) If the offset voltage of the op amp is 10 mV and V = 3 V, what is the effective reference voltage of this converter? (b) The integrator is used in a single-slope converter with an integration time of 1/30 s and a full-scale voltage of 5.12 V. What is the RC time constant? If R = 50 kΩ, what is the value of C?
answer: (a) effective reference voltage (offset +10 mV at the + input)
V − Vos = 2.99 V (the ramp slope is (V − Vos)/RC); for an offset of the opposite sign V + Vos = 3.01 V
(b) RC time constant (ramp reaches VFS in T = 1/30 s)
problems.how: Integrator (Fig. P12.90): vO = −(1/RC)∫(V − Vos)dt, so the offset appears as an error of the reference: Vref,eff = V − Vos. For a single-slope converter |vO| = V·t/RC must equal VFS at t = T: RC = V·T/VFS.
assume: The sign of the offset is not given: +10 mV at the + input is assumed (V − Vos); the opposite sign is also shown.
In (b) the reference V = 3 V of part (a) is used (nothing else is specified) and the offset is neglected.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.90 (p.766): ramp generator of an integrating converter: source V through R to the − input of an op amp with capacitor C in feedback (a reset switch across C), + input grounded; output vO.

problems.text: A ramp generator using the op amp integrator circuit in Fig. P12.90 is built using an operational amplifier with an open-loop gain Ao = 4×10^4. A 5-V step function is applied to the input of the integrator at t = 0. Write an expression for the output of the integrator in the time domain. What is the minimum RC product if the output ramp is to have an error of less than 1 mV at the end of a 200-ms integration interval?
answer: vO(t) = −A·V·[1 − exp(−t/((A + 1)RC))] = −2×10⁵·[1 − e^(−t/(40001·RC))] V (the ideal ramp is −V·t/RC)
Minimum RC for an error below 1 mV at t = 200 ms
RC ≥ 64.04 ms (64.04 ms); error at that RC = 1.0 mV
problems.how: Op amp with finite gain A: vO = −A·v−, KCL at the − node gives (A + 1)RC·dvO/dt + vO = −A·V, so vO(t) = −A·V(1 − e^(−t/τ)), τ = (A + 1)RC (a first-order lag, not a perfect ramp). The error |ideal − actual| at T = 0.2 s is ≈ V·T/(A·RC) + V·T²/(2A·RC²), decreasing with RC; the minimum RC is found by root finding on the exact expression. Numerical integration of the circuit equation reproduces the output.
assume: The error is the difference of magnitudes of the ideal ramp −V·t/RC and the actual output at t = 200 ms; "less than 1 mV" is taken as the equality limit for the minimum RC.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.90 (p.766): integrator: source V through R to the − input of an op amp with capacitor C in feedback (reset switch across C), + input grounded; a 5-V step is applied at t = 0.

problems.text: A 20-bit dual-ramp converter is to have an integration time T1 = 0.2 s. How rapidly must the unknown and reference voltage switches change state if this timing uncertainty is to be equivalent to less than 0.1 LSB?
problems.how: A timing error ΔT in T1 is a fractional error ΔT/T1 of full scale; 0.1 LSB = 0.1/2²⁰ of full scale.

title.vi: M06 · Bộ lọc tích cực: problem Jaeger không có đáp án in (site tự giải và kiểm)
title.en: M06 · Active filters: Jaeger problems without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site)

note.vi: Sách không in đáp án các problem này. Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. Bài có hình trong sách thì hình được cắt từ PDF và đặt dưới đề, kèm mô tả mạch bằng lời. Thời gian là giả định (8 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: (a) Repeat Design Example 12.6 for a maximally flat second-order low-pass filter with fo = 25 kHz, usingthecircuitinFig.12.5.AssumeC = 0.005μF. What is the filter bandwidth? (b) Use frequency scaling to change fo to 50 kHz.
answer: (a) R1 = R2 = 1/(√2·ωo·C) with C = C2 = 5 nF
R1 = R2 = 900.3 Ω, C1 = 10.0 nF, C2 = 5.0 nF (nearest standard 1 % value to be taken from Appendix A)
fo = 25.0 kHz, Q = 0.70711; −3 dB frequency of the exact circuit = 25.0 kHz
f_H = fo = 25.0 kHz (the low-pass filter extends from dc to f_H)
(b) frequency scaling KF = 2: every capacitor divided by 2, R unchanged
problems.how: Design Example 12.6 with C1 = 2C2 = 2C and R1 = R2 = R: ωo = 1/√(R1R2C1C2) = 1/(√2·RC), Q = √(C1/C2)·√(R1R2)/(R1 + R2) = 1/√2 (Eqs. 12.19), so R = 1/(√2·ωo·C). The exact circuit (Fig. 12.5 with an ideal follower) solved at s = jω confirms |A(jωo)| = Q and that the −3 dB frequency equals fo; frequency scaling (Eq. 12.37) halves the capacitors.
assume: "Assume C = 0.005 μF" is read as C2 = C = 5 nF, C1 = 2C = 10 nF (as in Example 12.6).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.5 (p.762): two-pole low-pass filter: vI → R1 → node v1 → R2 → node v2 (+ input of a voltage follower, output vo); C1 from v1 to the output; C2 from v2 to ground.

problems.text: Design a maximally flat second-order low-pass filter with a bandwidth of 2 kHz using the circuit in Fig. 12.5.
answer: R1 = R2 = 5.627 kΩ (the exercise in Sec. 12.3.1 for the same case gives 5.62 kΩ), C1 = 2C = 20.0 nF, C2 = 10.0 nF
fo = 2.0 kHz, Q = 0.70711, −3 dB frequency (bandwidth) = 2.0 kHz
problems.how: Maximally flat means Q = 1/√2, for which f_H = fo. Use C1 = 2C2 = 2C and R1 = R2 = 1/(√2·ωo·C) (Design Example 12.6); the value of C sets the impedance level. The exact circuit confirms the −3 dB frequency.
assume: The statement does not fix the capacitor: C2 = 10 nF is chosen as in Example 12.6 (any other C works with R scaled as 1/C).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.5 (p.763): two-pole low-pass filter: vI → R1 → v1 → R2 → v2 (+ input of a voltage follower); C1 from v1 to the output; C2 from v2 to ground.

problems.text: Design a high-pass filter with a lower-half power frequency of 24 kHz and Q = 1 using the circuit in Fig. 12.7.
answer: Amplifier gain K from Q = 1/(3 − K)
K = 3 − 1/Q = 2.0  (noninverting amplifier: (K − 1)R′ = R′, e.g. two equal resistors)
Natural frequency from the −3 dB condition
R and C (C1 = C2 = 1 nF chosen)
problems.how: High-pass filter of Fig. 12.7 with R1 = R2 = R, C1 = C2 = C: ωo = 1/(RC), Q = 1/(3 − K) (Eq. 12.26), so Q = 1 needs K = 2. The lower half-power frequency fL satisfies |A(jω)| = K/√2: with x = ω/ωo and Q = 1 it gives x⁴ + x² − 1 = 0, x = 0.786, so fo = fL/0.786. The −3 dB condition |A| = K/√2 reads x⁴/√((1 − x²)² + x²/Q²) = 1/√2. Verified by solving the exact circuit at s = jω (root of |A| = K/√2).
assume: "Lower-half power frequency" is taken as the exact −3 dB frequency (fo = 30.5 kHz). If one set fo = 24 kHz instead (the book says ωo approximately equals the lower cutoff), the real half-power frequency would be 18.87 kHz.
The capacitor value is not given: C1 = C2 = 1 nF chosen (R scales as 1/C).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.7 (p.763): high-pass filter with gain: vI → C1 → v1 → C2 → v2 → R2 to ground; R1 from v1 to the output; the output is vo = K·v2 from a noninverting amplifier with resistors (K − 1)R and R.

problems.text: (a) Calculate fo, Q, and the bandwidth for the band-pass filter in Fig. 12.9 if Rth = 1 kΩ, R2 = 200 kΩ, and C1 = C2 = 220 pF. (b) Use magnitude scaling to change the element values so that Rth = 3.3 kΩ. (c) Use frequency scaling to double fo for the filter in part (a).
answer: peak at 51.154 kHz, −3 dB edges 47.66 kHz and 54.9 kHz (width 7.234 kHz), peak gain 100.0 = 2Q²
(b) magnitude scaling KM = 3.3 (R × KM, C ÷ KM)
Rth = 3.3 kΩ, R2 = 660.0 kΩ, C1 = C2 = 66.67 pF; fo = 51.15 kHz and Q = 7.071 unchanged
problems.how: Band-pass filter of Fig. 12.9 with C1 = C2 = C (Eq. 12.32): ωo = 1/(C√(Rth R2)), Q = ½√(R2/Rth), BW = 2/(R2 C). Magnitude scaling (Eq. 12.35) multiplies R by KM and divides C by KM (fo, Q unchanged); frequency scaling (Eq. 12.37) divides C by KF. The exact circuit (Thévenin source) solved at s = jω gives the same fo, bandwidth and peak gain.
assume: Rth = R1‖R3 is the Thévenin resistance of Fig. 12.9(b); as given, R1 and R3 individually are not needed.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.9 (p.763): band-pass filter with the inverting op-amp configuration: vI → R1 (R3 from the node to ground, giving the Thévenin source vth with Rth = R1‖R3) → node v1; C1 from v1 to the output; C2 from v1 to the − input; R2 from the − input to the output; + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Design a band-pass filter with a center frequency of 600 Hz and Q = 5 using the circuit in Fig. 12.9 with R3 = ∞. What is the filter bandwidth? (b) Use frequency scaling to change fo to 2.25 kHz.
answer: (a) design with R3 = ∞ (Rth = R1) and C1 = C2 = C = 10 nF
peak 600.0 Hz, edges 543.0 Hz – 663.0 Hz, gain 50.0
(b) frequency scaling to 2.25 kHz: KF = 3.75, C ÷ KF
C1 = C2 = 2.667 nF, R1 and R2 unchanged; fo = 2.25 kHz, Q = 5, BW = 450.0 Hz
problems.how: From Eq. (12.32) with R3 = ∞: Q = ½√(R2/R1) ⇒ R2 = 4Q²R1, and ωo = 1/(C√(R1R2)) = 1/(2Q·R1·C) ⇒ R1 = 1/(2Q·ωo·C). Frequency scaling (Eq. 12.37): C′ = C/KF with KF = 2250/600. The exact circuit confirms fo, the bandwidth and the gain 2Q².
assume: The capacitor is not specified: C1 = C2 = 10 nF is chosen (R1, R2 scale as 1/C).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.9 (p.763): band-pass filter with the inverting op-amp configuration: vI → R1 → v1 (R3 omitted, R3 = ∞); C1 from v1 to the output; C2 from v1 to the − input; R2 from the − input to the output.

problems.text: (a) Two identical band-pass filters having ωo = 1 and Q = 3 are designed using the circuit in Fig. 12.9 with C1 = C2 and R3 = ∞. If the filters are cascaded, what are the center frequency, Q, and bandwidth of the overall filter? (b) Write the transfer function for the composite filter.
answer: ωo = 1.0 (unchanged; also the geometric mean of the band edges 0.89847 and 1.113)
BW = ωo·√(√2 − 1)/Q = 0.21453 (a single stage has ωo/Q = 0.33333)
A(s) = [−2Q·s·ωo/(s² + sωo/Q + ωo²)]² with 2Q = 6, ωo = 1: A(s) = 36 s² / (s² + s/3 + 1)²; center gain (2Q²)² = 324
problems.how: Each stage (C1 = C2, R3 = ∞) has A(s) = −2Q·sωo/(s² + sωo/Q + ωo²) with gain 2Q² at ωo (Sec. 12.3.3). The cascade is the product (Eq. 12.3), so the center frequency stays ωo; |A|/|A(jωo)| = [1 + Q²(x − 1/x)²]⁻¹ for two stages and the −3 dB condition gives (x − 1/x)² = (√2 − 1)/Q², i.e. BW = ωo·√(√2 − 1)/Q. Confirmed by root-finding on the exact product.
assume: Q of the overall filter is defined as center frequency / (−3 dB bandwidth).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.9 (p.763): band-pass filter with the inverting op-amp configuration (R3 = ∞, C1 = C2); two identical filters in cascade.

problems.text: The first stage of a two-stage filter consists of a band-pass filter with fo = 5 kHz and Q = 5. The second stage is also a band-pass filter, but it has fo = 6 kHz and Q = 5. If the filters use Fig. 12.9 with C1 = C2 and R3 = ∞, what are the center frequency, Q, and bandwidth of the overall filter?
answer: fo1 = 5 kHz, fo2 = 6 kHz, Q = 5 each (bandwidths fo/Q = 1 kHz and 1.2 kHz, peak gain 2Q² = 50 each)
Center frequency (maximum of the overall response)
5.4772 kHz (geometric mean of the −3 dB edges: 5.4772 kHz; geometric mean of fo1, fo2: 5.4772 kHz)
Q of the overall filter = fp/BW
1364.0 (62.69 dB; the response has a single hump)
problems.how: Overall response = product of the two single-stage band-pass responses A_k(jf) = −2Q·j(f/fo_k)/(1 − (f/fo_k)² + j(f/fo_k)/Q) (Eq. 12.3 with R3 = ∞). The peak is found by a one-dimensional search, the −3 dB frequencies relative to the peak by root finding. The same numbers come from solving the two filters of Fig. 12.9 as exact circuits (op amp, R, C) and multiplying their gains (the second filter does not load the first because the first output is an op-amp output).
assume: "Center frequency" is taken as the frequency of maximum gain (the response is not symmetric on a log scale); the geometric mean of the band edges is also shown. Q = center frequency / bandwidth.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.9 (p.763): band-pass filter with the inverting op-amp configuration (R3 = ∞, C1 = C2); two such filters in cascade, tuned to 5 kHz and 6 kHz, Q = 5 each.

title.vi: M07 · Mạch dao động và IC định thời 555: problem Jaeger không có đáp án in (site tự giải và kiểm)
title.en: M07 · Oscillators and the 555 timer: Jaeger problems without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site)

note.vi: Sách không in đáp án các problem này. Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập (mô phỏng số, mạch chính xác, FFT, nghiệm đa thức…); phần “Giả định” ghi chỗ đề chưa nói rõ. Bài có hình trong sách thì hình được cắt từ PDF và đặt dưới đề, kèm mô tả mạch bằng lời. Thời gian là giả định (8 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: The book prints no answer for these problems. The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route (numerical simulation, exact circuit solution, FFT, polynomial roots…); the “Assumptions” lines state what the statement leaves open. Where the problem refers to a figure of the book, the figure is cut from the PDF and shown under the statement with a description of the circuit in words. The time limit is an assumption (8 minutes per problem).

problems.text: Calculate the frequency and amplitude of oscillation of the Wien-bridge oscillator in Fig. 12.48 if R = 5.1 kΩ, C = 500 pF, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 14 kΩ, R3 = 6.8 kΩ, and R4 = 10 kΩ.
answer: Conditions for the amplitude network, Eq. (12.82)
Check: time-domain simulation of the same circuit (ideal op amp, diode drop 0.6 V)
frequency 62.37 kHz, amplitude 4.41 V (Eq. 12.85 is only an estimate)
problems.how: Wien bridge (Eq. 12.74–12.75): the loop gain is zero-phase at ωo = 1/RC where |T| = G/3, so oscillation needs G = 3. The diode network (Fig. 12.48) switches R4 in parallel with R3 at the peaks; the amplitude estimate of Eq. (12.85) follows from the equivalent circuit with D1 on (Fig. 12.49). Anchor: the book's own exercise with the Fig. 12.48 values (R = 10 kΩ, C = 1 nF, R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ, R3 = 12 kΩ, R4 = 24 kΩ, VD = 0.6 V) gives 15.9 kHz and 3.0 V, reproduced here.
assume: The diode on-voltage is not given: VD = 0.6 V as in the book's exercise is assumed (the amplitude is proportional to VD).

The time-domain simulation (piecewise-linear diodes) gives a larger amplitude than Eq. (12.85) because the book's formula is a peak-voltage estimate; the book's own SPICE value for its exercise is 3.33 V against 3.0 V from the formula.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.48 (p.767): Wien-bridge oscillator: series RC from the output to the + input and parallel RC from the + input to ground; the − input network R1 (to ground), R2, then R3 in parallel with R4 + back-to-back diodes D1/D2 to the output (the figure also shows the lamp version of Fig. 12.47).

problems.text: Calculate the frequency and amplitude of oscillation of the phase-shift oscillator in Fig. 12.50 if R = 5 kΩ, C = 1000 pF, R2 = 47 kΩ, R3 = 15 kΩ, and R4 = 68 kΩ.
answer: Start-up and limiting condition (RF must pass 12R = 60 kΩ)
RF (diodes off) = R2 + R3 = 62.0 kΩ > 12R; RF (diode on, R4 in parallel with R3) = 59.29 kΩ < 12R
Amplitude estimate (diode on, VD = 0.6 V; by the same method as Eq. 12.85)
Check: time-domain simulation (ideal op amp, diode drop 0.6 V)
problems.how: Phase-shift oscillator (Fig. 12.46, Eqs. 12.78–12.81): T(jωo) = RF/(12R) at ωo = 1/(√3RC), so RF must be 12R. With the diode network of Fig. 12.50 RF = R2 + R3 (> 12R, oscillation starts) and falls below 12R when a diode conducts, which limits the amplitude. The amplitude estimate sets the current through RF equal to the value that the RC network needs at the peak, vO/(12R), with the equivalent circuit of D1 on (R4 in series with VD, in parallel with R3), the − input being a virtual ground.
assume: The book gives no amplitude formula for the phase-shift oscillator: the estimate above is derived here by analogy with Eq. (12.85), and VD = 0.6 V is assumed. The time-domain simulation of the piecewise-linear circuit gives a somewhat larger amplitude (checked within 30 %).
No supply voltage is given; the amplitude of about 10 V assumes supplies larger than that.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.50 (p.767): phase-shift oscillator: three series capacitors C with two resistors R to ground (after the first and second capacitor) feeding the − input of an op amp; the feedback network RF = R2 in series with R3, with R4 and the anti-parallel diodes D1, D2 in parallel with R3.

problems.text: Four identical integrators from Fig. 10.34 are cascaded to form an oscillator. (a) Draw the circuit. (b) What is the frequency of oscillation if R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 pF, and the op amps are ideal? (c) If the output of the first integrator is Vo1 = 1 ^(̸) 0^(°), what are the phasor representations of the other three output voltages? (d) Add an amplitude stabilization network to one of the amplifiers and design it to set the output voltage to approximately 2 V.
answer: four identical inverting integrators (R from the input to the − input, C in feedback, + input grounded), each output driving the next; the output of the fourth is fed back to the input of the first (Fig. 10.34 integrator ×4)
T(s) = (−1/sRC)⁴ = 1/(sRC)⁴ has gain 1 and phase 0° at ωo = 1/RC = 1.0 Mrad/s: fo = 1/(2πRC) = 159.2 kHz
(c) phasors of the four outputs for Vo1 = 1∠0°
problems.how: Each ideal integrator has Vo/Vi = −1/(sRC); four in a ring give T(s) = 1/(sRC)⁴, which equals +1 at s = jωo with ωo = 1/RC (the phase of each stage is +90°, 4 × 90° = 360°). The characteristic equation s⁴ = (1/RC)⁴ has the roots ±jωo (and ±ωo); checked numerically. Part (d) (amplitude-stabilisation design for about 2 V) is a design choice and is not solved here.
assume: Part (a) is a drawing: it is described in words.
Part (d) is an open design (no specific stabilisation network is prescribed) and is not answered.
The ideal integrator ring also has a real root +ωo (a growing mode); the oscillation criterion used is the Barkhausen condition of the book.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.34 (p.767): inverting integrator: input resistor R to the − input of the op amp, capacitor C in feedback, + input grounded (four of them are cascaded in a ring in this problem).

problems.text: Design a Schmitt trigger to have its switching thresholds centered at 1 V with a hysteresis of ±0.05 V, using the circuit topology in Fig. P12.111.
answer: Design equations (output 0 V / 5 V; node on the + input)
VL = 5·RB‖RF/(RA + RB‖RF) with output low, VH = VL + 5/(RF·G) with G = 1/RA + 1/RB + 1/RF
Choice RA = 10 kΩ (as in the figure)
upper 1.05 V, lower 0.95 V: centre 1.0 V, hysteresis ±0.05 V
problems.how: Fig. P12.111 topology: the + input is the node of RA (to the 5-V supply), RB (to ground) and RF (to the comparator output, 0 V or 5 V), the input signal is applied to the − input. With the output high the node voltage is VH, with the output low VL; centre 1 V and hysteresis ±0.05 V need VL = 0.95 V and VH = 1.05 V, which give RF = 9.5·RA and RB = RA/4.158.
assume: Only two conditions (centre, hysteresis) for three resistors: RA = 10 kΩ is chosen as in Fig. P12.111; the others follow (the nearest standard values should be chosen in practice).
The comparator output swings 0 V to 5 V (supply pins +5 V and ground in the figure).
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.111 (p.769): Schmitt trigger: comparator (supply 5 V and ground); + input node with 10 kΩ to a 5-V source, 15 kΩ to ground and 100 kΩ to the output; the signal vS on the − input.

problems.text: (a) Design an astable multivibrator to oscillate at a frequency of 1 kHz. Use the circuit in Fig. 12.60 with symmetric supplies of ±5 V. Assume that the total current from the op amp output must never exceed 1 mA. (b) If the resistors have ±5 percent tolerances and the capacitors have ±10 percent tolerances, what are the worst-case values of oscillation frequency? (c) If the power supplies are actually +4.75 and −5.25 V, what is the oscillation frequency for the nominal resistor and capacitor design values?
answer: (a) peak output current (when the output switches)
(c) supplies +4.75 V and −5.25 V, nominal components
T1 = RC ln[(1 + βVEE/VCC)/(1 − β)], T2 = RC ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − β)]: f = 999.0 Hz
problems.how: Astable multivibrator (Eqs. 12.91, 12.94, 12.95): T = T1 + T2 with T1 = RC·ln[(1 + βVEE/VCC)/(1 − β)], T2 = RC·ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − β)]; symmetric supplies: T = 2RC·ln[(1 + β)/(1 − β)]. The current limit is met at the switching instant, when the capacitor is at −βVEE. Worst case = extreme over the 16 corners of the tolerance box (confirmed by 2000 random sets); exact event-driven numerical simulation of the capacitor reproduces the period of the design and of case (c).
assume: The statement leaves free β, R and C: β = 0.5 with R1 = R2 = 12 kΩ and R = 15 kΩ is chosen (any other choice meeting the 1 mA limit works; only the product RC·ln[(1+β)/(1−β)] matters for the frequency).
"Worst-case" means the minimum and maximum frequency over the tolerance extremes of R1, R2, R (±5 %) and C (±10 %).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.60 (p.769): astable multivibrator: comparator (op amp) with positive-feedback divider R2 (from the output) and R1 (to ground) on the + input, and R from the output to the − input with C from the − input to ground; supplies VCC and −VEE.

problems.text: Two diodes are added the circuit Fig. P12.116 to convert it to a monostable multivibrator similar to the circuit in Fig. 12.62, and the power supplies are changed to ±7.5 V. What are the pulse width and recovery time of the monostable circuit?
answer: Pulse width T = RC·ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]
Recovery time Tr = RC·ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − VD/VEE)]
problems.how: Monostable multivibrator (Eqs. 12.100 and 12.101): the capacitor starts at −VD (clamped by D2), charges toward VCC until it reaches βVCC (pulse width T) and then discharges from βVCC toward −VEE until D2 clamps it at −VD again (recovery time Tr). Numerical event simulation of the two exponentials gives the same times. Anchor: the book's exercise (Fig. 12.64: VCC = VEE = 5 V, R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 18 kΩ, R = 11 kΩ, C = 2 nF) gives 20.4 μs and 33.4 μs between triggers, which the formulas reproduce with VD = 0.7 V.
assume: The diode on-voltage is not given: VD = 0.7 V is used (it reproduces the book's exercise 20.4 μs / 33.4 μs).
R1 = 15 kΩ (to ground) and R2 = 27 kΩ (feedback) read from Fig. P12.116, with R = 51 kΩ and C = 0.033 μF; the supplies are ±7.5 V.
problems.circuit: Fig. P12.116 (p.769): astable-multivibrator comparator (op amp with the output-switching symbol): + input with 15 kΩ to ground and 27 kΩ from the output; 51 kΩ from the output to the − input with 0.033 μF from the − input to ground; supply +12 V (changed to ±7.5 V in this problem) and two diodes added as in Fig. 12.62.

problems.text: Design a monostable multivibrator to have a pulse width of 20 μs and a recovery time of 5 μs. Use the circuit in Fig. 12.62 with ±5 V supplies.
answer: RC from T = RC·ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]
T = 20.0 μs, Tr = 5.0 μs; stability condition βVEE = 4.79 V > VD
problems.how: Two equations (Eqs. 12.100, 12.101) fix β and RC: the ratio T/Tr = ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)] / ln[(1 + βVCC/VEE)/(1 − VD/VEE)] = 4 gives β by root finding, then RC = T/ln[(1 + VD/VCC)/(1 − β)]. R, C and R1 are then free choices.
assume: VD = 0.7 V is used (it reproduces the book's exercise 20.4 μs / 33.4 μs).
The requirement T/Tr = 4 forces β close to 1 (about 0.95): R2 must be only about 5 % of R1, so the design is sensitive to resistor tolerance; C = 100 pF and R1 = 19 kΩ are example choices.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.62 (p.769): monostable multivibrator: comparator with divider R2 (from the output) and R1 (to ground) on the + input, R from the output to the − input with C from the − input to ground; trigger diode D1 and clamp diode D2 on the − input.

title.en: M02 · The operational amplifier: book calculations without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site) · part 1 of 5

note.vi: Example, Related Problem, Section Checkup và problem chẵn của Floyd, Example của Jaeger: sách không in đáp án các bài này (đáp án Related Problem của Floyd nằm trên website nhà xuất bản). Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập; với Example, kết quả còn được so với lời giải in trong sách. Related Problem được kèm đề của Example mà nó dựa vào. Thời gian là giả định (6 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: Floyd Examples, Related Problems, Section Checkups and even-numbered Problems, and Jaeger Examples: the book prints no answer for these (Floyd's Related Problem answers are on the publisher's website). The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: Given the op-amp configuration in Figure 12–22, determine the value of Rf required to produce a closed-loop voltage gain of −100.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: |Acl(I)| = Rf/Ri, so Rf = 100 × 2.2 kΩ = 220 kΩ (Ri = 2.2 kΩ is read from Figure 12–22).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–22 (p.618): inverting amplifier, Ri = 2.2 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, feedback resistor Rf (unknown) from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Determine the input and output impedances of the amplifier in Figure 12–25. The op-amp datasheet gives Zin = 2 MΩ, Zout = 75 Ω, and Aol = 200,000. (b) Find the closed-loop voltage gain.
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier (Floyd §12–5): B = Ri/(Ri + Rf), Zin(NI) = (1 + Aol·B)·Zin, Zout(NI) = Zout/(1 + Aol·B). The book prints 17.4 GΩ, 8.6 mΩ and 23.0.
assume: The exact nodal solution of the op-amp model gives Zin = 17.4 GΩ and Zout = 8.7 mΩ.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–25 (p.621): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 220 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 10 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

problems.text: Find the values of the input and output impedances in Figure 12–28. Also, determine the closed-loop voltage gain. The op-amp has the following parameters: Aol = 50,000; Zin = 4 MΩ; and Zout = 50 Ω.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier (Floyd §12–5): Zin(I) ≈ Ri, B = Ri/(Ri + Rf), Zout(I) = Zout/(1 + Aol·B), Acl(I) = −Rf/Ri.
assume: BOOK ERROR: the printed solution gives B = 1.0 kΩ/101 kΩ = 0.001, but 1/101 = 0.0099; with B = 0.001 it prints Zout(I) = 980 mΩ. The correct value is 50 Ω/(1 + 50,000 × 0.0099) = 0.101 Ω (an exact KCL solution of the op-amp model confirms it). Still “zero for all practical purposes”.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Determine Aol for the following values of f. Assume fc(ol) = 100 Hz and Aol(mid) = 100,000. (a) f = 0 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²) (Floyd §12–7).
assume: The book prints 99,503 for (b): it truncates 99,503.7.

problems.text: Calculate the phase shift for an RC lag circuit for each of the following frequencies, and then plot the curve of phase shift versus frequency. Assume fc = 100 Hz. (a) f = 1 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz (e) f = 10,000 Hz
problems.how: RC lag circuit: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc); plot θ against f on a log axis.

problems.text: A certain op-amp has three internal amplifier stages with the following gains and critical frequencies: Stage 1: Av1 = 40 dB, fc1 = 2 kHz Stage 2: Av2 = 32 dB, fc2 = 40 kHz Stage 3: Av3 = 20 dB, fc3 = 150 kHz Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
answer: Total phase lag at f = fc1
problems.how: Stage gains add in dB; the phase lags of the stages add: −tan⁻¹(f/fc1) − tan⁻¹(f/fc2) − tan⁻¹(f/fc3).

problems.text: A certain amplifier has an open-loop midrange gain of 150,000 and an open-loop 3 dB bandwidth of 200 Hz. The attenuation (B) of the feedback loop is 0.002. What is the closed-loop bandwidth?
problems.how: Closed-loop bandwidth BWcl = BWol(1 + B·Aol(mid)) (Floyd §12–8).

problems.text: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth ( fT) of 3 MHz.
problems.how: BW(cl) = fT/|Acl| (Floyd Eq. 12–23): (a) Acl = 1 + 220 kΩ/3.3 kΩ = 67.7, (b) Acl = −47 kΩ/1.0 kΩ = −47. The book prints 44.3 kHz and 63.8 kHz.
assume: An exact single-pole solution gives 44.4 kHz and 62.5 kHz (the inverting amplifier's loop attenuation is 1/48 rather than 1/47, so the textbook value is about 2 % high).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–43 (p.635): (a) noninverting amplifier with Rf = 220 kΩ and Ri = 3.3 kΩ; (b) inverting amplifier with Rf = 47 kΩ and Ri = 1.0 kΩ.

problems.text: When a pulse is applied to an op-amp, the output voltage goes from −8 V to +7 V in 0.75 μs. What is the slew rate?
problems.ctx: Example 12–2: The output voltage of a certain op-amp appears as shown in Figure 12–12 in response to a step input. Determine the slew rate.
problems.how: ΔVout = +7 V − (−8 V) = 15 V in 0.75 μs.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–2, p.610 (PDF 628)

problems.text: If Rf in Figure 12–18 is increased to 150 kΩ, determine the closed-loop gain.
problems.ctx: Example 12–3: Determine the closed-loop voltage gain of the amplifier in Figure 12–18.
problems.how: Noninverting amplifier: Acl(NI) = 1 + Rf/Ri with Rf = 150 kΩ and Ri = 4.7 kΩ (read from Figure 12–18); the example gives 22.3 for Rf = 100 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–3, p.616 (PDF 634)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–18 (p.616): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 4.7 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: If Ri is changed to 2.7 kΩ in Figure 12–22, what value of Rf is required to produce a closed-loop gain with an absolute value of 25?
problems.ctx: Example 12–4: Given the op-amp configuration in Figure 12–22, determine the value of Rf required to produce a closed-loop voltage gain of −100.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–4, p.619 (PDF 637)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–22 (p.618): inverting amplifier, Ri = 2.2 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, feedback resistor Rf (unknown) from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: (a) Determine the input and output impedances in Figure 12–25 for op-amp datasheet values of Zin = 3.5 MΩ, Zout = 82 Ω, and Aol = 135,000. (b) Find Acl.
problems.ctx: Example 12–5: (a) Determine the input and output impedances of the amplifier in Figure 12–25. The op-amp datasheet gives Zin = 2 MΩ, Zout = 75 Ω, and Aol = 200,000. (b) Find the closed-loop voltage gain.
problems.how: Same circuit as Example 12–5 (Rf = 220 kΩ, Ri = 10 kΩ, so B = 0.0435) with the new op-amp values.
assume: Exact nodal solution: Zin = 20.5 GΩ, Zout = 14.0 mΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–5, p.622 (PDF 640)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–25 (p.621): noninverting amplifier, Rf = 220 kΩ from the output to the inverting input, Ri = 10 kΩ from the inverting input to ground, signal on the + input.

problems.text: Determine the input and output impedances and the closed-loop voltage gain in Figure 12–28. The op-amp parameters and circuit values are as follows: Aol = 100,000; Zin = 5 MΩ; Zout = 75 Ω; Ri = 560 Ω; and Rf = 82 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 12–7: Find the values of the input and output impedances in Figure 12–28. Also, determine the closed-loop voltage gain. The op-amp has the following parameters: Aol = 50,000; Zin = 4 MΩ; and Zout = 50 Ω.
problems.how: Same method as Example 12–7 with Ri = 560 Ω and Rf = 82 kΩ.
assume: Exact nodal solution: Zin = 560.8 Ω, Zout = 110.0 mΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–7, p.624 (PDF 642)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Find Aol for the following frequencies. Assume fc(ol) = 200 Hz and Aol(mid) = 80,000. (a) f = 2 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 2500 Hz
problems.ctx: Example 12–8: Determine Aol for the following values of f. Assume fc(ol) = 100 Hz and Aol(mid) = 100,000. (a) f = 0 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–8, p.630 (PDF 648)

problems.text: At what frequency, in this example, is the phase shift 60°?
problems.ctx: Example 12–9: Calculate the phase shift for an RC lag circuit for each of the following frequencies, and then plot the curve of phase shift versus frequency. Assume fc = 100 Hz. (a) f = 1 Hz (b) f = 10 Hz (c) f = 100 Hz (d) f = 1000 Hz (e) f = 10,000 Hz
problems.how: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc) = −60° ⇒ f = fc·tan 60°.
assume: fc = 100 Hz, as in Example 12–9.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–9, p.631 (PDF 649)

problems.text: The internal stages of a two-stage amplifier have the following characteristics: Av1 = 50 dB, Av2 = 25 dB, fc1 = 1500 Hz, and fc2 = 3000 Hz. Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
problems.ctx: Example 12–10: A certain op-amp has three internal amplifier stages with the following gains and critical frequencies: Stage 1: Av1 = 40 dB, fc1 = 2 kHz Stage 2: Av2 = 32 dB, fc2 = 40 kHz Stage 3: Av3 = 20 dB, fc3 = 150 kHz Determine the open-loop midrange gain in decibels and the total phase lag when f = fc1.
answer: Total phase lag at f = fc1
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–10, p.633 (PDF 651)

problems.text: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an Aol of 90 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth of 2 MHz.
problems.ctx: Example 12–12: Determine the bandwidth of each of the amplifiers in Figure 12–43. Both op-amps have an open-loop gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain bandwidth ( fT) of 3 MHz.
problems.how: Same amplifiers as Example 12–12 (Figure 12–43) with fT = 2 MHz; BW = fT/|Acl|. The open-loop gain (90 dB) only needs to exceed the closed-loop gain.
assume: Exact single-pole solution: 29.6 kHz and 41.7 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.12 Related Problem of Example 12–12, p.636 (PDF 654)
problems.circuit: Figure 12–43 (p.635): (a) noninverting amplifier with Rf = 220 kΩ and Ri = 3.3 kΩ; (b) inverting amplifier with Rf = 47 kΩ and Ri = 1.0 kΩ.

problems.text: Given that Rf = 100 kΩ; Ri = 2 kΩ; Aol = 120,000; Zin = 2 MΩ; and Zout = 60 Ω, what are Zin(I) and Zout(I) for an inverting amplifier configuration?
problems.how: Inverting amplifier (Floyd §12–4): Zin ≈ Ri; Zout(I) = Zout/(1 + B·Aol) with B = Ri/(Ri + Rf).
assume: Exact nodal solution gives Zin = 2.001 kΩ (the approximation Zin ≈ Ri is what the book uses).

problems.text: The upper critical frequency of a particular op-amp is 100 Hz. What is its open-loop 3 dB bandwidth?
problems.how: For a single-pole response starting at 0 Hz the open-loop 3 dB bandwidth equals the upper critical frequency fc(ol).
assume: The op-amp response is low-pass down to dc, so the bandwidth is fc(ol).

problems.text: If the individual stage gains of an op-amp are 20 dB and 30 dB, what is the total gain in decibels?
problems.how: Stage gains in dB add.

The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: If the individual phase lags are −49° and −5.2°, what is the total phase lag?
problems.how: Phase lags of the stages add: −49° + (−5.2°).

problems.text: A certain op-amp is used in a feedback configuration having a gain of 30 and a bandwidth of 100 kHz. If the external resistor values are changed to increase the gain to 60, what is the new bandwidth?
problems.how: Gain × bandwidth is constant: 30 × 100 kHz = 3 MHz, so at a gain of 60 the bandwidth is 3 MHz/60.
assume: The op-amp has a single-pole response (constant gain–bandwidth product).

problems.text: In Figure 12–28, if Rf is changed from 100 kΩ to 68 kΩ, the feedback attenuation will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
answer: Feedback attenuation B = Ri/(Ri + Rf): 100 kΩ → 68 kΩ
problems.how: B = Ri/(Ri + Rf) with Ri = 1.0 kΩ: a smaller Rf makes the divider ratio larger (0.0099 → 0.0145).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–28 (p.623): inverting amplifier, Ri = 1.0 kΩ in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Repeat Problem 19 for each circuit in Figure 12–69.
problems.how: Voltage follower: the feedback attenuation is B = 1, so Zin(VF) = (1 + Aol)·Zin and Zout(VF) = Zout/(1 + Aol) (Floyd §12–5, Eq. 12–17 and 12–18). Problem 19 asks the same for the noninverting amplifiers of Figure 12–68 (its printed answers 8.41 GΩ / 89.2 mΩ … follow the same formula).
assume: An exact KCL solution of the op-amp model agrees with the formulas to better than 0.1 %.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–69 (p.659): three voltage followers (output connected to the − input, signal on the + input). (a) Aol = 220,000, Zin = 6 MΩ, Zout = 100 Ω; (b) Aol = 100,000, Zin = 5 MΩ, Zout = 60 Ω; (c) Aol = 50,000, Zin = 800 kΩ, Zout = 75 Ω.

problems.text: A voltage-follower is driven by a voltage source with a source resistance of 75 Ω. (a) What value of compensating resistor is required for bias current, and where should the resistor be placed? (b) If the two input currents after compensation are 42 μA and 40 μA, what is the output error voltage?
answer: 75.0 Ω, in the feedback path (between the output and the inverting input)
problems.how: Bias-current compensation (Floyd §12–6): the resistor equals the resistance seen by the other input; the error is IOS × R.
assume: The two currents (42 μA and 40 μA) are the input currents after compensation: the error is the offset current × 75 Ω.

problems.text: A particular op-amp voltage-follower has an input offset voltage of 2 nV. What is the output error voltage?
problems.how: A voltage follower has unity gain, so the input offset voltage appears unchanged at the output.

problems.text: The midrange open-loop gain of a certain op-amp is 120 dB. Negative feedback reduces this gain by 50 dB. What is the closed-loop gain?
problems.how: Gains in dB subtract: 120 dB − 50 dB.

problems.text: An RC lag circuit has a critical frequency of 5 kHz. If the resistance value is 1.0 kΩ, what is XC when f = 3 kHz?
problems.how: RC lag circuit: XC = R at f = fc, and XC ∝ 1/f.

problems.text: The midrange open-loop gain of a certain op-amp is 80,000. If the open-loop critical frequency is 1 kHz, what is the open-loop gain at each of the following frequencies? (a) 100 Hz (b) 1 kHz (c) 10 kHz (d) 1 MHz
problems.how: Aol = Aol(mid)/√(1 + (f/fc(ol))²).

problems.text: An RC lag circuit has a critical frequency of 8.5 kHz. Determine the phase shift for each frequency and plot a graph of its phase angle versus frequency. (a) 100 Hz (b) 400 Hz (c) 850 Hz (d) 8.5 kHz (e) 25 kHz (f) 85 kHz
problems.how: θ = −tan⁻¹(f/fc) with fc = 8.5 kHz; plot θ against f on a log axis.

problems.text: A certain amplifier has an open-loop gain in midrange of 180,000 and an open-loop critical frequency of 1500 Hz. If the attenuation of the feedback path is 0.015, what is the closed-loop bandwidth?
problems.how: BWcl = fc(ol)(1 + B·Aol(mid)).

problems.text: Determine the effect on the output if the circuit in Figure 12–75 has the following fault (one fault at a time). (a) Output pin is shorted to the inverting input. (b) R3 is open. (c) R3 is 10 kΩ instead of 910 Ω. (d) R1 and R2 are swapped.
answer: (a) output pin shorted to the − input
Vout ≈ 0 V (≈ 37.0 nV for Vin = 100 mV, Aol = 200,000, Zout = 75 Ω): the op-amp holds the − input at the + input voltage (0 V) and sinks the source current Vin/R1 = 0.1 mA; no signal at the output
The + input has no dc path: its bias current charges the stray capacitance until the output drives into saturation at one supply rail; the ac gain (−10) is not available
Gain unchanged (−10); a dc offset appears: Vout(dc) = Ib·[R2 − R3(1 + R2/R1)] = -8.0 mV for Ib = 80 nA (instead of -0.8 μV with 910 Ω)
Gain becomes −R2/R1 = −1.0 kΩ/10 kΩ = -0.1 instead of -10.0: the output is 100 times smaller (still inverted); 100 mV in gives -10.0 mV
problems.how: Inverting amplifier with bias compensation (R3 ≈ R1 ‖ R2 = 909 Ω). Effects obtained from the ideal gain −R2/R1 and from the dc error of the input bias current, Vout(dc) = Ib·[R2 − R3(1 + R2/R1)] (exact nodal solution used as check).
assume: Ib = 80 nA is the typical LM741 value of Figure 12–77 (an assumption: the statement gives no op-amp); both inputs are taken to draw the same bias current.
The statement gives no input signal for this problem; Problem 41 uses 100 mV, which is used here only for the numbers of (a) and (d).
problems.circuit: Figure 12–75 (p.662): inverting amplifier, R1 = 1.0 kΩ from the input to the − input, R2 = 10 kΩ from the output to the − input, R3 = 910 Ω from the + input to ground (bias-current compensation).

problems.text: Refer to the partial datasheet in Figure 12–77. Determine the input impedances of a LM741 op-amp connected as an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop voltage gain of 100 and Rf = 100 kΩ.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: Ri = Rf/|Acl| = 1.0 kΩ and Zin(I) ≈ Ri (Floyd §12–5). The LM741 typical input resistance (2.0 MΩ, datasheet Figure 12–77) only matters for the noninverting configuration, where Zin(NI) = (1 + Aol·B)·Zin.
assume: Exact KCL solution with Aol = 200,000 and Zin = 2 MΩ gives 1.001 kΩ, i.e. Ri to 0.1 %.
The statement says “input impedances” (plural); the only input impedance of the inverting amplifier is Zin(I) ≈ Ri.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–77 (p.664): partial LM741 datasheet, “LM741” column, typical values: input resistance 2.0 MΩ, large-signal voltage gain 200 V/mV (200,000), slew rate 0.5 V/μs, input bias current 80 nA.

problems.text: Refer to Figure 12–77. How long does it typically take the output voltage of an LM741 to make a transition from −8 V to +8 V in response to a step input?
answer: Time for a −8 V → +8 V step at the slew rate
problems.how: Slew rate = ΔVout/Δt, so Δt = 16 V/(0.5 V/μs) = 32 μs (typical LM741 slew rate, Figure 12–77, unity gain).
assume: Slew-rate limited transition; the rise time of the small-signal response (0.3 μs typ) is much shorter.
problems.circuit: Figure 12–77 (p.664): partial LM741 datasheet; LM741 column, typical slew rate 0.5 V/μs (TA = 25 °C, unity gain).

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier using a 741 op-amp. The voltage gain must be 68 ± 5% and the input impedance must be approximately 10 kΩ. Include bias current compensation.
answer: Compensating resistor Rc = Ri‖Rf at the + input
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: |Av| = Rf/Ri, Zin ≈ Ri (Floyd §12–4); bias compensation Rc = Ri‖Rf (§12–6).
assume: One valid design (several are possible): the book's even-numbered problems have no printed answer.
Aol of the 741 taken as 200,000 for the check.

problems.text: What is the maximum closed-loop voltage gain that can be achieved with a 741 op-amp if the bandwidth must be no less than 5 kHz?
problems.how: Gain × bandwidth = fT: with BW ≥ 5 kHz the closed-loop gain cannot exceed fT/5 kHz.
assume: 741 unity-gain bandwidth fT = 1 MHz (typical datasheet value; the book's datasheet figure is an image).

problems.text: Calculate the voltage gain for an amplifier with the following parameters: A = 100, Rid = 100 kΩ, and Ro = 100 Ω, with RI = 10 kΩ and RL = 1000 Ω. Express the result in dB.
problems.how: Voltage gain of the differential amplifier model including the source resistance RI and the load RL (Jaeger Eq. 10.33).

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier (i.e., choose the values of R1 and R2) to have an input resistance of 20 kΩ and a gain of 40 dB.
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier: Rin = R1, Av = −R2/R1.
assume: Ideal op amp.

problems.text: Find the voltage gain Av, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.22 if R1 = 3 kΩ, R2 = 43 kΩ, and vi = +0.1 V.
problems.how: Ideal noninverting amplifier (Eq. 10.53): Av = 1 + R2/R1; the input current is zero, so the output current flows only through R2 + R1. The exact nodal solution gives the same vo and io.
assume: Ideal op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.22 (p.547): noninverting amplifier: vi on the + input, R2 from the output to the − input, R1 from the − input to ground; R1 = 3 kΩ, R2 = 43 kΩ, vi = +0.1 V.

problems.text: Find the values of VO, V+, V−, I1, I2, and IO for the difference amplifier in Fig. 10.25 with V1 = 5 V, V2 = 3 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, and R2 = 100 kΩ.
problems.how: Ideal difference amplifier: V+ from the divider on V2, V− = V+, I1 from Ohm's law on R1, VO from KVL around R1 and R2; check: VO = −(R2/R1)(V1 − V2) = −20 V. Exact nodal solution agrees.
assume: Ideal op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.25 (p.554): difference amplifier: V1 through R1 to the − input with R2 feedback; V2 through R1 to the + input with R2 to ground; V1 = 5 V, V2 = 3 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ.

note.en: Floyd Examples, Related Problems, Section Checkups and even-numbered Problems, and Jaeger Examples: the book prints no answer for these (Floyd's Related Problem answers are on the publisher's website). The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is designed to have a gain of 200 (46 dB) and is built using an operational amplifier with an open-loop gain of 80 dB. Find the values of the ideal gain, the actual gain, and the gain error. Express the gain error in percent.
problems.how: Finite open-loop gain: Av = Aideal·T/(1 + T), FGE = 1/(1 + T) (Jaeger §11.2).
assume: The op amp is ideal except for its finite open-loop gain A = 10,000 (80 dB).

problems.text: A noninverting amplifier is constructed with R1 = 1 kΩ and R2 = 39 kΩ using an operational amplifier with an open-loop gain of 80 dB and an output resistance of 50 Ω. Find the output resistance of the noninverting amplifier.
problems.how: Output resistance of the noninverting amplifier (Jaeger Eq. 11.25).
assume: The op amp is ideal except for finite A and nonzero Ro.
The book prints 0.198 Ω after “0.199 Ω ‖ 40 kΩ”; 50/251 = 0.1992 and the 40 kΩ in parallel changes nothing visible, so 0.199 Ω is the value (the book's last digit is a small arithmetic slip).

problems.text: Design a noninverting amplifier to have a gain of 35 dB and an output resistance of no more than 0.2 Ω. The only op amp available has an output resistance of 250 Ω. What is the minimum open-loop gain of the op amp that will meet the design requirements?
problems.how: Rout = Ro/(1 + Aβ) ≤ 0.2 Ω (Jaeger Eq. 11.26).
assume: The book rounds A to 7.03 × 10⁴ using 56.2; the exact value is 7.02 × 10⁴.

problems.text: The noninverting amplifier in Fig. 11.6 is built with an op amp having an input resistance of 2 MΩ and an open-loop gain of 90 dB. What is the amplifier input resistance if R1 = 20 kΩ and R2 = 510 kΩ?
problems.how: Eq. (11.31) for the series-shunt noninverting amplifier: Rin = Rid(1 + Aβ). The exact nodal solution of the circuit (Rid between the inputs) gives 2.39 GΩ; the small difference is the loading of Rid by R1‖R2, which the formula neglects.
assume: Op amp ideal except for the finite gain A = 90 dB and Rid = 2 MΩ (Ro = 0).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.6 (p.599): noninverting amplifier with a finite-gain op amp having input resistance Rid between the inputs: vx on the + input, R2 from the output to the − input, R1 from the − input to ground.

problems.text: Suppose the amplifier in Fig. 11.32 has |VOS| ≤3 mV and R2 and R1 are 99 kΩ and 1.2 kΩ, respectively. What is the quiescent dc voltage at the amplifier output?
answer: Range (the sign of VOS is not known)
problems.how: Offset of an otherwise ideal noninverting amplifier (Eq. 11.95): the offset voltage is amplified by the noninverting gain 1 + R2/R1 = 83.5. The exact nodal solution (offset source at the + input) agrees.
assume: The sign of VOS is not specified (only |VOS| ≤ 3 mV), so only the range is known.
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.32 (p.631): noninverting amplifier with the input grounded (vI = 0) and the op-amp offset voltage VOS modelled in series with the + input; R2 = 99 kΩ from the output to the − input, R1 = 1.2 kΩ from the − input to ground.

problems.text: The amplifier in Fig. 11.39 is to be designed to have a gain of 20 dB and must develop a peak output voltage of at least 10 V when connected to a minimum load resistance of 5 kΩ. The op amp output current specification states that the output current must be less than 2.5 mA. Choose acceptable values of R1 and R2 from the table of 5 percent resistor values in Appendix A.
answer: Load of the op amp for |vO| = 10 V: REQ = 10 V/2.5 mA
4 kΩ; with RL ≥ 5 kΩ the feedback resistor must satisfy RL‖R2 ≥ 4 kΩ, i.e. R2 ≥ 20 kΩ
problems.how: The op amp supplies the load current and the current in the feedback network: IO = vO/RL + vO/(R1 + R2). With RL = 5 kΩ the current limit forces R2 ≥ 20 kΩ; a gain of 10 sets R2 = 10·R1; R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ keeps Rin high. The exact nodal solution gives vO = 10 V and IO = 2.09 mA.
assume: Design example: several resistor pairs are acceptable (the book chooses 10 kΩ and 100 kΩ).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.39 (p.635): inverting amplifier: input resistor R1 to the − input, feedback R2, load RL = 5 kΩ at the output, + input grounded.

problems.text: Suppose the amplifier in Fig. 11.40 has a differential-mode gain of 2500 and a CMRR of 80 dB. What is the output voltage if V1 = 5.001 V and V2 = 4.999 V? What is the error introduced by the finite CMRR?
problems.how: Eq. (11.110): vO = A_d·vid + A_cm·vic with A_cm = A_d/CMRR. The common-mode term 2500·5.000/10⁴ = 1.25 V is a 25 % error.
assume: CMRR = +10⁴ (the sign of the CMRR is not specified, the book assumes +).
problems.circuit: Fig. 11.40 (p.640): differential amplifier with inputs V1 and V2 and differential gain A = 2500 (finite common-mode rejection).

problems.text: Calculate the gain error for a voltage follower that is built using an op amp with an open-loop gain of 80 dB and a CMRR of 60 dB.
problems.how: Voltage-follower gain error with finite gain and finite CMRR (Jaeger Eq. 12.38).
assume: CMRR = 60 dB = 1000.

problems.text: An op amp has a dc gain of 100 dB and a unity-gain frequency of 10 MHz. (a) What is the bandwidth of the op amp? (b) If the op amp is used to build a noninverting amplifier with a closedloop gain of 60 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? (c) Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. (d) Write an expression for the transfer function of the noninverting amplifier.
problems.how: Single-pole op amp: Av(s) = Ao·ωB/(s + ωB) with ωB = 2π·fT/Ao; closed loop: pole moves to ωB(1 + Ao·β).

problems.text: Anopamphasadcgainof200,000andaunity-gainfrequencyof500kHz.(a)Whatisthecutofffrequency of the op amp? (b) If the op amp is used to build an inverting amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 40 dB, what is the bandwidth of the feedback amplifier? (c) Write an expression for the transfer function of the op amp. (d) Write an expression for the transfer function of the inverting amplifier.
problems.how: Inverting amplifier: Av(s) = −(R2/R1)·Aoβ·ωB/(s + ωB(1 + Aoβ)), with the feedback factor β = 1/(1 + |Av|).
assume: Closed-loop gain 40 dB means |Av(0)| = 100.
