problems.text: The input signal in Figure 13–3(a) is applied to the comparator in Figure 13–3(b). Draw the output showing its proper relationship to the input signal. Assume the maximum output levels of the comparator are ±14 V.
answer: Reference voltage VREF = R2/(R1 + R2)·(+15 V)
+14.0 V whenever Vin > 1.63 V and −14.0 V whenever Vin < 1.63 V: a rectangular wave that is high for 39.4 % of each cycle of the ±5 V sine (switching at 19.0° and 161.0°)
problems.how: Zero-level detector shifted by the divider reference (Floyd §13–1); the output switches between the saturated levels ±14 V each time Vin crosses VREF. The book prints VREF = 1.63 V and draws the output in Figure 13–4.
assume: The duty cycle (39 %) is derived here; the book only draws the waveform.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–3 (p.670): (a) a sine wave Vin of 5 V peak (−5 V to +5 V); (b) an op-amp comparator with Vin on the + input and the reference on the − input, taken from a divider between +15 V and ground: R1 = 8.2 kΩ (from +15 V) and R2 = 1.0 kΩ (to ground).

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points for the comparator circuit in Figure 13–9. Assume that +Vout(max) = +5 V and − Vout(max) = −5 V.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 13–1/13–2; swept the input up and down in a state machine to find the switching points (independent check).
problems.circuit: Figure 13–9 (p.673): comparator with positive feedback (Floyd Fig. 13–7 arrangement): Vin on the − input, R1 from the output to the + input, R2 from the + input to ground; in Example 13–2 R1 = R2 = 100 kΩ.

problems.text: Determine the binary number sequence of the three-digit simultaneous ADC in Figure 13–16 for the input signal in Figure 13–17 and the sampling pulses (encoder enable) shown. Draw the resulting digital output waveforms.
answer: Comparator references (R-ladder, 8 equal resistors, VREF = 8 V)
Binary output sequence (D2 D1 D0) for the 12 samples
problems.how: A flash ADC with a ladder of 8 equal resistors: comparator k switches on when Vin exceeds k·VREF/8; the priority encoder outputs the number of the highest comparator that is on, i.e. floor(Vin/LSB). With VREF = 8 V the LSB is 1 V.
assume: The 12 sample values (3.7, 5.2, 6.2, 6.6, 4.7, 1.7, 0.6, 1.0, 2.7, 5.0, 6.6, 7.2 V) are read from the dots of Figure 13–17 to about ±0.1 V; samples 8 and 10 lie on a comparator threshold, where the book's code (001 and 101) is used.
VREF = 8 V is implied by the 0–8 V axis of Figure 13–17 and the printed codes (not stated in the example).
problems.circuit: Figures 13–16 and 13–17 (pp.677–678): a three-digit simultaneous (flash) ADC: a resistor ladder of 8 equal resistors R from VREF to ground gives 7 reference voltages to 7 op-amp comparators (Vin on the + inputs); a priority encoder (inputs 1–7, enable input) outputs D2D1D0. Vin is an analog waveform between 0 and 8 V sampled by 12 enable pulses.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage of the DAC in Figure 13–27(a). The sequence of fourdigit binary codes represented by the waveforms in Figure 13–27(b) are applied to the inputs. A high level is a binary 1, and a low level is a binary 0. The least significant binary digit is D0.
answer: Contribution of each bit (D0, D1, D2, D3) = −Rf·5 V/Rk
a staircase from 0 V to -3.75 V in steps of -0.25 V
problems.how: Binary-weighted scaling adder: the − input is a virtual ground, so each 1 sends 5 V/Rk through Rf (Floyd §13–2). The book prints −0.25, −0.5, −1, −2 V per bit and the 0 to −3.75 V staircase (Figure 13–28).
assume: All 16 codes were also solved by KCL with a finite open-loop gain.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–27 (p.684): four-digit binary-weighted DAC (scaling adder): input resistors D0 = 200 kΩ, D1 = 100 kΩ, D2 = 50 kΩ, D3 = 25 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded; a binary 1 is +5 V and a 0 is 0 V. The input waveforms D0…D3 form the straight binary count 0000 to 1111.

problems.text: (a) Determine the rate of change of the output voltage in response to the input square wave, as shown for the ideal integrator in Figure 13–35(a). The output voltage is initially zero. The pulse width is 100 μs. (b) Describe the output and draw the waveform.
answer: Rate of change of Vout, Vin = +2.5 V
a triangular wave between 0 V and −5 V (5 V peak-to-peak): a falling ramp while the input is +2.5 V and a rising ramp while it is −2.5 V; ΔVout = 25 mV/μs × 200 μs = 5 V
problems.how: Ideal integrator: ΔVout/Δt = −Vin/(Ri·C) = −2.5 V/(10 kΩ × 0.01 μF) = −25 mV/μs (Floyd §13–3).
assume: BOOK INCONSISTENCY: the statement says “the pulse width is 100 μs”, but Figure 13–35(b) and the printed solution use 200 μs per half-period (ΔVout = 25 mV/μs × 200 μs = 5 V). With literally 100 μs the output would swing only 2.5 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–35 (p.690): ideal integrator, Ri = 10 kΩ from the input to the − input, C = 0.01 μF from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a square wave between −2.5 V and +2.5 V; in the drawing each half-period is 200 μs.

problems.text: Determine the reference voltage in Figure 13–3 if R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 3.3 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 13–1: The input signal in Figure 13–3(a) is applied to the comparator in Figure 13–3(b). Draw the output showing its proper relationship to the input signal. Assume the maximum output levels of the comparator are ±14 V.
answer: Reference voltage VREF = R2/(R1 + R2)·(+15 V)
problems.how: Same divider as Figure 13–3(b) with R1 = 22 kΩ and R2 = 3.3 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–1, p.670 (PDF 688)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–3 (p.670): (a) a sine wave Vin of 5 V peak (−5 V to +5 V); (b) an op-amp comparator with Vin on the + input and the reference on the − input, taken from a divider between +15 V and ground: R1 = 8.2 kΩ (from +15 V) and R2 = 1.0 kΩ (to ground).

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points in Figure 13–9 for R1 = 68 kΩ and R2 = 82 kΩ. Also assume the maximum output voltage levels are now ±7 V.
problems.ctx: Example 13–2: Determine the upper and lower trigger points for the comparator circuit in Figure 13–9. Assume that +Vout(max) = +5 V and − Vout(max) = −5 V.
problems.how: Same circuit as Figure 13–9 with R1 = 68 kΩ, R2 = 82 kΩ and ±7 V output levels.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–2, p.673 (PDF 691)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–9 (p.673): comparator with positive feedback (Floyd Fig. 13–7 arrangement): Vin on the − input, R1 from the output to the + input, R2 from the + input to ground; in Example 13–2 R1 = R2 = 100 kΩ.

problems.text: Determine the upper and lower trigger points for Figure 13–13 if R1 = 150 kΩ, R2 = 68 kΩ, and the zener diodes are 3.3 V devices.
problems.ctx: Example 13–3: Determine the output voltage waveform for Figure 13–13.
answer: Voltage across the zener pair Vb = VZ + 0.7 V
problems.how: Example 13–3 method: the − input stands at Vout ∓ Vb and equals the + input voltage, so Vout − Vb = Vout·R2/(R1 + R2); hence Vout = Vb(R1 + R2)/R1 and VUTP = Vb·R2/R1. The same formulas give the book's ±7.94 V and ±2.54 V for 4.7 V zeners, 100 kΩ and 47 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–3, p.676 (PDF 694)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–13 (p.675): comparator with hysteresis and zener bounding: Vin (a ±5 V sine) through Ri to the − input; D1 and D2, two zener diodes in series (4.7 V each in the book example), between the − input and the output; R1 = 100 kΩ from the output to the + input and R2 = 47 kΩ from the + input to ground. One zener is always forward biased (0.7 V) while the other is in breakdown.

problems.text: If a fourth input of −0.5 V is added to Figure 13–22 with a 10 kΩ resistor, what is the output voltage?
problems.ctx: Example 13–5: Determine the output voltage in Figure 13–22.
problems.how: All input resistors and Rf are 10 kΩ, so the gain is −1 for every input and the output is the inverted sum: −(3 + 1 + 8 − 0.5) V.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–5, p.680 (PDF 698)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–22 (p.680): inverting summing amplifier, three inputs VIN1 = +3 V, VIN2 = +1 V, VIN3 = +8 V, each through 10 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded. Book result −12 V.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage in Figure 13–23 if the two input resistors are 2.2 kΩ and the feedback resistor is 18 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 13–6: Determine the output voltage for the summing amplifier in Figure 13–23.
problems.how: Figure 13–23 with VIN1 = 0.2 V and VIN2 = 0.5 V; R1 = R2 = 2.2 kΩ, Rf = 18 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–6, p.681 (PDF 699)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–23 (p.681): summing amplifier with VIN1 = 0.2 V and VIN2 = 0.5 V through R1 = R2 = 1.0 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded (book result −7 V).

problems.text: Determine the weight of each input voltage in Figure 13–25 if R1 = 22 kΩ, R2 = 82 kΩ, R3 = 56 kΩ, and Rf = 10 kΩ. Also find VOUT.
problems.ctx: Example 13–8: Determine the weight of each input voltage for the scaling adder in Figure 13–25 and find the output voltage.
problems.how: Scaling adder: the weight of each input is Rf/Rk; the inputs of Example 13–8 are +3 V, +2 V and +8 V (Figure 13–25).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–8, p.683 (PDF 701)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–25 (p.683): scaling adder, VIN1 = +3 V through R1, VIN2 = +2 V through R2, VIN3 = +8 V through R3, Rf = 10 kΩ; in Example 13–8 R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ (VOUT = −8.84 V).

problems.text: If the 200 kΩ resistor in Figure 13–27(a) is changed to 400 kΩ, would the other resistor values have to be changed? If so, specify the values.
problems.ctx: Example 13–9: Determine the output voltage of the DAC in Figure 13–27(a). The sequence of fourdigit binary codes represented by the waveforms in Figure 13–27(b) are applied to the inputs. A high level is a binary 1, and a low level is a binary 0. The least significant binary digit is D0.
answer: Do the other resistors have to change?
Yes. Binary weighting needs R(D0) : R(D1) : R(D2) : R(D3) = 8 : 4 : 2 : 1, so with 400 kΩ for D0 the others must be 200 kΩ, 100 kΩ and 50 kΩ (all doubled)
Effect of changing only D0 to 400 kΩ
D0 would count 1/4 as much as D1 instead of 1/2: code 0001 → -0.125 V, 0010 → -0.5 V, 0011 → -0.625 V: the staircase is no longer uniform
Output step after doubling all four input resistors (Rf = 10 kΩ)
−0.125 V per count (0 to −1.875 V); Rf = 20 kΩ restores −0.25 V per count (0 to −3.75 V)
problems.how: The weight of an input is Rf/Rk; for a binary DAC the weights must be in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4 : 8, so all the input resistors scale together (Floyd §13–2).
assume: The statement does not say whether the original output step (−0.25 V) must be kept; both options are given.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–9, p.685 (PDF 703)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–27 (p.684): four-digit binary-weighted DAC (scaling adder): input resistors D0 = 200 kΩ, D1 = 100 kΩ, D2 = 50 kΩ, D3 = 25 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 10 kΩ, + input grounded; a binary 1 is +5 V and a 0 is 0 V. The input waveforms D0…D3 form the straight binary count 0000 to 1111.

problems.text: Modify the integrator in Figure 13–35 to make the output change from 0 to −5 V in 100 μs with the same input.
problems.ctx: Example 13–10: (a) Determine the rate of change of the output voltage in response to the input square wave, as shown for the ideal integrator in Figure 13–35(a). The output voltage is initially zero. The pulse width is 100 μs. (b) Describe the output and draw the waveform.
answer: C for 0 → −5 V in 100 μs with Ri = 10 kΩ, Vin = 2.5 V
problems.how: The slope must be 5 V/100 μs = 50 mV/μs = Vin/(Ri·C), so Ri·C = 2.5 V/(50 mV/μs) = 50 μs: halve the time constant (C = 5 nF with Ri = 10 kΩ, or Ri = 5 kΩ with C = 0.01 μF).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–10, p.690 (PDF 708)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–35 (p.690): ideal integrator, Ri = 10 kΩ from the input to the − input, C = 0.01 μF from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a square wave between −2.5 V and +2.5 V; in the drawing each half-period is 200 μs.

problems.text: What would the output voltage be if the feedback resistor in Figure 13–40 is changed to 3.3 kΩ?
problems.ctx: Example 13–11: Determine the output voltage of the ideal op-amp differentiator in Figure 13–40 for the triangular-wave input shown.
answer: Vout during the rising ramp / falling ramp
problems.how: Differentiator: Vout = −Rf·C·(ΔVin/Δt) = −(3.3 μs)(2 V/μs) = −6.6 V on the rising ramp (the book gets −4.4 V for Rf = 2.2 kΩ).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–11, p.693 (PDF 711)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–40 (p.692): ideal op-amp differentiator, C = 0.001 μF in series with the input to the − input, Rf = 2.2 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded. Vin is a triangular wave between −5 V and +5 V, 5 μs per ramp (10 μs period).

problems.text: In Figure 13–47, R5 = 47 kΩ. What is the output voltage if R1 opens?
problems.ctx: Example 13–13: (a) What is the normal output voltage in Figure 13–47? (b) What is the output voltage if R2 opens? (c) What happens if R5 opens?
problems.how: With R1 open the 1 V input is disconnected; the remaining inputs are amplified by −Rf/R = −47 kΩ/10 kΩ = −4.7.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.13 Related Problem of Example 13–13, p.697 (PDF 715)
problems.circuit: Figure 13–47 (p.697): summing amplifier, four inputs VIN1 = 1 V, VIN2 = 0.5 V, VIN3 = 0.2 V, VIN4 = 0.1 V, each through 10 kΩ (R1…R4) to the − input, feedback R5 = 10 kΩ in the book example (−1.8 V).

problems.text: A certain scaling adder has two inputs, one having twice the weight of the other. If the resistor value for the lower-weighted input is 10 kΩ, what is the value of the other input resistor?
problems.how: In a scaling adder the weight of an input is Rf/Rk, so twice the weight needs half the resistance: 10 kΩ/2.
assume: The lower-weighted input has the larger resistor (10 kΩ).

problems.text: If VIN2 is changed to −1 V in Figure 13–22, the output voltage will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
problems.how: VOUT = −(VIN1 + VIN2 + VIN3): VIN2 falls from +1 V to −1 V, the sum falls from 12 V to 10 V and VOUT rises from −12 V to −10 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–22 (p.680): inverting summing amplifier, VIN1 = +3 V, VIN2 = +1 V, VIN3 = +8 V, three 10 kΩ input resistors, Rf = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: If VIN3 is changed to −7 V in Figure 13–24, the output voltage will (a) increase (b) decrease (c) not change
problems.how: Averaging amplifier, Rf/R = 1/4: VOUT = −(1/4)(VIN1 + VIN2 + VIN3 + VIN4); the sum drops from 10 V to 0 V, so VOUT goes from −2.5 V to 0 V.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–24 (p.682): averaging amplifier, four inputs VIN1…VIN4 = +1, +2, +3, +4 V each through 100 kΩ to the − input, Rf = 25 kΩ, + input grounded (book result −2.5 V).

problems.text: The waveforms given in Figure 13–71(a) are observed at the indicated points in Figure 13–71(b). Is the circuit operating properly? If not, what is a likely fault?
answer: Healthy circuit (zener pair drop Vb = 4.3 + 0.7 = 5.0 V)
Vout = ±10.0 V, VC = ±5.0 V: it should switch between +10 V and −10 V with trigger points ±5 V
VB = +10 V / −1.4 V and VC = +5 V / −0.7 V: the positive half is correct, the negative half is not

One of the zener diodes is shorted (the one that should be in breakdown when the output is negative): the negative output is then limited by a single 0.7 V junction, giving Vb = 0.7 V, Vout = −2·0.7 = -1.4 V and VC = −0.7 V, exactly the observed values
problems.how: Zener-bounded comparator with hysteresis (Example 13–3): Vout = ±Vb(R1 + R2)/R1 and VUTP/VLTP = ±Vb·R2/R1 with Vb = VZ + 0.7 V. The observed negative levels fit Vb = 0.7 V, i.e. one zener replaced by a short.
assume: An open zener would stop the output from switching to that level at all; the observation shows a limited negative level, so a short is more consistent.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–71 (p.715): (b) a comparator with hysteresis and zener bounding (Figure 13–13 type): input A through Ri = 100 kΩ to the − input, two 4.3 V zeners D1 and D2 in series between the − input (node) and the output B, R1 = 10 kΩ from B to the + input (node C) and R2 = 10 kΩ from C to ground. (a) the observed waveforms: VA a ±6 V sine; VB switches between +10 V and −1.4 V; VC between +5 V and −0.7 V; the output switches high when VA falls to −0.7 V and low when VA reaches +5 V.

problems.text: Assume that a 1.0 kΩ resistor is inadvertently used for R1 in Figure 13–50. What effect does this have on the circuit operation?
answer: Reference range with R1 = R3 = 56 kΩ (as drawn)
Effect on the duty cycle (10 V peak sine)

minimum 0 % (the reference exceeds the 10 V peak, so over the top 9.08 % of the potentiometer travel the output never goes high), maximum 90.8 % instead of 93.7 %: the range is no longer symmetrical and part of the control is wasted
problems.how: Reference voltage = +12 V − I·(R1 + x·R2) with I = 24 V/(R1 + R2 + R3); the pulse is high while the sine exceeds the reference, duty = (π − 2·asin(Vref/Vp))/(2π). The 10 V peak sine of Problem 27 is used (Application Activity text).
assume: The effect is derived here (the book gives no answer for this even-numbered problem); the duty cycles are computed by sampling the sine wave.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–50 (p.700): sine/pulse generator: a 10 V peak sine wave goes to the + input of an LM111 comparator; the − input is the wiper of a 500 kΩ potentiometer R2 between R1 = 56 kΩ (to +12 V) and R3 = 56 kΩ (to −12 V); output pulled up to +5 V by R4 = 1 kΩ.

problems.text: Redesign the circuit in Figure 13–50 for a 5 V peak sine wave.
answer: Required reference range (same 98 % of the sine peak as the original)
R1 = R3 for that range (R2 = 500 kΩ, ±12 V supplies)
362.0 kΩ (standard value 360 kΩ gives ±4.92 V and a duty-cycle range of 5.77 % … 94.2 %)
problems.how: The reference at the ends of the potentiometer is ±(12 V − I·R1) with I = 24 V/(2R1 + R2). The original design (R1 = 56 kΩ) gives ±9.8 V for a 10 V peak sine (duty 6.4 %–93.6 %); for a 5 V peak sine the same fractions need ±4.9 V.
assume: A design problem: the book prints no answer. Assumed: the pot R2 = 500 kΩ and the ±12 V supplies stay, only R1 = R3 change, and the duty range of the original design is kept (the pulse spec of Table 13–1 is 15 %–85 %, which any R1 above this value also meets).
Another valid design would change R2 or the supply instead.
problems.circuit: Figure 13–50 (p.700): sine/pulse generator: 10 V peak sine on the + input of an LM111; − input from the wiper of a 500 kΩ potentiometer R2 between R1 = 56 kΩ (to +12 V) and R3 = 56 kΩ (to −12 V); R4 = 1 kΩ pull-up to +5 V.

problems.text: Design an inverting amplifier (i.e., choose the values of R1 and R2) to have an input resistance of 20 kΩ and a gain of 40 dB.
problems.how: Ideal inverting amplifier: Rin = R1, Av = −R2/R1.
assume: Ideal op amp.

problems.text: Find the voltage gain Av, output voltage vo, and output current io for the amplifier in Fig. 10.22 if R1 = 3 kΩ, R2 = 43 kΩ, and vi = +0.1 V.
problems.how: Ideal noninverting amplifier (Eq. 10.53): Av = 1 + R2/R1; the input current is zero, so the output current flows only through R2 + R1. The exact nodal solution gives the same vo and io.
assume: Ideal op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.22 (p.547): noninverting amplifier: vi on the + input, R2 from the output to the − input, R1 from the − input to ground; R1 = 3 kΩ, R2 = 43 kΩ, vi = +0.1 V.

problems.text: Find the values of VO, V+, V−, I1, I2, and IO for the difference amplifier in Fig. 10.25 with V1 = 5 V, V2 = 3 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, and R2 = 100 kΩ.
problems.how: Ideal difference amplifier: V+ from the divider on V2, V− = V+, I1 from Ohm's law on R1, VO from KVL around R1 and R2; check: VO = −(R2/R1)(V1 − V2) = −20 V. Exact nodal solution agrees.
assume: Ideal op amp.
problems.circuit: Fig. 10.25 (p.554): difference amplifier: V1 through R1 to the − input with R2 feedback; V2 through R1 to the + input with R2 to ground; V1 = 5 V, V2 = 3 V, R1 = 10 kΩ, R2 = 100 kΩ.

problems.text: Find the magnitude and phase of this voltage transfer function for ω = 0 and ω = 3 rad/s.
problems.ctx: Transfer function of the example: Av(s) = 50(s² + 4)/(s² + 2s + 2).
problems.how: Substitute s = jω and take magnitude and phase of the complex number.

problems.text: Design an active low-pass filter (choose the values of R1, R2, andC) with fH = 2 kHz, Rin = 5 kΩ, and Av = 40 dB.
answer: With standard values R1 = 5.1 kΩ, R2 = 510 kΩ, C = 160 pF
problems.how: Active low-pass filter: inverting amplifier with C in parallel with R2; Rin = R1, |Av| = R2/R1, fH = 1/(2π·R2·C).
assume: Standard values are the nearest of the Appendix A tables, as in the book.

problems.text: Calculate the base-to-collector voltage gain of the amplifier in Figure 6–16 when a load resistance of 5 kΩ is connected to the output. The emitter is effectively bypassed and re′ = 6.58 Ω.
answer: ac collector resistance Rc = RC ‖ RL
problems.how: RC = 1.0 kΩ is read from Figure 6–16; with the emitter bypassed Av = Rc/r′e where Rc = RC ‖ RL (Floyd §6–6). The book prints 833 Ω and 127.
assume: The unloaded gain was 152 in Example 6–5 (RC/r′e).
problems.circuit: Figure 6–16 (p.284): voltage-divider biased 2N3904 common-emitter amplifier. VCC = +12 V, R1 = 22 kΩ (VCC to base), R2 = 6.8 kΩ (base to ground), RC = 1.0 kΩ, RE = 560 Ω with the bypass capacitor C2 across it; input coupling C1, output coupling C3.

problems.text: Determine the base-to-collector voltage gain in Figure 6–16 when a 10 kΩ load resistance is connected from collector to ground. Change the resistance values as follows: RC = 1.8 kΩ, RE = 1.0 kΩ, R1 = 33 kΩ, and R2 = 6.8 kΩ. The emitter resistor is effectively bypassed and re′ = 18.5 Ω.
problems.ctx: Example 6–6: Calculate the base-to-collector voltage gain of the amplifier in Figure 6–16 when a load resistance of 5 kΩ is connected to the output. The emitter is effectively bypassed and re′ = 6.58 Ω.
answer: ac collector resistance Rc = RC ‖ RL
problems.how: Rc = 1.8 kΩ ‖ 10 kΩ; Av = Rc/r′e with the given r′e = 18.5 Ω (the emitter is bypassed). The changed R1, R2, RE only change the dc bias, which the statement already gives as r′e.
assume: R1, R2 and RE affect only r′e, which is given.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.6 Related Problem of Example 6–6, p.286 (PDF 304)
problems.circuit: Figure 6–16 (p.284): voltage-divider biased 2N3904 common-emitter amplifier. VCC = +12 V, R1 = 22 kΩ (VCC to base), R2 = 6.8 kΩ (base to ground), RC = 1.0 kΩ, RE = 560 Ω with the bypass capacitor C2 across it; input coupling C1, output coupling C3.

problems.text: If the multistage amplifier in Figure 6–57 is driven by a 75 Ω, 50 μV source and the second stage is loaded with an RL = 18 kΩ, determine (a) voltage gain of each stage (b) overall voltage gain (c) Express the gains found in (a) and (b) in dB.
answer: (a) Av1 (stage 1, loaded by the input resistance of stage 2)
(a) Av2 (stage 2 with RL = 18 kΩ: Rc = RC ‖ RL)
Av1 = 39.4 dB, Av2 = 48.1 dB, Av = 87.55 dB (= sum of the stage dB values)
Extra: output for the 50 μV, 75 Ω source (the source resistance only divides the input)
problems.how: DC: VB = VCC·R2/(R1 + R2) = 2.985 V, IE = (VB − 0.7 V)/RE = 2.285 mA, r′e = 25 mV/IE = 10.94 Ω. Rin(tot) of a stage = R1 ‖ R2 ‖ β·r′e = 1.482 kΩ; Av1 = (RC ‖ Rin(tot2))/r′e, Av2 = (RC ‖ RL)/r′e (Floyd §6–6).
assume: Gains are voltage gains base-to-collector of the amplifier as in Problem 31; the 75 Ω source resistance does not change them (it only reduces the signal at the input, shown as an extra).
Same figure as Problem 31, whose printed answers (Av1 = 93.6, Av2 = 303 unloaded) are reproduced within 1 % (r′e rounding).
The 50 μV is taken as the same kind of value (rms or peak) as the output.
problems.circuit: Figure 6–57 (p.331): two identical capacitively coupled voltage-divider biased common-emitter stages, VCC = +15 V. Stage 1: R1 = 33 kΩ, R2 = 8.2 kΩ, RC = R3 = 3.3 kΩ, RE = R4 = 1.0 kΩ bypassed by C2. Stage 2 (after coupling capacitor C3): R5 = 33 kΩ, R6 = 8.2 kΩ, RC = R7 = 3.3 kΩ, RE = R8 = 1.0 kΩ bypassed by C4; output through C5. βac = βDC = 175.

problems.text: Determine the efficiency of the power amplifier in Figure 7–5 (Example 7–1).
answer: Input resistance Rin(tot) = R1 ‖ R2 ‖ β(RE1 + r′e)
problems.how: Floyd Example 7–2 with the circuit of Example 7–1: Av1 = Rc1/(RE1 + r′e) = 27.9; PDC = ICC·VCC with IE(Q3) = VE(Q3)/RE3 = 8.2 V/33 Ω ≈ 0.25 A; η = Pout/PDC. Pout is also checked as Vout²/RL (Vout = Av·Vin).
assume: BOOK ERROR 1: the printed solution says 50 mV peak-to-peak is 35.4 mV rms. 35.4 mV rms is 50 mV PEAK (100 mV pp); 50 mV pp is 17.7 mV rms. The book's numbers (Pin = 149 nW, Pout = 122 mW, η ≈ 4 %) are reproduced here for 35.4 mV to confirm the circuit values, but the figure says 50 mV pp, which gives η ≈ 1 %.

BOOK ERROR 2 (also in Example 7–1): the printed Rin(tot) = 56 kΩ ‖ 10 kΩ ‖ 200(68 Ω + 14 Ω) = 8.4 kΩ is only 56 kΩ ‖ 10 kΩ; with the 16.4 kΩ branch it is 5.6 kΩ, so the power gain of Example 7–1 is about 5.5·10⁵, not 817,330. Pout does not depend on it.
Either way the lesson is the same: a class A power stage is very inefficient.
problems.circuit: Figure 7–5 (p.344, Example 7–1): VCC = +12 V. Stage 1 = voltage-divider biased common-emitter Q1 with R1 = 56 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, RC = 4.7 kΩ, swamping RE1 = 68 Ω in series with RE2 = 560 Ω (RE2 bypassed by C2). Stage 2 = Darlington emitter follower Q2–Q3 biased by R3 = 5.6 kΩ and R4 = 22 kΩ (R3 from VCC, R4 to ground), emitter resistor RE3 = 33 Ω (2 W); the load is an 8 Ω speaker through C4. Source Vs = 50 mV pp at 1 kHz. βac = 200 for all transistors.

problems.text: What is the maximum peak output voltage and current if the supply voltages are changed to +15 V and −15 V?
problems.ctx: Example 7–3: Determine the ideal maximum peak output voltage and current for the circuit shown in Figure 7–15.
problems.how: Ideal limits of the push-pull stage: Vout(peak) ≈ VCC, Iout(peak) ≈ VCC/RL.
assume: RL = 150 Ω from Figure 7–15 (Example 7–3).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.7 Related Problem of Example 7–3, p.352 (PDF 370)

problems.text: A certain class C amplifier has a power dissipation of 100 mW and an output power of 1 W. What is its percent efficiency?
problems.how: Power taken from the supply = output power + power dissipated in the transistor; η = Pout/(Pout + PD(avg)) (Floyd §7–3).
assume: The 100 mW is the average power dissipated in the transistor.

problems.text: Refer to the class AB amplifier in Figure 7–46. (a) What is the maximum power that could be delivered to the load resistor? (b) Assume the power supply voltage is raised to 24 V. What is the new maximum power that could be delivered to the load resistor?
problems.how: Single-supply class AB: VCEQ = VCC/2 and the ideal maximum peak output voltage is VCEQ, so Pout(max) = (0.707·Ic)(0.707·VCEQ) = VCC²/(8·RL) (Floyd §7–2). Ideal: transistor saturation voltage neglected.
assume: Ideal limit; the actual maximum is slightly smaller because VCE(sat) of the transistors is not zero.
RL = 75 Ω and VCC = +15 V are read from Figure 7–46 and confirmed by the printed answer of Problem 15(b) (167 mW for a 10 V pp input).
problems.circuit: Figure 7–46 (p.379): class AB push-pull emitter-follower output stage on a single supply VCC = +15 V. R1 = 1.0 kΩ from VCC to the base of the upper (npn) transistor Q1, diodes D1 and D2 in series between the two bases, R2 = 1.0 kΩ from the base of the lower (pnp) transistor Q2 to ground; Q1 collector at VCC, Q2 collector at ground, the emitters joined at the output, which drives RL = 75 Ω through the coupling capacitor C3. The source Vs is coupled to the two bases through C1 and C2.

problems.text: If a 1 V rms signal source with an internal resistance of 50 Ω is connected to the amplifier in Figure 7–46, what is the actual rms signal applied to the amplifier input? Assume βac = 200.
answer: Input resistance Rin = β(r′e + RL) ‖ R1 ‖ R2
Actual rms signal at the amplifier input
problems.how: ICQ = 6.8 mA, so r′e = 25 mV/ICQ = 3.68 Ω. Eq. 7–8: Rin = β(r′e + RL) ‖ R1 ‖ R2 (the diode ac resistances are negligible, as in Example 7–6). The 50 Ω source and Rin form a voltage divider: Vin = Vs·Rin/(Rs + Rin).
assume: r′e from the dc current 6.8 mA of Problem 15(a); ignoring r′e changes the result in the third digit.
problems.circuit: Figure 7–46 (p.379): class AB push-pull emitter-follower output stage on a single supply VCC = +15 V. R1 = 1.0 kΩ from VCC to the base of the upper (npn) transistor Q1, diodes D1 and D2 in series between the two bases, R2 = 1.0 kΩ from the base of the lower (pnp) transistor Q2 to ground; Q1 collector at VCC, Q2 collector at ground, the emitters joined at the output, which drives RL = 75 Ω through the coupling capacitor C3. The source Vs is coupled to the two bases through C1 and C2.

problems.text: The op amps in the circuit on the next page operate from ±12-V power supplies, but are ideal otherwise. (a) What are the voltage gain, input resistance, and output resistance of the overall amplifier? (b) If input voltage vI = 5 mV, what are the voltages at each of the 10 nodes in the circuit? (c) Now suppose that vI = 10 mV. What are the voltages at the outputs of the three op amps? (d) Suppose vI = Vi sin 2000πt. What is the largest value of input voltage Vi that corresponds to linear operation of the amplifier?
answer: 75.0 kΩ (the 75 kΩ resistor; the + input of the first op amp is ideal)
vOA = 110.0 mV, vOB = -2.2 V; the third output would be −13.2 V, so it saturates at -12.0 V and v−C = -2.0 V
problems.how: Three stages (noninverting, inverting, noninverting) with ±12-V supplies: gains multiply, Rin is the 75 kΩ shunt resistor, Rout = 0 (Eq. 12.2); nodes follow vOA = 11 vI, vOB = −20 vOA, vO = 6 vOB. When vO would exceed the rail, the output is clamped at −12 V, the loop of the third stage is open and v−C = −12·20/120 = −2 V. The exact nodal solution with the clamped output as a fixed source gives all the printed values.
assume: The book counts 10 nodes (including V+, V− and ground), here the seven circuit nodes are given.
The output saturates at exactly the supply voltage.
problems.circuit: Three-stage amplifier of the worked example (p.688; the figure has no number): noninverting stage (R1 = 15 kΩ to ground, R2 = 150 kΩ feedback; input tied to ground by R7 = 75 kΩ), inverting stage (R3 = 21 kΩ in, R4 = 420 kΩ feedback), noninverting stage (R5 = 20 kΩ to ground, R6 = 100 kΩ feedback); supplies ±12 V.

problems.text: Determine the value of the external gain-setting resistor RG for a certain IC instrumentation amplifier with R1 = R2 = 25 kΩ. The closed-loop voltage gain is to be 500.
problems.how: Instrumentation amplifier: Acl = 1 + 2R/RG (Floyd §14–1).

problems.text: Calculate the voltage gain and determine the bandwidth using the graph in Figure 14–6 for the instrumentation amplifier in Figure 14–7.
answer: ≈ 80 kHz (the book's reading of the point where the curve begins to drop)
problems.how: AD622: Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1 = 50.5 kΩ/510 Ω + 1 = 100 (Floyd Eq. 14–1). The gain-100 curve of Figure 14–6 is flat up to about 80 kHz and then falls.
assume: Read from the vector drawing of Figure 14–6, the gain-100 curve stays flat to 60.1 kHz and is 3 dB down (gain 70.7) at 112.0 kHz; the book's 80 kHz lies between the two (it is a rough reading).
problems.circuit: Figures 14–7 and 14–6 (pp.722–723): AD622 instrumentation amplifier, supplies +15 V (pin 7) and −15 V (pin 4), inputs +IN (pin 3) and −IN (pin 2), gain resistor RG = 510 Ω between pins 1 and 8, REF pin 5, output pin 6. Gain: Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1; Figure 14–6 is the graph of gain versus frequency of the AD622 for gains 1, 10, 100 and 1000.

problems.text: If an OTA has a gm = 1000 μS, what is the output current when the input voltage is 25 mV?
problems.how: OTA: Iout = gm·Vin; 1 μS × 1 mV = 1 nA.

problems.text: The input to the OTA amplitude modulator in Figure 14–25 is a 50 mV peak-to-peak, 1 MHz sine wave. Determine the output signal, given the modulation voltage shown is applied to the bias input.
answer: a 1 MHz carrier whose amplitude follows the 1 kHz modulating sine between 1.23 V and 2.51 V (amplitude modulation)
problems.how: OTA amplitude modulator: the bias current follows VMOD, so the gain does (Floyd §14–3). Maximum at VMOD = +10 V, minimum at +1 V; Vout = Av·Vin with Vin = 50 mV as in the book.
assume: The book multiplies the 50 mV peak-to-peak input by the gain, so the quoted values are peak-to-peak amplitudes of the carrier.
problems.circuit: Figure 14–25 (p.733): OTA amplitude modulator, supplies +9 V and −9 V; carrier Vin = 50 mV pp at 1 MHz through R1 = 10 kΩ to the − input, R2 = 10 kΩ from the + input to ground, RL = 10 kΩ; the bias input takes VMOD (1 kHz sine between +1 V and +10 V) through RBIAS = 56 kΩ.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage for the log amplifier in Figure 14–31. Assume IR = 50 nA.
problems.how: Log amplifier of Figure 14–31.
assume: Values read from Figure 14–31: Vin = +2 V, R1 = 100 kΩ; IR = 50 nA given in the example.

problems.text: What is Vout for a transistor log amplifier with Vin = 3 V and R1 = 68 kΩ? Assume IEBO = 40 nA.
problems.how: Transistor log amplifier (Floyd §14–4): use the natural logarithm.

problems.text: For the antilog amplifier in Figure 14–34, find the output voltage. Assume IEBO = 40 nA.
problems.how: Antilog amplifier (Floyd §14–4): Vout = −Rf·IEBO·antilog(Vin/25 mV) = −(68 kΩ)(40 nA)(1101) = −3 V. It undoes the log amplifier of Example 14–9, whose output for a 3 V input is −175.1 mV.
problems.circuit: Figures 14–34 and 14–33 (p.740): antilog amplifier: the input +175.1 mV is applied to the emitter of a grounded-base transistor whose collector goes to the − input; feedback resistor Rf = 68 kΩ (Example 14–10).

problems.text: What value of external gain-setting resistor is required for an instrumentation amplifier with R1 = R2 = 39 kΩ to produce a gain of 325?
problems.ctx: Example 14–1: Determine the value of the external gain-setting resistor RG for a certain IC instrumentation amplifier with R1 = R2 = 25 kΩ. The closed-loop voltage gain is to be 500.
problems.how: RG = 2R/(Acl − 1) with R = 39 kΩ.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–1, p.720 (PDF 738)

problems.text: Modify the circuit in Figure 14–7 for a gain of approximately 45.
problems.ctx: Example 14–2: Calculate the voltage gain and determine the bandwidth using the graph in Figure 14–6 for the instrumentation amplifier in Figure 14–7.
problems.how: Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1, so RG = 50.5 kΩ/44 = 1.15 kΩ (printed answer to the similar Problem 7: for a gain of 24 “change RG to 2.2 kΩ”, 50.5 kΩ/23 = 2.20 kΩ).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–2, p.723 (PDF 741)
problems.circuit: Figures 14–7 and 14–6 (pp.722–723): AD622 instrumentation amplifier, supplies +15 V (pin 7) and −15 V (pin 4), inputs +IN (pin 3) and −IN (pin 2), gain resistor RG = 510 Ω between pins 1 and 8, REF pin 5, output pin 6. Gain: Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1; Figure 14–6 is the graph of gain versus frequency of the AD622 for gains 1, 10, 100 and 1000.

problems.text: Select resistor values in Figure 14–15 that will produce a total voltage gain of approximately 100.
problems.ctx: Example 14–4: Determine the total voltage gain of the 3656KG isolation amplifier in Figure 14–15.
answer: A choice with total gain ≈ 100 (input stage unchanged, Av1 = 11)
Rf2 = 82 kΩ with Ri2 = 10 kΩ: Av2 = 9.2, total = 101.2
Ri1 = 3.3 kΩ (Av1 = 7.67) with the original output stage gives 43.7: too low, so change the output stage
problems.how: The total gain is the product of the stage gains, Av(tot) = (Rf1/Ri1 + 1)(Rf2/Ri2 + 1) (Eq. 14–3, 14–4); for 100 with Av1 = 11 the output stage needs Av2 = 9.1, i.e. Rf2/Ri2 = 8.1.
assume: A design exercise: many resistor pairs give “approximately 100”; one is given.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–4, p.728 (PDF 746)
problems.circuit: Figure 14–15 (p.728): 3656KG isolation amplifier. Input stage: Rs = 10 kΩ (pin 7), Rf1 = 22 kΩ (pin 10 to 6), Ri1 = 2.2 kΩ from pin 6 to ground; output stage: Ri2 = 10 kΩ, Rf2 = 47 kΩ (pin 14 to 15), output at pin 15; supply +15 V.

problems.text: If the OTA in Figure 14–23 is operated with dc supply voltages of ±12 V, will this change the voltage gain and, if so, to what value?
problems.ctx: Example 14–6: The OTA in Figure 14–23 is connected as an inverting fixed-gain amplifier where +VBIAS = +V. Determine the approximate voltage gain.
answer: IBIAS = (12 V + 12 V − 1.4 V)/33 kΩ for ±12 V
New gm = K·IBIAS and Av = gm·RL
11.0 mS, Av = 110.0: yes, the gain increases from 80.5 to about 110.0
problems.how: The bias current, and so gm and the gain, depend on the supply voltages through IBIAS = (+V − (−V) − 1.4 V)/RBIAS (Floyd §14–3, Example 14–6).
assume: K = 16 μS/μA is taken constant (the book's value for this current); at the larger bias current the graph of Figure 14–18 may differ slightly.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–6, p.733 (PDF 751)
problems.circuit: Figure 14–23 (p.731): OTA (LM13700) amplifier, supplies +9 V and −9 V, RBIAS = 33 kΩ from +9 V to the bias input, R1 = 10 kΩ from Vin to the − input, R2 = 10 kΩ from the + input to ground, load RL = 10 kΩ. IBIAS = (+V − (−V) − 1.4 V)/RBIAS, gm = K·IBIAS with K ≈ 16 μS/μA (Figure 14–18), Av = gm·RL (book result 80.5).

problems.text: Calculate the output voltage of the log amplifier with a +4 V input.
problems.ctx: Example 14–8: Determine the output voltage for the log amplifier in Figure 14–31. Assume IR = 50 nA.
problems.how: Vout = −0.025 ln(Vin/(IR·R1)).
assume: R1 = 100 kΩ and IR = 50 nA as in Example 14–8 (Figure 14–31).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–8, p.739 (PDF 757)

problems.text: Calculate Vout if R1 is changed to 33 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 14–9: What is Vout for a transistor log amplifier with Vin = 3 V and R1 = 68 kΩ? Assume IEBO = 40 nA.
problems.how: Vout = −0.025 ln(Vin/(IEBO·R1)).
assume: Vin = 3 V and IEBO = 40 nA as in Example 14–9.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–9, p.739 (PDF 757)

problems.text: Determine Vout for the amplifier in Figure 14–34 if the feedback resistor is changed to 100 kΩ.
problems.ctx: Example 14–10: For the antilog amplifier in Figure 14–34, find the output voltage. Assume IEBO = 40 nA.
problems.how: Vout is proportional to Rf: −3 V × 100 kΩ/68 kΩ.
assume: Provided the op-amp output can reach this value (the supply voltages are not given).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.14 Related Problem of Example 14–10, p.741 (PDF 759)
problems.circuit: Figures 14–34 and 14–33 (p.740): antilog amplifier: the input +175.1 mV is applied to the emitter of a grounded-base transistor whose collector goes to the − input; feedback resistor Rf = 68 kΩ (Example 14–10).

problems.text: In a certain AD622 configuration, RG = 10 kΩ. What is the voltage gain?
For the constant-current source in Figure 14–36, the input reference voltage is 6.8 V and Ri is 10 k load? To a 5 kΩ load?
answer: 0.68 mA (the same: IL does not depend on RL)
problems.how: Op-amp constant-current source: the − input is a virtual ground, so Ii = VIN/Ri flows through the load RL in the feedback path (Eq. 14–11): 6.8 V/10 kΩ = 0.68 mA.
assume: The output must reach 3.4 V for the 5 kΩ load, which a ±12 V to ±15 V supply allows (supplies are not given).
problems.circuit: Figure 14–36 (p.742): constant-current source: the input voltage VIN is applied through Ri to the − input, the + input is grounded and the load RL is connected in the feedback path between the output and the − input.

problems.text: Determine the approximate bandwidth of the amplifier in Figure 14–54 if the voltage gain is set to 10. Use the graph in Figure 14–6.
answer: Bandwidth from the gain-10 curve of Figure 14–6
≈ 400.0 kHz (3 dB down: the curve peaks at 11.0 near 204.0 kHz and falls to 7.07 at 399.0 kHz)
problems.how: Gain 10 needs RG = 50.5 kΩ/9 = 5.6 kΩ; the bandwidth is read from the gain-10 curve of Figure 14–6 at the −3 dB point (gain 7.07).
assume: The graph reading comes from the vector drawing of Figure 14–6 (the curve points were converted with the log-log axes, calibration checked on the flat levels 1, 10, 100, 1000). If the book's rougher rule of Example 14–2 (“where the curve begins to drop”) is used the answer is about 0.3 MHz.
The statement says the gain is “set to 10” (RG would be 5.6 kΩ) although the figure shows 1.0 kΩ.
problems.circuit: Figures 14–54 and 14–6 (pp.758, 723): AD622 instrumentation amplifier, supplies ±15 V, +IN pin 3, −IN pin 2, RG = 1.0 kΩ between pins 1 and 8, output pin 6, REF pin 5. Gain Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1 (51.5 as drawn). Figure 14–6 is the AD622 graph of gain versus frequency (curves for gains 1, 10, 100, 1000).

problems.text: Determine the value of RG in Figure 14–54 for a voltage gain of 20.
answer: 2.658 kΩ (nearest standard value 2.7 kΩ gives Av = 19.7)
problems.how: Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1 (Floyd Eq. 14–1) gives RG = 50.5 kΩ/19 = 2.66 kΩ.
problems.circuit: Figures 14–54 and 14–6 (pp.758, 723): AD622 instrumentation amplifier, supplies ±15 V, +IN pin 3, −IN pin 2, RG = 1.0 kΩ between pins 1 and 8, output pin 6, REF pin 5. Gain Av = 50.5 kΩ/RG + 1 (51.5 as drawn). Figure 14–6 is the AD622 graph of gain versus frequency (curves for gains 1, 10, 100, 1000).

problems.text: Specify how you would change the total gain in Figure 14–55(b) to approximately 440 by changing only the gain of the output stage.
answer: 4.94 kΩ; standard values: 4.7 kΩ → total 434.7, 5.1 kΩ → 443.5
problems.how: Total gain = Av1·Av2 with Av1 = 330 kΩ/1.0 kΩ + 1 = 331 and Av2 = Rf2/Ri2 + 1; only Rf2 (or Ri2) of the output stage may change: Rf2/Ri2 = 0.329, i.e. Rf2 ≈ 4.9 kΩ for Ri2 = 15 kΩ.
assume: Figure 14–55(b) is read as Rs = 10 kΩ, Rf1 = 330 kΩ, Ri1 = 1.0 kΩ, Ri2 = 15 kΩ and Rf2 = 47 kΩ; the same figure, part (a), is checked by Problem 11 whose printed answer (change 18 kΩ to 68 kΩ) follows from the same formulas.
problems.circuit: Figure 14–55(b) (p.759): 3656KG isolation amplifier, supply +15 V. Input stage: Rs = 10 kΩ, Rf1 = 330 kΩ (pin 10 to 6), Ri1 = 1.0 kΩ from pin 6 to ground; output stage: Ri2 = 15 kΩ, Rf2 = 47 kΩ (pin 14 to 15), output pin 15.

problems.text: If a 10 kΩ rheostat is added in series with the bias resistor in Figure 14–56, what are the minimum and maximum voltage gains?
problems.how: IBIAS = (+V − (−V) − 1.4 V)/RBIAS, gm = K·IBIAS with K = 16 μS/μA, Av = gm·RL (Example 14–6/14–7 method).
assume: NOTE: the printed answer of Problem 17 (same circuit without the rheostat) is Av ≅ 11.6, about 4 % above the 11.2 given by the book's own method (1.4 V drop in the bias path); with that 4 % scaling the range would be about 11.1 to 11.6. Cause not found in the book.
problems.circuit: Figure 14–56 (p.759): OTA amplifier, supplies +12 V and −12 V, RBIAS = 220 kΩ from +12 V to the bias input, R1 = 10 kΩ from Vin to the − input, R2 = 10 kΩ from the + input to ground, load RL = 6.8 kΩ (K = 16 μS/μA).

problems.text: Using your calculator, find the natural logarithm (ln) of each of the following numbers: (a) 0.5 (b) 2 (c) 50 (d) 130
problems.how: Natural logarithms.

problems.text: Determine the output voltage for the antilog amplifier in Figure 14–61. Assume IEBO = 60 nA.
problems.how: Antilog amplifier (Floyd §14–4): Vout = −(100 kΩ)(60 nA)·e^(0.225/0.025) = −6 mV × 8103 = −48.6 V.
assume: This is the ideal result; it is larger than any normal op-amp supply, so the real output would saturate near the negative supply (the supply voltage is not given).
problems.circuit: Figure 14–61 (p.760): antilog amplifier: the input +0.225 V is applied to the emitter of a grounded-base transistor whose collector goes to the − input; Rf = 100 kΩ from the output to the − input, + input grounded.

problems.text: Find the values of VO, VA, and VB for the instrumentation amplifier in Fig. 12.4 if V1 = 2.5 V, V2 = 2.25 V, R1 = 15 kΩ, R2 = 150 kΩ, R3 = 15 kΩ, and R4 = 30 kΩ.
problems.how: Instrumentation amplifier (Eq. 12.13): the ideal op amps ① and ② put V1 and V2 on the ends of 2R1, so I = (V1 − V2)/2R1 and VA, VB are I·R2 above and below; the difference amplifier gives VO = −(R4/R3)(VA − VB). The exact nodal solution of the three-op-amp circuit agrees.
assume: Ideal op amps.
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.4 (p.700): instrumentation amplifier: V1 and V2 on the + inputs of op amps ① and ②; R2, 2R1, R2 in series between their outputs; op amp ③ with R3, R4 forms the difference amplifier; V1 = 2.5 V, V2 = 2.25 V, R1 = 15 kΩ, R2 = 150 kΩ, R3 = 15 kΩ, R4 = 30 kΩ.

problems.text: A certain band-pass filter has a center frequency of 15 kHz and a bandwidth of 1 kHz. Determine Q and classify the filter as narrow-band or wide-band.
problems.how: Band-pass filter: Q = f0/BW; Q > 10 is narrow-band (Floyd §15–1).

problems.text: If resistor R2 in the feedback circuit of an active single-pole filter of the type in Figure 15–6 is 10 kΩ, what value must R1 be to obtain a maximally flat Butterworth response?
problems.how: Damping factor DF = 2 − R1/R2; Butterworth needs DF = 1.414, so R1/R2 = 0.586 (Floyd Table 15–1). The book prints R1 = 5.86 kΩ and picks 5.6 kΩ.
assume: The independent check uses an exact Sallen-Key response: with R1/R2 = 0.586 its gain at fc is 1/√2 of the dc gain (maximally flat).
problems.circuit: Figure 15–6 (p.770): general active single-pole (first-order) filter block: a frequency-selective RC circuit drives the + input of a noninverting op-amp whose gain and damping factor are set by the feedback resistors R1 (from the output to the − input) and R2 (from the − input to ground).

problems.text: For the four-pole filter in Figure 15–12(b), determine the capacitance values required to produce a critical frequency of 2680 Hz if all the resistors in the RC low-pass circuits are 1.8 kΩ. Also select values for the feedback resistors to get a Butterworth response.
problems.how: Both stages need the same fc, so with equal R the capacitors are equal: C = 1/(2πR·fc); the feedback ratios of Table 15–1 for a four-pole Butterworth filter are R1/R2 = 0.152 and R3/R4 = 1.235 with R2 = R4 = 1.8 kΩ.
assume: The exact response of the two cascaded sections with the book's values is 3 dB down at 2.68 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–12(b) (p.775): four-pole Sallen-Key low-pass filter made of two cascaded two-pole stages: stage 1 with RA1 = RB1 (RC low-pass circuit), CA1 = CB1 and feedback resistors R1 and R2; stage 2 with RA2 = RB2, CA2 = CB2 and feedback resistors R3 and R4.

problems.text: Choose values for the Sallen-Key high-pass filter in Figure 15–15 to implement an equal-value second-order Butterworth response with a critical frequency of approximately 10 kHz.
answer: C = CA = CB = 1/(2πR·fc) with R = RA = RB = R2 = 3.3 kΩ
If R1 = 3.3 kΩ is chosen instead
problems.how: Equal-value Sallen-Key high-pass: fc = 1/(2πRC), R1/R2 = 0.586 for a Butterworth response (Floyd §15–4). The book prints 0.0048 μF and 1.93 kΩ.
assume: The exact response is 3 dB down at 9.998 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–15 (p.777): Sallen-Key high-pass filter: input through CA to a node, CB from that node to the + input, RA from the node to the output (feedback), RB from the + input to ground; gain-setting resistors R1 (output to − input) and R2 (− input to ground).

problems.text: Verify that the band-stop filter in Figure 15–26 has a center frequency of 60 Hz, and optimize the filter for a Q of 10.
answer: R5 for Q = 10 with R6 = 3.3 kΩ: R5 = (3Q − 1)·R6
problems.how: The band-stop filter uses the state-variable filter: f0 equals the critical frequency of the integrators and Q = (1/3)(R5/R6 + 1), so R5 = (3Q − 1)R6 (Floyd §15–6). R6 is free to choose.
assume: Exact solution of the whole circuit (state-variable filter + summing amplifier): notch at 60.29 Hz, depth > 60 dB, Q = 10.0.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–26 (p.786): band-stop (notch) filter made from a state-variable filter and a summing amplifier: R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ, integrators R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ with C1 = C2 = 0.22 μF, Q-setting resistors R5 (from the BP output) and R6 (to ground); the high-pass and low-pass outputs are added by R8 = R9 = R10 = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: What is the damping factor for R2 = 10 kΩ and R1 = 5.6 kΩ?
problems.ctx: Example 15–2: If resistor R2 in the feedback circuit of an active single-pole filter of the type in Figure 15–6 is 10 kΩ, what value must R1 be to obtain a maximally flat Butterworth response?
problems.how: Damping factor of the two-pole Sallen-Key filter: DF = 2 − R1/R2 (Floyd §15–2).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–2, p.771 (PDF 789)

problems.text: Determine fc for Figure 15–11 if RA = RB = R2 = 2.2 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.01 μF. Also determine the value of R1 for a Butterworth response.
problems.ctx: Example 15–3: Determine the critical frequency of the Sallen-Key low-pass filter in Figure 15–11, and set the value of R1 for an approximate Butterworth response.
problems.how: Equal-value Sallen-Key: fc = 1/(2πRC) with RA = RB = 2.2 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.01 μF; R1/R2 = 0.586 for DF = 1.414 (Example 15–3 method).
assume: The exact response with R1 = 0.586·R2 is 3 dB down at 7.235 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–3, p.774 (PDF 792)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–11 (p.774): Sallen-Key low-pass filter: input through RA to a node, RB from that node to the + input, CA from the node to the output (feedback), CB from the + input to ground; gain-setting resistors R1 (output to − input) and R2 (− input to ground). In Example 15–3 RA = RB = R2 = 1.0 kΩ and CA = CB = 0.022 μF (fc = 7.23 kHz, R1 = 586 Ω).

problems.text: For the filter in Figure 15–12(b), determine the capacitance values for fc = 1 kHz if all the filter resistors are 680 Ω. Also specify the values for the feedback resistors to produce a Butterworth response.
problems.ctx: Example 15–4: For the four-pole filter in Figure 15–12(b), determine the capacitance values required to produce a critical frequency of 2680 Hz if all the resistors in the RC low-pass circuits are 1.8 kΩ. Also select values for the feedback resistors to get a Butterworth response.
answer: 840.0 Ω (nearest standard 820 Ω or 840 Ω → 820 Ω)
problems.how: Same method as Example 15–4 with R = 680 Ω and fc = 1 kHz.
assume: The exact response with the computed (not rounded) values is 3 dB down at 1.0 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–4, p.775 (PDF 793)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–12(b) (p.775): four-pole Sallen-Key low-pass filter made of two cascaded two-pole stages: stage 1 with RA1 = RB1 (RC low-pass circuit), CA1 = CB1 and feedback resistors R1 and R2; stage 2 with RA2 = RB2, CA2 = CB2 and feedback resistors R3 and R4.

problems.text: Select values for all the components in the high-pass filter of Figure 15–15 to obtain an fc = 300 Hz. Use equal-value components with R = 10 kΩ and optimize for a Butterworth response.
problems.ctx: Example 15–5: Choose values for the Sallen-Key high-pass filter in Figure 15–15 to implement an equal-value second-order Butterworth response with a critical frequency of approximately 10 kHz.
answer: 53.1 nF (standard value 0.056 μF gives fc = 284.0 Hz; 0.047 μF gives 339.0 Hz)
problems.how: Same method as Example 15–5 with R = 10 kΩ and fc = 300 Hz.
assume: The exact response with the computed values is 3 dB down at 300.0 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–5, p.778 (PDF 796)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–15 (p.777): Sallen-Key high-pass filter: input through CA to a node, CB from that node to the + input, RA from the node to the output (feedback), RB from the + input to ground; gain-setting resistors R1 (output to − input) and R2 (− input to ground).

problems.text: If R2 in Figure 15–19 is increased to 330 kΩ, determine the gain, center frequency, and bandwidth of the filter?
problems.ctx: Example 15–6: Determine the center frequency, maximum gain, and bandwidth for the filter in Figure 15–19.
problems.how: Multiple-feedback band-pass (Floyd §15–5): f0 = (1/2πC)·√((R1 + R3)/(R1R2R3)), A0 = R2/2R1, Q = π·f0·C·R2, BW = f0/Q; Example 15–6 (R2 = 180 kΩ) gives 736 Hz, 1.32 and 177 Hz.
assume: The exact transfer function of the circuit gives a peak at 544.0 Hz, gain 2.43 and a −3 dB bandwidth of 96.5 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–6, p.782 (PDF 800)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–19 (p.781): multiple-feedback band-pass filter: input through R1 = 68 kΩ to a node; from that node C1 = 0.01 μF to the output, R3 = 2.7 kΩ to ground and C2 = 0.01 μF to the − input; R2 = 180 kΩ from the output to the − input; + input grounded.

problems.text: Determine f0, Q, and BW for the filter in Figure 15–22 if R4 = R6 = R7 = 330 Ω with all other component values the same as shown on the schematic.
problems.ctx: Example 15–7: Determine the center frequency, Q, and BW for the passband of the state-variable filter in Figure 15–22.
problems.how: State-variable band-pass (Floyd §15–5): f0 = fc of the integrators, Q = (1/3)(R5/R6 + 1), BW = f0/Q. Example 15–7 (R4 = R6 = R7 = 1.0 kΩ) gives 7.23 kHz, 33.7 and 215 Hz.
assume: Exact solution of the three-op-amp circuit: peak at 21.92 kHz, Q = 101.0.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–7, p.784 (PDF 802)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–22 (p.783): state-variable filter with three op-amps: R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ around the first (summing) op-amp, two integrators with R4 = R7 = 1.0 kΩ and C1 = C2 = 0.022 μF, band-pass output taken from the second op-amp; Q-setting resistors R5 = 100 kΩ (from the BP output) and R6 = 1.0 kΩ (to ground) feed the + input of the first op-amp.

problems.text: How would you change the center frequency to 120 Hz in Figure 15–26?
problems.ctx: Example 15–8: Verify that the band-stop filter in Figure 15–26 has a center frequency of 60 Hz, and optimize the filter for a Q of 10.
answer: 6.03 kΩ (standard 6.2 kΩ gives 116.7 Hz; 6.0 kΩ gives 120.6 Hz)
Or keep R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ and change C1 = C2
problems.how: f0 = 1/(2πRC) of the integrators is inversely proportional to R·C: doubling the centre frequency halves R4 = R7 (both, so the integrators stay matched) or halves C1 = C2; R5/R6 (the Q) need not change.
assume: Exact solution of the circuit with R4 = R7 = 6.03 kΩ: notch at 120.0 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.15 Related Problem of Example 15–8, p.786 (PDF 804)
problems.circuit: Figure 15–26 (p.786): band-stop (notch) filter made from a state-variable filter and a summing amplifier: R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ, integrators R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ with C1 = C2 = 0.22 μF, Q-setting resistors R5 (from the BP output) and R6 (to ground); the high-pass and low-pass outputs are added by R8 = R9 = R10 = 10 kΩ.

problems.text: Without changing the response curve, adjust the component values in the filter of Figure 15–45 to make it an equal-value filter. Select C = 0.22 μF for both stages.
answer: Critical frequency of each stage fc = 1/(2π·√(R1R2C1C2))
Equal-value stage with C = 0.22 μF: R = 1/(2π·fc·C)
3.81 kΩ (standard 3.9 kΩ gives fc = 185.5 Hz; 3.6 kΩ gives 201.0 Hz)

R1 = R2 = R5 = R6 = 3.8 kΩ (≈ 3.9 kΩ), C1 = C2 = C3 = C4 = 0.22 μF; the gain-setting resistors R3/R4 = 0.147 (DF = 1.853) and R7/R8 = 1.214 (DF = 0.786) are unchanged: they are the four-pole Butterworth ratios of Table 15–1 (0.152 and 1.235), so the response curve is kept
problems.how: In the book's model the response (damping factor) of an equal-value Sallen-Key stage depends only on R3/R4 (R7/R8) and fc = 1/(2πRC); the unequal-value circuit has fc = 1/(2π√(R1R2C1C2)) = 190 Hz. Replacing both resistors by R = 1/(2π·fc·C) with C = 0.22 μF keeps fc and the feedback resistors keep the Butterworth shape.
assume: Exact check of the new circuit: the cascade is 3 dB down at 187.0 Hz.

This follows the textbook equal-value model; the exact response of the original unequal-value circuit is not identical (its damping depends on the component ratios), so “without changing the response curve” is interpreted as keeping fc and the Butterworth feedback ratios.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–45 (p.805): two cascaded Sallen-Key low-pass sections, each with unequal values. Stage 1: R1 = 4.7 kΩ, R2 = 6.8 kΩ, C1 = 0.22 μF (feedback capacitor), C2 = 0.1 μF (to ground), gain resistors R3 = 1.0 kΩ and R4 = 6.8 kΩ. Stage 2: R5 = 4.7 kΩ, R6 = 6.8 kΩ, C3 = 0.22 μF, C4 = 0.1 μF, gain resistors R7 = 6.8 kΩ and R8 = 5.6 kΩ.

problems.text: Optimize the state-variable filter in Figure 15–48 for Q = 50. What bandwidth is achieved?
problems.how: State-variable band-pass: Q = (1/3)(R5/R6 + 1), so R5 = (3Q − 1)R6 = 149·R6; with R6 = 1.0 kΩ, R5 = 149 kΩ. BW = f0/Q = 1.326 kHz/50.
assume: R5 and R6 are not in the figure (they are to be chosen); only their ratio matters: R6 = 1.0 kΩ is an arbitrary choice.
Exact solution of the three-op-amp circuit gives f0 = 1.326 kHz and Q = 50.0.
problems.circuit: Figure 15–48 (p.806): state-variable filter, R1 = R2 = R3 = R4 = R7 = 12 kΩ, C1 = C2 = 0.01 μF; R5 (from the BP output) and R6 (to ground) set Q and are left to be chosen.

problems.text: Design a low-pass filter using the circuit in Fig. 12.5 with an upper cutoff frequency of 5 kHz and a maximally flat response.
answer: fo = 4.98 kHz, Q = 0.7071; −3 dB frequency of the exact circuit 4.98 kHz
problems.how: Maximally flat second-order low-pass filter (Q = 1/√2): C1 = 2C2 = 2C, R1 = R2 = R = 1/(√2·ωo·C); then fH = fo. The exact circuit (Fig. 12.5 with an ideal follower) solved at s = jω confirms |A(jωo)| = Q and fH ≈ fo = 4.98 kHz.
assume: Ideal op amp (voltage follower).
problems.circuit: Fig. 12.5 (p.704): two-pole low-pass filter: vI → R1 → v1 → R2 → v2 (+ input of a voltage follower); C1 from v1 to the output; C2 from v2 to ground.

problems.text: Determine the resonant frequency for the Wien-bridge oscillator in Figure 16–12. Also, calculate the setting for Rf assuming the internal drain-source resistance, rd′ s, of the JFET is 500 Ω when oscillations are stable.
answer: Rf for a closed-loop gain of 3: Rf = (Av − 1)(R3 + r′ds)
problems.how: Wien-bridge: fr = 1/(2πRC); oscillations need a closed-loop gain of 3 to offset the lead-lag attenuation 1/3, and the amplifier is a noninverting stage with Ri = R3 + r′ds (Floyd §16–2). The book prints 1.59 kHz and 3.0 kΩ.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–12 (p.814): Wien-bridge oscillator with automatic gain control: lead-lag network R1 = R2 = 10 kΩ, C1 = C2 = 0.01 μF on the + input; negative feedback from the output to the − input through the 10 kΩ potentiometer Rf, with a JFET (2N5458, drain-source resistance r′ds) and R3 = 1.0 kΩ in the source in series to ground; diode D1 (1N914), R4 = 10 kΩ and C3 = 1.0 μF rectify the output to bias the JFET gate.

problems.text: (a) Determine the frequency for the oscillator in Figure 16–21. Assume there is negligible loading on the feedback circuit and that its Q is greater than 10. (b) Find the frequency if the oscillator is loaded to a point where the Q drops to 8.
problems.how: Colpitts oscillator: the tank capacitors C1 and C2 are in series, fr = 1/(2π√(L·CT)); a loaded tank lowers it by √(Q²/(Q² + 1)) (Floyd §16–4). The book prints 0.0091 μF, 7.46 kHz and 7.40 kHz.
assume: Exact lossy-tank solution for Q = 8: 7.406 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–21 (p.821): Colpitts oscillator, +12 V: bias resistors R1, R2, collector resistor R3, emitter resistor R4, coupling/bypass capacitors C3, C4, C5; the tank is L = 50 mH with C1 = 0.1 μF and C2 = 0.01 μF in series (the capacitive divider gives the feedback).

problems.text: Determine the frequency of oscillation of the circuit in Figure 16–30. To what value must R1 be changed to make the frequency 20 kHz?
problems.how: Triangular-wave oscillator (Floyd Eq. 16–10); the book prints 8.25 kHz and 4.13 kΩ.
assume: The simulation of the integrator + comparator confirms both frequencies.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–30 (p.827): triangular-wave oscillator with two op-amps: an integrator with R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 μF (input from the comparator output) and a comparator with hysteresis whose positive-feedback resistors are R2 = 33 kΩ and R3 = 10 kΩ; the comparator output swings between +Vmax and −Vmax. Book formulas: VUTP = +Vmax·(R3/R2), fr = (1/(4R1C))(R2/R3).

problems.text: (a) Find the amplitude and frequency of the sawtooth output in Figure 16–32. Assume that the forward PUT voltage, VF, is approximately 1 V. (b) Sketch the output waveform.
answer: Gate voltage VG = R4/(R3 + R4)·(+V) = peak of the sawtooth
a sawtooth ramping from about 1 V up to 7.5 V in 1.59 ms, then dropping back quickly when the PUT fires
problems.how: PUT sawtooth generator (Floyd §16–5): the ramp slope is |VIN|/(Ri·C) and the PUT fires when the output reaches VG. The book prints 7.5 V, 6.5 V, 628 Hz and 1.59 ms.
assume: The book neglects the loading of the 68 kΩ/10 kΩ divider by Ri (the current is taken as |VIN|/Ri); including it lowers the frequency to about 579.0 Hz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–32 (p.828): sawtooth generator with a PUT: an op-amp integrator whose input resistor Ri = 100 kΩ is fed from a divider between −15 V: R1 = 68 kΩ (to −15 V) and R2 = 10 kΩ (to ground); feedback capacitor C = 0.0047 μF; the PUT (anode at the − input, cathode at the output through the gate network) has its gate at the divider R3 = 10 kΩ (from +15 V) and R4 = 10 kΩ (to ground), so VG = 7.5 V.

problems.text: A 555 timer configured to run in the astable mode (oscillator) is shown in Figure 16–41. Determine the frequency of the output and the duty cycle.
problems.how: 555 astable (Floyd Eq. 16–12 and 16–13). The book prints 5.64 kHz and 59.5 %.
assume: A time-stepped simulation gives 5.652 kHz and 59.5 % (the book's 1.44 is 1/0.694).
problems.circuit: Figure 16–41 (p.834): astable 555 timer on +5.5 V: R1 = 2.2 kΩ (VCC to the discharge pin), R2 = 4.7 kΩ (discharge pin to the threshold/trigger pins), Cext = 0.022 μF to ground, 0.01 μF on the control pin. Figure 16–40: a diode D1 across R2 makes Cext charge through R1 only.

problems.text: (a) If R1, R2, and R3 in Figure 16–14 are changed to 8.2 kΩ, what value must Rf be for oscillation? (b) What is the value of fr?
problems.ctx: Example 16–2: (a) Determine the value of Rf necessary for the circuit in Figure 16–14 to operate as an oscillator. (b) Determine the frequency of oscillation.
problems.how: Phase-shift oscillator: the three-section network attenuates by 29 at fr = 1/(2π√6·RC) with a phase shift of 180°, so the inverting amplifier needs Acl = 29: Rf = 29·R3 (Floyd §16–2).
assume: Exact solution of the unloaded three-section network: 180° at 7.924 kHz with attenuation 29.0.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–2, p.816 (PDF 834)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–14 (p.816): three-section RC phase-shift oscillator: an inverting op-amp with feedback resistor Rf; the feedback network is three series capacitors C1 = C2 = C3 = 0.001 μF with shunt resistors R1 = R2 = R3 = 10 kΩ in Example 16–2; the loop gain needs Acl = 29, B = R3/Rf = 1/29.

problems.text: What frequency does the oscillator in Figure 16–21 produce if it is loaded to a point where Q = 4?
problems.ctx: Example 16–3: (a) Determine the frequency for the oscillator in Figure 16–21. Assume there is negligible loading on the feedback circuit and that its Q is greater than 10. (b) Find the frequency if the oscillator is loaded to a point where the Q drops to 8.
problems.how: The resonant frequency of a loaded tank is fr = f0·√(Q²/(Q² + 1)) (Floyd §16–4, Example 16–3 uses it for Q = 8: 7.40 kHz): for Q = 4, fr = 7.46 kHz × 0.9701.
assume: An exact admittance calculation of a coil with Q = 4 gives 7.228 kHz (the textbook factor is an approximation).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–3, p.821 (PDF 839)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–21 (p.821): Colpitts oscillator, +12 V: bias resistors R1, R2, collector resistor R3, emitter resistor R4, coupling/bypass capacitors C3, C4, C5; the tank is L = 50 mH with C1 = 0.1 μF and C2 = 0.01 μF in series (the capacitive divider gives the feedback).

problems.text: What is the amplitude of the triangular wave in Figure 16–30 if the comparator output is ±10 V?
problems.ctx: Example 16–4: Determine the frequency of oscillation of the circuit in Figure 16–30. To what value must R1 be changed to make the frequency 20 kHz?
answer: Peak-to-peak amplitude of the triangular wave
problems.how: The comparator trigger points set the triangle: VUTP = +Vmax(R3/R2), VLTP = −Vmax(R3/R2) (Floyd §16–5): ±10 V × 10 kΩ/33 kΩ. The frequency (8.25 kHz) does not depend on Vmax.
assume: A time-stepped simulation of the integrator and comparator gives a peak of 3.03 V and 8.24 kHz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–4, p.827 (PDF 845)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–30 (p.827): triangular-wave oscillator with two op-amps: an integrator with R1 = 10 kΩ and C = 0.01 μF (input from the comparator output) and a comparator with hysteresis whose positive-feedback resistors are R2 = 33 kΩ and R3 = 10 kΩ; the comparator output swings between +Vmax and −Vmax. Book formulas: VUTP = +Vmax·(R3/R2), fr = (1/(4R1C))(R2/R3).

problems.text: If Ri is changed to 56 kΩ in Figure 16–32, what is the frequency?
problems.ctx: Example 16–5: (a) Find the amplitude and frequency of the sawtooth output in Figure 16–32. Assume that the forward PUT voltage, VF, is approximately 1 V. (b) Sketch the output waveform.
answer: the slope is inversely proportional to Ri: 628 Hz × 100 kΩ/56 kΩ
problems.how: Same method as Example 16–5: VIN = −1.92 V, Vp − VF = 6.5 V, now with Ri = 56 kΩ.
assume: Including the loading of the divider by Ri (not done in the book) the frequency would be about 973.0 Hz.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–5, p.829 (PDF 847)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–32 (p.828): sawtooth generator with a PUT: an op-amp integrator whose input resistor Ri = 100 kΩ is fed from a divider between −15 V: R1 = 68 kΩ (to −15 V) and R2 = 10 kΩ (to ground); feedback capacitor C = 0.0047 μF; the PUT (anode at the − input, cathode at the output through the gate network) has its gate at the divider R3 = 10 kΩ (from +15 V) and R4 = 10 kΩ (to ground), so VG = 7.5 V.

problems.text: Determine the duty cycle in Figure 16–41 if a diode is connected across R2 as indicated in Figure 16–40.
problems.ctx: Example 16–6: A 555 timer configured to run in the astable mode (oscillator) is shown in Figure 16–41. Determine the frequency of the output and the duty cycle.
answer: Duty cycle with the diode across R2: tH = 0.694·R1·C, tL = 0.694·R2·C
problems.how: With D1 across R2, Cext charges through R1 only and discharges through R2: duty cycle = R1/(R1 + R2) (Floyd §16–6).
assume: The diode forward drop (≈ 0.7 V) is neglected, as in the book; a time-stepped simulation confirms the duty cycle.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.16 Related Problem of Example 16–6, p.834 (PDF 852)
problems.circuit: Figure 16–41 (p.834): astable 555 timer on +5.5 V: R1 = 2.2 kΩ (VCC to the discharge pin), R2 = 4.7 kΩ (discharge pin to the threshold/trigger pins), Cext = 0.022 μF to ground, 0.01 μF on the control pin. Figure 16–40: a diode D1 across R2 makes Cext charge through R1 only.

problems.text: A certain lead-lag circuit has R1 = R2 and C1 = C2. An input voltage of 5 V rms is applied. The input frequency equals the resonant frequency of the circuit. What is the rms output voltage?
problems.how: At the resonant frequency the lead-lag network has B = 1/3 and 0° phase shift (Floyd §16–3).

problems.text: Calculate the frequency of oscillation for each circuit in Figure 16–60 and identify the type of oscillator. Assume Q > 10 in each case.
answer: Colpitts oscillator (one inductor, two capacitors C1 and C3 forming the capacitive divider)
Hartley oscillator (two inductors L1 and L2 with one capacitor C2)
problems.how: Colpitts: fr = 1/(2π√(L·CT)) with the two tank capacitors in series; Hartley: fr = 1/(2π√(LT·C)) with LT = L1 + L2 (Floyd §16–4). Q > 10 so loading is neglected.
assume: The two inductors of the Hartley circuit are taken as uncoupled (no mutual inductance is given).
The coupling and bypass capacitors (1 μF) are taken as ac shorts.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–60 (p.848): (a) a transistor oscillator whose tank is L1 = 5 mH with C1 = 100 pF (from the inductor's lower end to ground) and C3 = 1000 pF (from the collector to ground, ac), feedback taken from the C1 junction through C2 = 1 μF to the base (C4 = 1 μF bypass); (b) a transistor oscillator with L1 = 1.5 mH and L2 = 10 mH each from a side of the tank to ground and C2 = 470 pF across both (C1, C3, C4 = 1 μF coupling/bypass capacitors).

problems.text: Determine the amplitude and frequency of the output voltage in Figure 16–63. Use 1 V as the forward PUT voltage.
answer: Gate voltage VG = R5/(R4 + R5)·(+12 V) = peak of the output
Input voltage VIN = R2/(R1 + R2)·(−12 V)
problems.how: PUT sawtooth generator solved as Example 16–5: the gate divider R4 = 100 kΩ, R5 = 47 kΩ from +12 V sets the firing level VG; the input divider R1 = 100 kΩ, R2 = 22 kΩ from −12 V sets the ramp current through R3 = 100 kΩ into C = 0.0022 μF.
assume: As in the book's Example 16–5 the loading of the input divider by R3 is neglected; including it the frequency would be 2.94 kHz.
problems.circuit: Figure 16–63 (p.849): PUT sawtooth generator: an op-amp integrator with C = 0.0022 μF; the input R3 = 100 kΩ is fed from the divider R1 = 100 kΩ (to −12 V) and R2 = 22 kΩ (to ground); the PUT gate is set by R4 = 100 kΩ (from +12 V) and R5 = 47 kΩ (to ground).

title.vi: M08 · Ổn áp và IC ổn áp: bài tính trong sách không có đáp án in (site tự giải và kiểm) · phần 1/2
title.en: M08 · Voltage regulators and IC regulators: book calculations without a printed answer (solved and checked by this site) · part 1 of 2

note.vi: Example, Related Problem, Section Checkup và problem chẵn của Floyd, Example của Jaeger: sách không in đáp án các bài này (đáp án Related Problem của Floyd nằm trên website nhà xuất bản). Đáp án do site tính theo công thức của chính sách và kiểm lại bằng một cách độc lập; với Example, kết quả còn được so với lời giải in trong sách. Related Problem được kèm đề của Example mà nó dựa vào. Thời gian là giả định (6 phút mỗi bài).
note.en: Floyd Examples, Related Problems, Section Checkups and even-numbered Problems, and Jaeger Examples: the book prints no answer for these (Floyd's Related Problem answers are on the publisher's website). The answers were computed by this site with the book's own formulas and re-checked by an independent route; for the Examples the result is also compared with the worked solution printed in the book. A Related Problem is shown with the statement of the Example it builds on. The time limit is an assumption (6 minutes per exercise).

problems.text: When the ac input voltage of a certain power supply changes, the input to the voltage regulator decreases by 5 V as a result, and the output of the regulator decreases by 0.25 V. The nominal output is 15 V. Determine the line regulation in %/V.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 17–2: line regulation = (ΔVOUT/VOUT)·100 %/ΔVIN.

problems.text: A certain voltage regulator has a 12 V output when there is no load (IL = 0).When there is a full-load current of 10 mA, the output voltage is 11.9 V. Express the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.how: Floyd Eq. 17–3: load regulation = (VNL − VFL)/VFL·100 %; the load current changes by 10 mA.

problems.text: In Figure 17–15, what power rating must R1 have if the maximum input voltage is 12.5 V?
answer: Worst case: output shorted, VR1 = VIN
7.1 W → use a resistor rated at least 10 W
problems.how: With the output short-circuited VOUT = 0, so VR1 = 12.5 V and PR1 = 12.5²/22 Ω = 7.10 W; choose the next standard rating, 10 W (Floyd §17–2).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–15 (p.862): series regulator with current limiting: R1 = 22 Ω in series with the input (VIN to the output), the pass transistor Q1 with R2 = 1.0 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and R4 = 10 kΩ; the worst case for R1 is a short-circuited output (VOUT = 0), when all of VIN appears across R1.

problems.text: Determine the minimum and maximum output voltages for the voltage regulator in Figure 17–30. Assume IADJ = 50 μA.
answer: VOUT(max), R2 = 5 kΩ: VREF(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2
problems.how: LM317 (Floyd §17–5): the regulator holds VREF = 1.25 V across R1, so the current through R1 plus IADJ flows in R2. The book prints 1.25 V and 29.9 V.
assume: The 35 V input is high enough for 29.9 V out (a dropout margin of a few volts is needed).
problems.circuit: Figure 17–30 (p.872): adjustable LM317 regulator: input +35 V; R1 = 220 Ω between the output and the adjustment terminal; R2 = 5 kΩ (maximum) potentiometer from the adjustment terminal to ground; decoupling capacitors C1, C2, C3. VOUT = VREF(1 + R2/R1) + IADJ·R2 with VREF = 1.25 V.

problems.text: What value is Rext if the maximum current to be handled internally by the voltage regulator in Figure 17–34 is set at 700 mA?
problems.how: Qext turns on when the voltage across Rext reaches its base-emitter voltage 0.7 V, which happens at Imax = 0.7 V/Rext; so Rext = 0.7 V/0.7 A = 1 Ω (Floyd §17–6). Check with the printed answer of Problem 25: 0.7 V/250 mA = 2.8 Ω.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–34 (p.876): fixed three-terminal regulator (78xx) with an external pass transistor Qext (pnp): Rext is connected between the input terminal of the regulator and the base/emitter of Qext so that Qext turns on when the current through the regulator (and Rext) makes VRext = 0.7 V; the load current is IL = Iext + Imax.

problems.text: What must be the minimum power rating for the external pass transistor used with a 7824 regulator in a circuit such as that shown in Figure 17–34? The input voltage is 30 V and the load resistance is 10 Ω. The maximum internal current is to be 700 mA. Assume that there is no heat sink for this calculation. Keep in mind that the use of a heat sink increases the effective power rating of the transistor and you can use a lower rated transistor.
answer: Current through Qext: Iext = IL − Imax
10.2 W → choose a transistor rated at least 15 W
problems.how: External pass transistor (Floyd §17–6): the regulator handles Imax = 0.7 A and Qext the rest of the load current, dropping VIN − VOUT = 6 V. The book prints 2.4 A, 1.7 A and 10.2 W.
assume: No heat sink is assumed, as stated.
problems.circuit: Figure 17–34 (p.876): fixed three-terminal regulator (78xx) with an external pass transistor Qext (pnp): Rext is connected between the input terminal of the regulator and the base/emitter of Qext so that Qext turns on when the current through the regulator (and Rext) makes VRext = 0.7 V; the load current is IL = Iext + Imax.

problems.text: What value of R1 is necessary in a 7805 regulator to provide a constant current of 0.5 A to a variable load that can be adjusted from 1 Ω to 10 Ω?
problems.how: The 7805 holds 5 V between its output and ground terminals, so the current-setting resistor is R1 = 5 V/IL (neglecting IG).
assume: The regulator ground-terminal current IG is neglected.

problems.text: The input of a certain regulator increases by 3.5 V. As a result, the output voltage increases by 0.42 V. The nominal output is 20 V. Determine the regulation in %/V.
problems.ctx: Example 17–1: When the ac input voltage of a certain power supply changes, the input to the voltage regulator decreases by 5 V as a result, and the output of the regulator decreases by 0.25 V. The nominal output is 15 V. Determine the line regulation in %/V.
problems.how: Eq. 17–2 with ΔVOUT = 0.42 V, VOUT = 20 V, ΔVIN = 3.5 V.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–1, p.853 (PDF 871)

problems.text: A regulator has a no-load output voltage of 18 V and a full-load output of 17.8 V at a load current of 50 mA. Determine the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.ctx: Example 17–2: A certain voltage regulator has a 12 V output when there is no load (IL = 0).When there is a full-load current of 10 mA, the output voltage is 11.9 V. Express the voltage regulation as a percentage change from no-load to full-load and also as a percentage change for each mA change in load current.
problems.how: Eq. 17–3 with VNL = 18 V, VFL = 17.8 V, ΔIL = 50 mA.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–2, p.854 (PDF 872)

problems.text: The following changes are made in the circuit in Figure 17–7: A 3.3 V zener replaces the 5.1 V zener, R1 = 1.8 kΩ, R2 = 22 kΩ, and R3 = 18 kΩ. What is the output voltage?
problems.ctx: Example 17–3: Determine the output voltage for the regulator in Figure 17–7.
problems.how: Series regulator: the op-amp keeps the voltage at the divider R2/R3 equal to the zener voltage, so VOUT = (1 + R2/R3)·VREF = (1 + 22/18) × 3.3 V (Floyd Eq. 17–3, Example 17–3 gives 10.2 V for 5.1 V and equal resistors).
assume: R1 only sets the zener current (6.5 mA), which is enough to keep the zener in breakdown.
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–3, p.858 (PDF 876)
problems.circuit: Figure 17–7 (p.857): series voltage regulator with an op-amp: the 5.1 V zener D1 (fed from VIN = +15 V through R1 = 1.0 kΩ) is the reference VREF on the + input; the pass transistor Q1 is driven by the op-amp; the feedback divider R2 = 10 kΩ (output to − input) and R3 = 10 kΩ (− input to ground). VOUT = (1 + R2/R3)·VREF (book result 10.2 V).

problems.text: In Figure 17–15, R1 is changed to 33 Ω. What must be the power rating of R1 if the maximum input voltage is 24 V?
problems.ctx: Example 17–5: In Figure 17–15, what power rating must R1 have if the maximum input voltage is 12.5 V?
answer: Power in R1: PR1 = VIN²/R1 (output shorted)
17.5 W → use a resistor rated at least 20 W
problems.how: Worst case again VOUT = 0: PR1 = 24²/33 Ω = 17.5 W; the next standard rating is 20 W (the printed answer to Problem 15, same method: 6.25 W for 25 V across 100 Ω).
problems.ref: Floyd 9e Ch.17 Related Problem of Example 17–5, p.863 (PDF 881)
problems.circuit: Figure 17–15 (p.862): series regulator with current limiting: R1 = 22 Ω in series with the input (VIN to the output), the pass transistor Q1 with R2 = 1.0 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and R4 = 10 kΩ; the worst case for R1 is a short-circuited output (VOUT = 0), when all of VIN appears across R1.
